Those of you who have faint hearts go no further... today we bring you the story of "Slim the Milkman," i.e., Sgt. Calvin Bourgeault of Conshohocken, PA. It's near Philadelphia. Slim has been in the army 27 months and has spent 13 of them overseas. He came over as a T/5, worked at it too believe it or not. He then became a power unit man and finally came to the AES in December of '44 (alas, he had no more rest camps to go to), and has been happy ever since... it says here. As a civilian, Cal was an aircraft worker. The only one of his former hobbies that is printable is flying. He holds a student license. Right now he spends his time looking at bulletin boards for shipping lists with his name on them. When he does find one and gets back to that place near Philly, he wants to study electronics. Up here the lad is occupied every morning from 7:00 AM till 8:15 with his Slim the Milkman program.

May it never be said that the Woody Herman band doesn't come on like gangbusters. The band won both the Silver Award and the New Stars award in this year's Esquire jazz poll. It's hard to pick out the most important thing in the Herman band... there are too many of them. Chubby Jackson and Bill Harris both won Gold awards as tops on bass and trombone. Red Norvo was voted top vibe man, Pete Candoli (trumpet) and Frances Wayne (vocalist) won awards as New Stars. The new star arranger had to be Ralph Burns, he's done so much wonderful and revolutionary work. In fact, I think I'd pick Burns as the most important part of the Herd. The small 22-year-old pianist did almost all of the arrangements that brought so much attention to the band... from the lovely "Happiness is Just a Thing Called Joe," through the jumpy "Caldonia, and Your Father's Mustache," to the magnificent "Bijou." It was these that made the great Stravinsky write a concerto especially for the Herman band's concert in Carnegie Hall last March. Burns also wrote a concerto for rhythm section which I'm told was the hit of the evening. Ralph was one of the first to recognize the genius of Dizzy Gillespie and be influenced by it, and yet not copy it, just adapt it to his own style. He's done many great things for the future of jazz and the world is going to hear it and like it. I also have to mention the wonderful drums of Don Lamond, guitar of Billy Bauer, and if I had room, I could write a book about Joe "Flip" Phillips and the knocked-out way he kicks a tenor sax around. I've almost done something that everyone seems to do, and that is forget about leader-man Herman. The band couldn't have gotten to the top without his wonderful singing and showmanship. He's about the most personable guy in the business and one of the swellest too.

Tuesday evening at 11 PM comes a swell program, "Topics and Tunes." It features news bits from the hometown as well as news from the sport and entertainment worlds, and appropriate tunes from your favorite bands. Roy Arndt is the man who does it on "Topics and Tunes" every Tuesday evening from 2300 to 2330 hours.

Have you heard the Information Please program in which one of the questions needed the location of Foggia as part of an answer... and someone, James Ramsey Ullman to be exact, knew it? Upon a note of awe at Mr. Ullman's knowledge of trivia, I leave you until next week.

Nights 'Round Foggia By Eddie M. Dunaj

AT THE NEW YORKER — Making its debut in the town of Foggia is the 803rd M.P.'s addition to nightlife. As the majority of the original members of the 803rd came from New York, the club was christened the New Yorker. First in Casablanca, then Naples and Bari, and today in Foggia, the club continues to entertain the boys off duty. Pfc. Wilbert Amb sketched the Varga Girls, which add a certain touch to the atmosphere. The Atomica orchestra plays nightly except Monday. "They live up to their reputation as far as the name goes," remarked manager Cliff Waldo. The C.O. Lt. Edwin C. Stephen added, "They make a lot of noise anyhow." The White Helmeted Gestapo, as defined by Axis Sally, extends a cordial invitation to all military personnel of the F.A.A.B. For the coolest place in town, take your date to the New Yorker.

AT THE 779th E.M. CLUB — A drawing card is the weekly Saturday night dance attended by a cosmopolitan crowd. Characters of all types orientate themselves at the bar, putting on sketches and impersonations of well-known wheels around town. Gaiety and laughter with an occasional hiccup conclude a well-spent evening.

AT THE FORTRESS CLUB — The snack bar is open six nights weekly, with a menu that offers versatility in lunches, sandwiches, and five flavors of ice cream sundaes. Sgt. Nick Pavis, N.C.O. in charge of the club, dropped a note of interest: De Grazia's band is to play in the near future at the Siponto Annex. Capt. Tupper, a commercial artist in civilian life, drew the sketches for the modernistic bar at Siponto. With a full crew of Italian workers, Lt. Blessing is turning the paper drawings into the real thing.

AT THE RIPPLE LOUNGE — Mac's assistant, Cpl. Richard F. Welter, informed us of the dinner music as a special feature of the Ripple. "Chow time," he said in reference to the Italian orchestra that plays at the mess hall, is between five and seven in the afternoon. Soon to be seen in aprons and jackets are the waiters and waitresses at the club. Twenty uniforms of blue material will sport "The Ripple" on one pocket and the individual's initials on the other. Among other things, coffee is on the house, so Sgt. James Utter drenched himself with java and avoided that uncertain stimulation of alcohol. His excuse: tomorrow is a day of work.

AT THE WONDER BAR — Thursday night was the big event of night club history in Foggia. The Starlit Terrace, located on the roof of the 55th Station Hospital, opened for the summer season. A mural depicting night life in dreams was designed by manager Leibowitz and put into paint under the artistic touches of Luigi Longo. Located in the center of activities is the U-shaped bar, claimed by the management as the biggest in Italy.

AT THE SIPONTO E.M. BEACH CLUB — Rumors have it that the females dominated the beach last Sunday. Hmmm. Selling at popular prices is the assortment of sandwiches, such as pork lunch meat, roast beef, and eggs and chips for the hungry appetites. "What do you got?" asked a patron. "Everything you want," was the cheerful reply.

AT THE STORK CLUB — Replacing the movies on Monday is Freddy's band, which also plays on Saturdays. From Tuesday to Thursday, the Foggia band supplies the music. Added to the usual run of Italian liquor is American whiskey. "It was a hard struggle, but we finally got it," manager Bill Vance happily announced. Plans are in the preparatory stage for redecorating the club.

AT THE EMBASSY CLUB — The girl at the check room takes pride in her excellent memory of the frequent patrons, so doing away with checks. But the other day, a peculiar barfly spent some time getting his hat back. The signorita explained the situation, "There are so many heads tonight with size 7 1/8."

Erlangen Defeats Foggia All-Stars 4-2 In Season Opener Sparkplugs Beat ETO Men 7-6 In Warm Up Game

Ken Mullis, lanky tobacco-chewing hurler for the 40th Bomb Wing baseball team, held the Foggia All-Stars to seven scattered hits last Sunday, taking a close 4-2 victory after Colonel Robert K. Martin threw the ball onto the diamond to open the official Foggia baseball season.

Foggia Misplays Seven Times

Opposing Mullis was Red Cooke, 955 pitcher, who also pitched a neat eight-hitter, but Cooke watched his team commit seven errors and throw the game away. In the third inning, when the Erlangen squad scored its first two runs, Al Reaud, Foggia third baseman who plays for the 779 Rebels, overthrew two balls in succession to first base, letting one score and putting another in scoring position. Dave Carr was then substituted for Reaud. Later in the game, Bob Caley committed four misplays, repeatedly putting Red Cooke in a hole. Cooke pitched his way out of most of it, leaving eleven men on bases during the game.

Star during the game, however, was Ken Mullis. Mullis, who has played minor league ball, has a steaming fastball and a fast-breaking curve. Big Mullis remained calm throughout the game, except for a few typical blow-ups at Umpire Kopinsky's decisions.

ETO Scores First

The 40th Bombers scored first in the last half of the third. With one out, Lowell Mondon, second sacker, got on base on the first of Al Reaud's overthrows. When Reaud misplayed Williams' slam to short, Mondon came across with the first run and Williams, left fielder, went to second. Williams was driven across the plate by Ed Roberts, shortstop from Los Angeles, who lined one into centerfield.

In the fourth, the Foggia All-Stars got one run back when Burgess came across the plate. After Burgess walked, Johnson's hit dropped between three Erlangen fielders. Lowell Mondon picked up the ball and threw to third baseman Leonard, and both runners advanced. Dave Carr brought Burgess across the plate on an infield out.

After two more scoreless innings, the Germany squad picked up another unearned run when Ed Roberts got on base on Caley's error, stole second, and came across the plate when Bob Markley lined a ball into left. Cooke later retired the side with two men on by striking out Gat Leonard, third baseman. In the previous inning, Cooke ended the inning, striking out first baseman Dowdy with bases loaded.

Gray Strikes Out

In the beginning of the eighth, with the score 3-1, the Foggians picked up another run when Red Cooke scored on Mel Burgess' timely bingle, but the 40th Bombers clinched the game in the last of the eighth when Lowell Mondon crossed the plate. In the ninth, Bill Gray lost a chance to tie the game. With two men on, potential tying runs, Gray struck out. It was his third strikeout for the day.

Sparkplugs Defeat 40th Bomb Wing, 7-6 In Tenth Inning of Saturday's Warmup Opening the two-game Foggia series, the 40th Bomb Wing baseball team went down to defeat at the hands of the 955th Sparkplugs Saturday in a game that stretched out into ten innings. In the warmup match for Sunday's official opener, hurler Moose Varga unveiled a steaming fastball and a roundhouse curve that held the top-heavy 40th Bombers to ten hits. With the score 6-3 in the top half of the ninth, the 40th Bombers scored three runs and tied up the ball game. Although they did not get a hit during the inning, they made the runs on errors by catcher Bull Johnson and third baseman Ingenite. Two new pitchers came into the game as a result of the rally. Lefty Owen of the Sparkplugs retired the 40th Bombers in the tenth without a hit. But the Erlangen relief pitcher, Fireman Mel Saari, then blew up and walked four men, Bull Johnson coming across with the winning run. Big men with the bat for the day were Sparkplugs Red Cooke, who made three for four, and Bull Johnson who poled three for five.

Special Services Building New Swimming Pool

May 16 — The construction of a new swimming pool for the use of American military personnel in the city of Foggia was announced by Special Services this week. The pool will be located adjacent to the 803rd MP area and will be completed in three weeks. A labor crew of twenty to thirty men is working on the pool in three shifts, twenty-four hours a day. Sergeant John Russel, FAAB Gym director, is supervising the construction.

Sport Shots Stan Gomberg

The most interesting sports character we had seen in a long time was Ken Mullis, a four-fingered, tobacco-chewing speedballer who came to Foggia with the 40th Bomb Wing team last week. Mullis is a Winston Salem boy who had met 955's Red Cooke in high school leagues. In their Sunday mound battle, Cooke and Mullis broke almost even. Cooke gave up eight hits and Mullis seven.

Before coming to this side of the pond, Ken Mullis had held down the catching position on the Beaumont team in the Texas Leagues. While catching, Mullis split the middle finger on his right hand so badly that it had to be amputated. But long, lanky Mullis had developed a strong arm through his catching experience, and his new grip on the ball gives it plenty of speed and hop.

Mullis sauntered down to Foggia with a fabulous record of having given up one hit in seventeen innings of ETO ball and having struck out twenty-three men. Foggia's boys were a bit more difficult, although Mullis sent twelve men back from the plate without letting them get their bat on the horsehide.

Bob Barientos, who held down the hot corner for the 40th Bombers, is another man on the Erlangen squad who had minor-league experience. He played AA ball with the Louisville Colonels about three years ago. Bob has a bad trick knee; however, after Moose Varga knocked him down in Saturday's game, he went limping back to Germany.

Big Bill Gray, who has no trouble at all getting announcers on Foggia's AES to refer to him as "Foggia's best athlete," still has to find his batting eye this season. With Gray's size, he should be one of the few to pole a ball over the right field wall at the Foggia Stadium. But Gray loses the ball out in front of him, and in the big game Sunday, Bill went down three times with his bat on his shoulder.

As usual, some of Foggia's sports fans have been crying about the choices of John Russel and some of the local talent for the Foggia All-Star team that was fielded last Sunday. The boys at one of the local bars were moaning that nasty things like politics and the like had entered into the choosing. Well, let's see. Of the ten players who got into the game, three were 779 players, two Special Services men, two from Security, and three from the 955 Sparkplugs. Put away your towels, boys.

The MTO Volleyball Championship, originally scheduled to be played off next week in Leghorn, has been postponed to May 29, 30, and 31. At that time, Foggia's winners and runners-up, the 779 Rebels and the Finance Redliners, will make the trip to Leghorn, it was announced by Special Services this week.

Rebels Take Opening League Game 16-3

"Lefty" Elliott Hurls 4-Hitter As Barons Trounce Reds 14-2 In Second Game

May 15 — Rebels' Slovick and Janovick had perfect days at bat, and Falk's three-run homer gave the 779 team a 16-3 win over the 529 Yankees in the opening game of the American League. Tommy Thompson, the winning pitcher, struck out nine men in the six innings he pitched.

The four-hit hurling of Lefty Elliott in the second game gave the Security Barons a smashing defeat over the 803 MPs Reds with a score of 14-2. The Barons' triple threat—Childs, Damato, and Austinson—hit three homers, leading their teammates into a victorious hard-hitting baseball game.

Rebels 16, Yankees 3

Slugging their way into a victorious sixteen-run game, the Rebels started in the last of the first with Slovick's double that drove in Boyle and Janovick for the first two runs scored. Caley's single, on a strong ground hit between short and second base in the third inning, brought Boyle and Janovick across the plate. Batting 1.000 in the opening game with four times at bat, Janovick, the second baseman, added another three runs. In the last of the sixth, Falk hit a home run, driving Thompson in as the Rebels picked their first win in the opening game of the season.

Hard luck hit Rebel pitcher Tommy Thompson in today's game. Failing to touch second, Thompson was put out on a long fly into deep left field that would have been good for a homerun in the fourth. An injury sustained on a pitched ball in the last of the sixth inning forced Thompson to retire from the ball game, with Bill Falk pitching in the seventh. Falk allowed a base hit while fanning three in a row.

Barons 14, Reds 2

May 15 — In the second game of the day, Baron hurler Elliott pitched a four-hit, two-run game and struck out ten men, winning the nightcap game for the Security Barons, 14-2, over the 803 MPs Reds. Tom McCorkal, of the Reds, got three hits off pitcher Elliott with a double in the fourth, a single in the second and sixth, bringing Ray Moore from third base in for a run, while Bill Wharehime took a base hit in the fourth that drove McCorkal, at second, across the plate. Pitcher Bogacki of the Reds gave the Barons twelve hits and struck out ten men.

With the bases full, a Baron triple play in the first of the fourth pulled pitcher Elliott out of a tight spot and killed a menacing threat that would have given the Reds a one-run lead provided the batter hit a homerun. As it happened, Mutchler flied out to left fielder Welker, who threw the ball to second baseman McGrain for an out on runner Berrnocco. McGrain then hurled the ball to catcher Childs, which caught Wharehime out in an attempted dash for home plate and retired the side. From there on, the Barons developed into three-run rallies for the remaining three innings: Barons beating the Reds, 14-2.

Dick Harris Strikes Out 14 As Bulldozers Beat Specials

May 17 - Dick Harris, sensational Bulldozer hurler, set a new local mark for pitchers when he struck out eight Specials batters in a row to pace his team to a 5-4 victory. Harris, who struck out 14 men, walked Doliner, the first man to face him, and then continued to strike out the next eight men: McDonald, Ruzich, Burgess, Fournet, Hannon, Sellers, Maslyck, and Avilla. Again, Doliner came to bat. He walked for the second time, stopping the consecutive string at eight.

Ed Gray scored the winning run for the Bulldozers when he doubled in the last of the seventh, stole third, and went home when Doliner, the Specials' pitcher, tried to pick him off third base.

Bulldozers Score First

The Bulldozers scored first on a hit by Solenberger, a passed ball, and a stolen base. Solenberger then scored when Pruitt hit to deep short. In the third, the 'Dozers picked up two more runs on a triple by Solenberger and hits by Gray and Pruitt.

Specials got their first run on Doliner's base on balls, a stolen base, and an error by Pruitt. The Specials then went ahead in the fifth when Accardo came to bat and got the first hit off Harris, a driving single to left. Feltenberger, the next batter, was hit with a pitched ball, and Doliner singled Accardo home. Then Red McDonald doubled a ground ball between second and first, bringing in Feltenberger and Doliner.

In the sixth, the Engineers tied the score, combining a base on balls, error, and a single. The Specials threatened to win out in the first of the seventh when Doliner was caught off third base on a squeeze bunt play when Ruzich, the batter, was not able to get a chance on the ball. French pitched the last inning for the Bulldozers when Harris developed a sore arm in the sixth. The box score is above.

WIVES ARRIVE IN NAPLES HARBOR ABOARD VULCANIA (See pages 2, 5)

Vulcania Brings 122 Wives To Italy

When the Vulcania pulled into Naples Harbor Tuesday, one hundred and twenty-two wives of MTO soldiers ran down the gangplank in a reunion that was surely the happiest this side of the Atlantic since the war ended. There was a band playing and dozens of photographers were eagerly trying to capture the first tender moments, but the overjoyed wives and husbands saw only each other as they fell into each other's arms for the first hysterically happy greeting and then dashed into waiting automobiles.

The reunited couples, plus seventy children, were from many different units in the MTO and by far the greatest bulk were officers and their wives. As soon as they had left the boat, the couples were spirited away from the dock area in waiting staff cars to their various destinations in the city of Naples and other places in Italy. The group from Foggia consisted of fifteen wives and two children, sons of Lts. Archibald F. McCasland and Charles Worrall.

Lt. Rose M. Morss of Foggia had been in the 300th General Hospital but was given a 24-hour pass in order to meet his wife at the dock. Other wives who arrived here Tuesday are: Mrs. Robert K. Martin, Mrs. Hollis J. Palmer, Mrs. James B. Sadler, Mrs. John F. Cotter, Mrs. Leroy W. Grote, Mrs. Paul Cole, Mrs. Eugene B. Cruce, Mrs. Archibald F. McCasland, Mrs. Peter Pawluk, Mrs. Thomas A. Horse Taxis To Be Placed 'Off Limits'

Foggia - In the near future, white 'off-limits' signs will be painted on all horse-drawn Italian taxis, and disciplinary action will be taken against military personnel who ride in them, Captain R. W. Clark, Provost Marshal, revealed this week. Surveys have disclosed that the vehicles are seldom used by military personnel and that when they are, it is largely to lead to immoral establishments. Violations using these 'off-limits' taxis will be reported to Unit Commanding Officers for disciplinary action.

Fly to Tripoli for Crash Boat

Foggia — A crew of airmen led by Major Harold Thayer took off from Foggia today in a B-17 for Tripoli, North Africa, in order to get an Army crash boat. The passengers include men 'best qualified' to bring the boat back to Manfredonia. When it arrives here, it will be kept in readiness for Air Sea Rescue purposes. Mechanics are among the men flying to Tripoli, and they will determine after an inspection of the 68-foot craft whether it is seaworthy enough to make the thousand-mile sea voyage back to Manfredonia. If not, repairs will be made, and the boat brought back on another flight.

Miss FAAB Crowned Tomorrow "Occupators" Play - AES To Broadcast "Who is the fairest one of all?" That's what they'll be asking at the gymnasium tomorrow night when the seven lovelies who won the voting appear before the solemn tribunal of judges that will decide who among them is to wear the crown of Miss FAAB 1946. The setting for the proclamation will be a monster dance at the FAAB Gymnasium. Fifteen hundred invitations have been printed and are being distributed by ARC girls and through offices in Foggia. LOCAL ITEMS

There's My Husband! 

The Vulcania docked at Naples Tuesday morning, and we saw the long-awaited reunion as the wives ran down the gangway into the arms of their husbands. It was a happy scene, although there was plenty for a sentimentalist to get sentimental about, especially when the husbands and wives began recognizing each other as the liner moved up to the crowded wharf. The husbands were almost exclusively officers, and a good percentage of these were high enough to be considered "brass." But the atmosphere was down to earth. They were just a bunch of men darned glad to see their women again.

At eight-thirty in the damp gray morning, berth 5, where the Vulcania was to dock, was already populous with military personnel. The MPs were there, along with a band, staff cars, buses, and six-by-six trucks. The husbands stood around in small groups or wandered off to the edge of the wharf to peer into the misty harbor for the Vulcania, due to arrive at ten o'clock. An hour and a half later, the bulk of the luxury liner moved into view from around a bend in the harbor, and in a few moments, the wives could be seen as a line of color along the ship's gray side.

The ship moved silently closer, and suddenly there was a cry of, "There's my husband!" and an arm began to wave. Two liberty ships blew tremendous blasts on their whistles, and when the echoes died down, the band was playing, more arms were waving, and some of the girls were holding up infants and pointing to the crowded dock. As the liner was fastened to the pier, the couples were close enough to shout to each other. "Were you seasick?" we heard, and "I'm broke flat," "I can't wait," "Come up here!"

"Oh beautiful!" we heard a feminine voice shout as the band started playing again. The gangway moved into position, and a loudspeaker blared, "Foggia wives will be the first to debark. Please give Foggia husbands freedom of movement." Then the first, the wife of Lt. Gen. John C. H. Lee, came down the gangway followed by the wives of the other generals. The flashbulbs popped as they were happily greeted and introduced all around.

Immediately after this, the wives of the Foggia officers came down. There was a rush down the gangplank, a swooping into their husbands' arms, a few intense moments, and an oblivious walk to the car! We tried to get one of those "great" pictures where the happy couple are in each other's arms looking ecstatically into each other's faces in full view of the camera. But the couples were more inclined to spend those first fleeting moments in a long kiss than in ecstatic looks. Photog John Cogswell saw Mrs. Martin reach the Colonel, but the crowd got in the way of the picture. He followed after and called, "Oh, Colonel Martin." The Colonel turned around, and Cogswell said, "How about a real good kiss?" There wasn't an instant's hesitation as the Colonel smilingly obliged.

In ten minutes, the couples were in their cars off to their new home. The last we saw was a trim girl in blue transferring a large baby to the arms of her husband.

"Isn't he heavy?" we heard, "And I've carried him for two and a half years!"

A New Deal for Security Section

Among the many people of this community that have won our sympathy and tears are the FBI boys of the Security Section. We too have read Carnegie's "How to Win Friends and Influence People." But the other day, we dispensed with the crying towel upon hearing the cheerful news that has befallen these forgotten men, A NEW DEAL.

Just what did that mean, we did not know, so tossing a coin, two out of three, fate brought us to the exile of many a good soul, among the scattered 'goof-offs' so to speak. Once behind the forbidden walls of the Security Section, we searched for the Orderly Room. City Service would be making a thriving business here; nevertheless, without the aid of road maps or guides, after a number of flights up and down, hitting a good many dead-end walls, we achieved our goal by tapping the walls for growls and barks.

Opening a nearby door, we caught the I/Sgt. T.A. Neely's atomic announcement, "It's revolutionizing the whole show." Just what do you mean by that statement? we boldly inquired, as a squad of guards, forty-fives in hand, blocked all exits. Reassuring the men that we were representatives of the press, the sergeant ordered his men to cock their guns. The interview continued under extreme conditions.

"Now that we are working directly with S-2," the sergeant went on to say, "all precautions must be taken." Neely continued his report in a dignified manner associated with his rank. "Yes, a hundred and fifty men will be affected by this new program. The original thirty-six posts have dwindled down to four with the boys pulling convoy duty now, and by the way, they'll be working three days with one off, discontinuing the old regime, where a trooper stood guard duty as much as eight before receiving his day of gratis."

Good Deal All Around

Upon conclusion of his short but potent tidings, the old Infantryman gave the boys a ten-minute break. His sharp retort startled the daydreaming individualists, who sprang on us, armed with comments and confirmations. Pfc. John Nagel poured forth his views. "I definitely think the change was needed for a long time. This place was known for low morale and a haven for undesirables, but now it's changed, we have a good bunch of guys." Among the many others was Cpl. Thomas Caron, KP pusher, whose considerate heart dictated, "It's a good deal for the men after all the shoving around they got."

Holding off a rear guard of WHEELS with pencil and pad, we departed the scene of recent reshuffling. Who are we to doubt their veracity beyond the point of questioning?

The Native Returns From The States

The first thing we heard Joe O'Neill say after he returned to Foggia was a heartfelt, "How can I get home again?" As far as we were concerned, that was a perfectly legitimate question—coming from anyone but Captain O'Neill because that day he had returned to Foggia from the States. He might have waited a day or so to ask.

In the February 20th issue of the Occupator, we featured a story headlined "Five Officers Leave For States On TDY." Captain Joseph O'Neill, Special Services head, who at that time had twenty-four months overseas, was one of the returning.

"We left Foggia for Naples, and in a couple of days were on board ship going west. They were eleven miserable too. The boat didn't have enough ballast, and it just rolled and tossed enough to show me what a poor sailor I am. But then we hit New York, and everything was all right again, though I didn't weigh as much."

After two years, the States looked good to the dark-haired Captain. Foggia seemed like a long way back when he journeyed down to Fort Dix in New Jersey to get the official okay.

Back To The Great White Way

Then, with leave papers in hand, Captain O'Neill hopped a train up to Woodhaven, New York, to see his mother, then back to the Great White Way to catch up on some of the night life that is only a fond memory in Foggia. There was a lot to be crowded into only forty-five days' freedom.

"It was plenty good seeing New York again. I went back to some of the old bars, like the Merry-Go-Round Bar up near Queens Boulevard, and some of those in the 57th Street section. Then, like I told you when I left, I saw several good New York shows. Oh, yes, when you get back, don't miss 'Carousel.' It's terrific.

"But I'll tell you," he went on, "New York disappointed me in a lot of ways. It's as dirty and as filthy as Naples, I think. And the liquor situation is plenty bad. You just can't get it. It took me two weeks to find a bottle of Bacardi Rum!"

Young Goes West

The situation was so bad that Captain O'Neill was hastened to the next leg of his leave tour—Los Angeles. Los Angeles, as he put it, "for sixteen lovely days."

"Now California is something else again. In the restaurants, I found all the good food I wanted. Delicious steaks, over an inch thick, that you cut with your fork. And when you get enough of that you alternate it with thick roast beef covered with juicy cranberry sauce—"

In his travels about the California empire, O'Neill found his way to Santa Barbara, Catalina, Long Beach, and, of course, Hollywood. "I remember running into Errol Flynn with some bag on his arm," he reminisced wryly. "Of course, Ken Murray's 'Blackouts' is still going strong, just like 'Mike Romanoff's' in Beverly Hills, 'Melody Lane,' 'Chi-Chi's,' and all those places you know if you've ever been out there."

We edged a bit closer to the captain, looked about the room furtively, lowered our voice to a secretive tone, and whispered, "Well, tell us, Captain O'Neill, the real dope, how are things back in the States? We mean, are things really hard to get, and is everyone spending his money as fast as he can find something to buy with it? You know..."

The captain lit a cigarette, took a puff, and began slowly. "Well, like I said about the Bacardi Rum, there are a lot of things that are hard to get. Not cigarettes or gasoline, they're easy, but things like houses and apartments are impossible to find. And as hard as they are, they're no easier than trying to get a simple thing like a white shirt. Clothes are difficult to find, and when you do find them, they are expensive and probably not as good quality as you are used to. Sugar is rationed still, and butter—well, we got a quarter of a pound a week while I was home.

Still The USA

"But money is being spent freely and the people are happy. The bars and restaurants are always crowded, and it takes about eight weeks to get a reservation on a Pullman. Yet it doesn't seem to matter much. The people just want to get the war out of their minds. They're not interested in politics, and they don't know as much about world goings-on as the average GI. As for the occupation, well, the impression I got was that they didn't care very much. Some just say get them out of there and get it over with. In New York, not much was said about the Security Council meetings, except such trivial things as where they were going to house them in the future, the Sperry Gyroscope Building or the old World's Fair or both.

"But that doesn't mean as much to me as my wanting to go home. With all the shortages, believe me, it's still the United States. And so far as I'm concerned, the only place to live. So, go ahead, ask me if I want to go right home again, go ahead—and the answer is YES."

FOGGIA AND THE PROVINCE

A New Leader  
To the agricultural city of Foggia, a tall middle-aged man with a nod in his eye came to speak to his followers. He was tired from campaigning and irritable with those of his followers who had come from Cerignola, Lucera, San Severo, from all over the province to shake the hand of the great man who was promising them a new life. He came to the Grand Hotel Ciccolella to rest and eat. Police, both in uniform and out of uniform, kept his public away from the great man. One could not tell who was police or a member of his party. His followers and the curious watched the street for a sight of the great man. As the crowds watched the front of the hotel door, he slipped out of the back way in a strange mysterious car. The crowd who had gathered to see him as he entered the front of the old Ensa theater was disappointed, for he came in the back with the strange mysterious car.

The Audience  
Inside the theater, an enthusiastic crowd cheered as he came to the stage. Most of the audience were young people, less than 25 years old. It was difficult to get in, for you had to have a special pass issued to enter. Every precaution had been taken: soldiers and police with machine guns had been posted in and out of the theater since seven o'clock that morning. The 'great man' was given protection to speak. He spoke: "That which you love of me is just the idea and not the person, we must not personify the ideas. When the ideas are incarnated in a single man it is very dangerous. We must follow the idea, we are all equal. Our enemies accuse us of personalism..." When the great man finished the speech, his audience shouted 'Viva Il Nostro Eroe' (Long Live our Hero). The great man returned to the Grand Hotel Ciccolella in a strange mysterious car.

Left Parties Hold Slight Edge In Province

Returns of the administrative elections held in 54 of the 60 communities in Foggia Province give the Left Wing parties, composed of the Communist, Socialist, Action, and Republican parties, a slight lead over the Right Wing group of the Liberal, Democrat Christian, Democrat Labor, and Qualunquisti parties, in an analysis of votes made. The total vote cast for Left Parties totaled 91,240, the Right Parties 85,744, and the so-called Center Parties 8,387 votes.

The Democrat Christian Party gained the most votes for a single party - 37,208 - followed by the Communist Party, which was able to obtain 25,391 votes on their own ticket. The Socialists proved to be the third strongest party with a total single vote of 6,759.

In 32 out of the 54 communities, the Democratic Christian Party presented a single list composed of their candidates only, while the Communists only presented in 6 out of the 154 communities their list. In the other 48 communities, they combined with the Socialists, Actionists, and Republican parties.

Right, Center or Left

It is interesting to note the grouping made by the local analysts. Actually, the Democrat Christian is not a right-wing party in the sense of the Liberal and Qualunquisti parties. Nationally, it is better recognized as a Center party. In the same sense, the interpretation of the Action and Republican parties as left-wing groups is hardly justifiable as Professor Balsamo, in his very excellent speech here in Foggia on May 12th, declared that "the Italian Republican Alliance has been formed to let the people know of the dictatorship of the Communist Party and to avoid the danger of an uncertain monarchical minority."

Foggia Votes In September

The City of Foggia will vote for its local officials in the month of September. Of the five other cities in the province that have not voted as yet are Margherita di Savoia, San Ferdinando, San Giovanni Rotondo, S. Nicandro Garganico, and Trinitapoli. The total vote of these five communities is about twenty percent of the Foggia Province. In this respect, such a high percentage of those that have not voted as yet makes it difficult to determine the outcome of the elections here for the Constituent Assembly.

You can start anyplace... with the old standbys. Johnny Hodges, who has won more polls as the top alto man than anyone I know of... It would be silly to try and talk about Duke... there's too little paper and too few words. And then there are the new men in the band... one of the best bass men there is, Oscar Pettiford... Taft Jordan playing better trumpet than he ever has before… and last, there is Cat Anderson, recently out of the Hampton band. The range and power of this great new trumpet star are incredible... he hits notes an octave above the highest note on a piano; his phenomenal range combined with his fine technique and extreme sensitivity make him one of the greatest discoveries of the year. A lot more will be heard from this great musician. And a lot more will be heard from Duke Ellington because there is a lot that Ellington has to say in his music, and there is no one else to do it for him. Something about a Black man and a white man and sitting in street cars and living in houses and walking on streets and getting jobs and lynchings and a lot of other things... we'll keep on hearing more from Duke Ellington. I just hope the people will listen and understand.

For something we can all listen to, it's "Yesterday In Music" taken care of by Roy Arnold every Wednesday eve from 11:00 to 11:30 PM. Everyone likes old songs, and that's what the program is composed of... old favorites of yesteryear, songs we can associate with the good old days, so come 11:00 PM Wednesday eve... relax, listen, and reminisce. That's the ration of yah ta ta yah ta ta for today. So long till next week.

Sport Shots by Stan Gomberg

The opening of the American League on the local lots a week and a half ago gave a good indication of the kind of conditions Foggia's ball teams are going to be playing under this summer season. The inaugural game between the 529 Yankees and the 779 Rebels, and several games since then, have been hampered by gusty winds and clouds of dust that blew across the diamond. Those who were in Valley Forge last year remember that the afternoon winds are characteristic of this area during the hot season, and the local talent is going to have to buck against it.

Will Rogers, who was also a ball fan, reminded us that we can't do anything about the weather, but Foggia's diamond men could use a little cooperation from upstairs in contriving some means to deal with the blowing dust. Unless there is a water shortage, it shouldn't be too difficult to find a means to wet down the infield before game time.

Manager Donovan lets us know that his officers' baseball team is now to be known as the Pickups in memory of the pickup officer basketball squad that played in the Foggia Tournament during the winter. Donovan was the manager of that team, too. (The Pickups only won one game during the cage season, but already the Pickups have upset the highly favored 955 Sparkplugs by an 11-6 count in their first league game.)

A lot of the local ball fans are wondering about the above-mentioned outcome of what was supposed to have been an easy contest for the powerful Sparkplugs. The biggest controversy revolves around the Sparkplugs manager, Red Cooke. Cooke has lost a lot of favor among Sparkplug fans because, they say, of the arbitrary methods with which Cooke has been running the team. Sometimes playing left field, sometimes pitching, Cooke shifted to first base for the Pickup game and handled himself without too much finesse, getting credit for three misplays. According to the riders in the grandstand, the Sparkplugs have lost their zip under Cooke's handling.

The fact that the Sparkplugs hadn't worked out for almost a week before the game might also have had something to do with the loss. Then, too, several of the boys had been hitting the local bars the previous evening. And Lefty Boik, the smooth first baseman, was in the hospital during the game. Oh, yes, there was also Olin Kach, Pickup hurler, who allowed one hit in the five innings he toed the mound.

What about the Softball League? National Leaguers have been asking. It seems to us that Special Services is making a mistake in figuring that the softballers don't drum up as much interest as the senior league. Since the highly touted 955 Turbos have been knocked over three times by the 529 Giants and once by the formerly hapless FAAB Band Downbeats, interest has perked up. It should be a close race for the pennant and the trip to Leghorn.

One of the new ballclubs on the Foggia lots came up with a dandy pitcher last week. In the most exciting game of the American League play thus far, Dick Harris of the 1898 Dozers pitched a pretty six-hit win and took the game by a 5-4 count. Harris, a Detroit, Michigan boy, gathered up fourteen strikeouts in the nine-inning game, and early in the play struck out eight men in a row. Dick's best pitch is a fast-breaking hook.

Probably the most diamond-wise player in Foggia's American League is silent, smooth-working Mike Demato, utility man of the Security Barons. Mike has plenty of experience behind him, including a berth on a New York Giants farm team. So far, in Foggian league play, Demato has a neat batting average of .444, having gotten four for nine, including a home run and two doubles. In his five-hit win over the Special Service team last Sunday, Mike showed a good fastball that should cause plenty of trouble for the rest of the league. With a pitching staff of Lefty Elliot, Johnny Bowman, and Mike Demato, Security is a sudden strong contender for the American League pennant.

Eight Hundred And Fifty Civilians Dropped From FIAB Payroll

June 1 — Naples Air Force General Depot has ordered a thirty percent cut in the total civilian employees of the Foggia Army Air Base to take effect today, according to an announcement made by Lt. Paul F. Kirby, Civilian Personnel Officer. Eight hundred and fifty employees will be dropped from the payrolls due to a shortage of funds caused by FAAB spending more money during this fiscal year than had been allotted. The dismissals, explained Lt. Kirby, are necessary in order that this command may meet its financial budget by the end of June 1946.

Another Cut July 1st

A further cut of 850 civilian employees is expected on July 1, 1946, due to the omission of Foggia Army Air Base from the appropriations made by Congress to the War Department. The cause developed after the War Department had changed the supervision of this command from MTOUSA to the United States Air Forces, Europe. MTOUSA dropped Foggia from its appropriation, and, through an error, USAFE did not appropriate new funds for FAAB.

Major Benjamin C. Bowman, Budget and Fiscal Officer, will fly immediately to USAFE with an estimate for necessary funds for the next fiscal year to obtain an emergency appropriation from Washington to meet the requirements of this command. FAAB officials doubt, however, that Congress will consent to a full appropriation for the same number of employees that will be retained on the payroll during the month of June 1946, but instead will force the additional 850 reduction on July 1, 1946.

Military Personnel Must Avoid Interference In Local Elections AFHQ, May 27 - Allied Headquarters in Caserta has ordered that military personnel should be directed to avoid any kind of intervention or appearance of intervention in the Italian elections. In a wire received by FAAB from Allied Force Headquarters, the following is extracted: "The Italian National Elections will be held throughout Italy on June 2nd and 3rd. Personnel of all military formations will be directed to avoid any kind of intervention or appearance of intervention in these elections."

New Trainer for Flying Men A newly built Radar Navigation trainer is expected to be in operation within a week for navigators and bombardiers in the Foggia area, according to a statement by Captain Norman Sanger of the FAAB S-3 section. A team of six newly trained radar men will instruct each officer one hour weekly at Foggia Main in the old 4291st Squadron shack. Four navigators in the Flight Section will also be instructed in "Mickey" operation through a new temporary trainer.

Italy Goes to Polls to Decide Political Future

Twenty million men and women of Italy will decide the future political government of their country when they cast their ballots for delegates to the Constituent Assembly and vote for either the republican form of government or the monarchical form of government. All citizens born in 1924 or before that year will be compelled to vote or forfeit their right for five years. Only those members of the Fascist government who held responsible or policy-making positions and civilian police who were connected with the Mussolini regime will be denied the right to vote.

Monarchy or Republic

Today, the new Italy will decide whether she shall continue to cast her future with the House of Savoy, which has ruled the Kingdom of Italy from 1861 to the present, or whether she shall form a republican government and send King Umberto II and his family to join the exiled Vittorio Emanuele III in Egypt.

573 delegates will be elected to the Constituent Assembly where they will sit for a period of six to twelve months to abolish the old constitution and to ratify the new constitution. Each delegate will represent 35,000 voters.

In electing the Constituent delegates, the voters will choose their representative by casting a ballot for the political party list they prefer. At the same time, they will select two men from that list whom they desire to represent their party. The delegates will be elected by the proportional system.

Honor Those Who Sacrificed, Memorial Day Services

In a simple ceremony, the memory of soldiers who sacrificed their lives was honored as a special detachment of troops from Foggia Army Air Base journeyed to the U.S. Military Cemetery in Bari for Memorial Day Services.

Italians Join at Services

All Allied peoples were invited to join, and with the detachment from Foggia went Italian civilians with flowers for the graves. At the cemetery, a large group of local people watched the quiet service take place.

In the group was a sound truck, and when the convoy passed through towns on the road to Bari, it halted for a brief period while a talk on the purpose of the mission and the meaning of Memorial Day was made to the people. Large signs on the trucks proclaimed the mission as one to honor the memory of all those who gave their lives in Italy.

The service at the Bari Cemetery was not lengthy but moving. First, the units assembled, and while the FAAB Band played, the processional marched to position before the flagstaff. Chaplain J. B. Sadler read the Invocation and Psalms, and then Major Berg made an address. Large wreaths of flowers were placed at the flagstaff and then three volleys were fired by a squad of Military Police. Taps was played; there was a minute of silence; the Flag was raised to full mast as the band played the Star-Spangled Banner.

Beside each grave, a small American flag fluttered over a simple spray of carnations. The sun was bright upon the white gravel walks and neat green plots. The Italians and their children walked slowly away as the soldiers marched toward their trucks. The ceremony was over for Memorial Day 1946.

LOCAL ITEMS The American Red Cross, modestly reporting its laurels, tells us that Lieutenant General Lee wrote personal letters to the parents of all the girls here after having visited the local ARC last month. Said the General in one letter: "She is giving her charming best so splendidly that we shall never forget our debt to her and to you for letting her serve over here." Miss FAAB, 1946 Nineteen-year-old Silvana Cioni was crowned Miss FAAB of 1946 Monday night, and as she nervously stepped up to the judges' stand to receive the bouquet of white lilies, she whispered, "I'm so happy, I don't know what to do." Far over the anticipated fifteen hundred guests arrived at the FAAB Gym Monday evening, and as they danced to the music of Frerick De Orazia's orchestra, the topics of conversation were theories on the winner of the contest. Four girls had arrived as finalists in the Miss FAAB contest (seven of those polling the top number of Foggia votes had been chosen as finalists, but only four accepted the invitation): Lina Vinelli, Pina Rige, Aida Dal Cin, and Silvana Cioni. The four pretenders to the throne arrived shortly before the ceremonies were to begin at 2200 hours local time. They all wore newly made evening gowns and all forgot most of the English they knew in the last-minute excitement, much to the distress of the master of ceremonies who tried to give them their only rehearsal fifteen minutes before contest time.

Cooperative Effort The nervousness of the last minute was the climax to the past days of hasty preparations. The dance, an innovation in Italian-American relations, was a cooperative effort that had enlisted the help of Foggia AES, the FAAB newspaper Portavoce, the FAAB Civilian Club, Frenck De Grazia and his orchestra, the 55th Station Hospital ARC, and personnel from Flagella Theater, the Gymnasium, Special Services, and numerous other units. As the lights dimmed at 2200 hours and Sergeant Lou Cook told the radio audience what was about to happen, a large number of people in Foggia had a personal desire to see the outcome of their work.

Each of the girls and her escort walked slowly down the aisle through the packed dance floor, and the judges looked briefly at the girls in the light of an airport signal lamp manned by an electrician behind the band. When the last girl walked off the floor, the De Orazia orchestra took over for twenty minutes as the judges added up the points and the master of ceremonies told the winner to be ready to come out.

As the perspiring MC told Silvana Cioni to be ready to come out when the music started again, she still did not know who had won. "But who should I follow?" she asked. Not until judge Peg Staring handed her the huge bouquet was she sure that she was Miss FAAB of 1946.

Florence-born little Silvana with the large brown eyes and chestnut hair is five feet four inches tall and weighs 117 pounds. She came to Foggia in 1939 when her railroad engineer father was transferred to Southern Italy, left again in 1943 during the bombardment, and returned in 1945. This shifting about gave her a high school education in both Florence and Foggia, where she studied French, English, and Italian. When she is not working in the Civilian Personnel Office, Silvana tells us that she likes to study literature—in each of the three languages—play an accordion, and cook. Her ambitions are not positive, she said, but within the limitations of wars and other European troubles, she hopes to travel and study "and get married, but not right away of course."

He Likes His Work

There has been lots of enthusiastic talk recently about the changes at the Headquarters Officers' Mess and about the 529 Officers' Club, now the sensational Castle Bar. Looking for the reason behind things, we hunted up Sgt. Vincent Siano, the new force behind it all.

We found him sitting in one of his new wine-colored sofas at the Castle while in the next room the din of construction work kept things lively. The first sight greeting a visitor to the Castle is the stone formations. We tapped one of the stone posts and heard a hollow thud. "Is it strong?" we asked Siano.

"Like iron," he replied.

When did all this start?

Wanted Something Different

"Well, I had a kind of inspiration. Like a fantasy. What do you call those fellows who draw crazy things, like half a girl on one side of a room and half an apple on the other? Surrealist! That's the word. I had a surrealist fantasy. It started when I first started running this club in Foggia back when the 324th Service Group was here. The name changed a few times and the management and when the 529th took over we had a nice fund available."

"And then you thought of making the change?"

"Yes. Remember when the Fortress Club opened up? I was really surprised at the piece of work they did there. Very nice. But it wasn't anything really different and when I got the go-ahead on the plans from Lt. King, I called in the professor."

"What professor is that?"

"Professor Luigi Zaccheria. He's the one who helped me make the old Blue Grotto Ballroom and after that the Streets Of Paris Room. So I told the professor that I wanted something fantastic, out of this world, something people will talk about. We have lots of arches here so I wanted to make a castle. The professor began digging around in books and came up with a copy of The Three Musketeers that had just the illustrations we needed. Well, this is what we got. It's not done yet. There's lots of little things to put in and of course we have to finish the other section, the City Of The Future."

Past Or Future Available

We walked into the other section where Sgt. Siano has his workers completing the future section of the club. 

"It will give the opportunity of being in the past," he indicated the ancient section, "or the future," with a wave toward the new work. "See that painting? That's a window overlooking the city of the future, with underground living quarters to give protection against atomic bombs. The inside here will be modernistic with indirect lighting, a raised bandstand, and a movable stage."

Was Jack Of All Trades

We wondered where Sgt. Siano had learned all this.

"I never did this work professionally," he explained, "was mostly interested in sports when I was a kid, played baseball, football, and basketball in high school in New York. Did lots of different jobs after that. Pitched for different companies, worked in a children's camp, and was finally a salesman before I came into the Army four years ago."

"And then?"

"I got into the Recreation Department. It wasn't called Special Services then. I umpired ballgames, gave lectures, and was a drill sergeant too, for a while. When I came overseas I got right into club managing and messes. Used to referee fights around here too.

"Are you going to open a nightclub when you go home?"

"No. Running a nightclub in civilian life isn't the same as in the Army. It's a tough racket. First of all, you couldn't go around and scrounge junk material like we did. You'd have to buy it. And then besides labor troubles, you'd have to buck racketeers. Nope, I'm not going into nightclubs. I'm not sure what I'll do, but it'll be a job I like. That's important. You have to like what you do, have ideas, realize it's no cinch, and work. But that suits me."

Master Sergeants of The Regular Army

We spoke to two "zebras" this week, but our reasons for tracking them down were not to find out what makes a master sergeant, but rather to discover what prompted these bestriped gentlemen to re-enlist for three years. Their names are Samuel L. Hoffmeir, new Base Sergeant Major, and William V. De Rosa, Unit Personnel chief clerk (names given in order of height and weight).

Bill De Rosa, a blonde-haired, ruddy-faced Master Sergeant from Washington, D.C., surprises everyone when he says he is of Italian origin. With a slight drawl, he explains that he has many relatives in Italy and that he likes the Army, which were his reasons for coming to Italy and re-enlisting, respectively. A reason for his liking the Army was the twenty-year retirement plan offered to him in the fall of 1945 when he was discharged as a Warrant Officer, Junior Grade. He already had five years of service that took him to India in 1943 and got him a job as Chief Clerk for General Stratemeyer and the 10th and 14th Air Forces. On top of his Army time, he has seven years with the Federal Works Agency, so that his Army time can be used toward a Federal Works pension in case he should choose to take the government's thirty-year civilian pension plan instead.

A B-17 Man

Base Sergeant Major Hoffmeir, on the other hand, has been in the Army since 1938, and he feels a personal relationship to the Second Bomb Group, with which he served for two and a half years in Langley Field, Virginia. Transferred to the 43rd Bomb Group when the Second was to go to Europe, he made his path to the South Pacific. His 43rd Bomb Group flew B-17s until June 1943 when some strategist decided B-17s would do a better job. According to M/Sgt. Hoffmeir, the old B-17 pilots disagreed with the strategist and blew up a few planes on take-off just to prove their point. The strategist apparently won the argument, though, because things settled down in six months and the B-24s proved to be better suited to Pacific flying.

He too re-enlisted because of the twenty-year retirement plan, picked ETO, and finally ended up in the MTO. He says about Italy: "It's much nicer than the Pacific as a whole, but it doesn't compare to Australia. Then again, a lot of parts of the States don't compare with parts of Australia."

A Quarterly Report On Humanity, Sex, Conscience And Church Schedules

Mail is a nice thing to get whether it comes from a girl you love down in North Carolina or whether it comes from somebody telling you, "Brother, you stink." It's a nice feeling to know that somebody is thinking about you. For example, we always feel like sitting down and telling Roy Arndt that we like the music he plays on his program every Thursday night called Reflections in Music, but we never get around to doing that because he may sit down and write us a long letter telling us about his beautiful wife in Wisconsin, and then we have to sit down and tell him in words how nice!

The other day, we got one of those letters that we knew we should reply to, but we didn't know exactly what to say, so we haven't answered it yet. Our correspondent calls to our attention the fact that we never publish church notices or discuss religious topics in our paper. You see what we mean? You get a letter like that, and you don't know what to do but sit around thinking about it, file the letter, pull it out of the files, study it, and put it back in the files again.

The truth of the matter is that we haven't got the 'guts' to handle a letter like that. If we did, we would say that every time we sit down to prepare the church schedule for next week, a guy comes along and tells you about this fellow and that fellow selling coffee, selling gasoline, selling uniforms, selling everything that doesn't belong to him. So we say, what the hell - put in the movie schedule instead. Sunday comes along, and we get that religious fervor going again, and we set up the church schedule for next week. In comes a character complaining that "...she is a nice stupid girl who believes in marriage and all her family are stupid because they won't let me at her alone." There goes that church schedule in the basket again!

So what do we do? We go down to chat with the Chaplain for a couple of hours. It's like penicillin. It makes you feel new again. This time we are going to put that church schedule in because there are a lot of other guys who ought to listen to that man.

With renewed vigor, out we go strolling down towards Piazza Settembre, when one of those little things they call 'jeeps,' buzzes by us at a rate of 1000 miles an hour, jerks back to where we are, trying to move out of the place where we were frozen, and an apologetic voice belonging to one of the members of humanity that President Truman said paid 25 cents at a corner drugstore to get his license whispers, "I am really sorry, I thought that you were a civilian when I spotted you crossing the street a mile back." "Brotherly love!"

That ain't all! In comes a traveler with a nice juicy tale of his visit to Paris. What women! What life! What an experience! The kid is a magnificent lover! He's got the inside dope on the women of Paris! Terrific copy!

And yet, there is that letter staring you in the face. Church schedule, religious discussion. What are you going to do about it? You take the easy way out. You don't write about that Paris affair, and you don't print the church schedule. In this way, you are still one of the 'broad-minded boys,' one of the fence sitters, one of the mob who always take the easy way out.

It's so much easier to write about the nice things. In that way, we don't have to worry about our conscience. My god, man, you only live once. Get in step, let the next guy print that church schedule!

Tires Are Still At A Premium

The tire racket is still one of large proportion in Italy, and Foggia comes in for its share. We interviewed CID Agent Harry Manicas this week to get some information about this activity. In both the MP and CID offices, there are large stocks of recovered stolen tires awaiting return to the proper depots—mutilated tires, revulcanized tires, tires in all stages of attempted disguise. At CID headquarters, in a large bin marked "evidence," are kits of tire-disguising tools. There are curved plates with the letters "Pirelli" and "Michelin" cut into them which are used for molds, and crude knives used to cut new treads into military tires. To combat these well-organized rings, the CID and Military Police are constantly on the lookout.

"The MPs do most of the spotting," Agent Manicas explained. "They pick up lots of tires as they ride around on patrol. Whenever they come up against one that they can't be sure of, they call us, and we have a man who knows every tire made. He can spot an altered one every time." In the storage room at headquarters, we looked at a dozen tires awaiting return. Spotting a spurious tire is much like spotting a counterfeit piece of paper money. There is always evidence of the crude job of burning in new trade names, or the scraped places where old names have been cut off; phony treads have sharp lines from the knife instead of molded grooves from vulcanization. And, very often, there is no attempt to cover up military treads.

A Twist To It

The tire situation in Italy has a twist not generally known. Civilian motorists can legally possess military tires if they have a permit. This is acquired if the tires are legally purchased from a surplus sale. If a civilian has a tire that bears evidence of having been altered, he may get a permit if he takes his tire to Italian Police and 'denounces' it. Then he pays a fee and receives a permit. There have been certain 'respites' ordered during which time the CID and MPs did not recover tires. Civilians were notified that they must denounce all their doubtful tires and get permits during that time. After the period was over, the two agencies went back to work again, and again the steady trickle of illegal and permitless ones began. "They are being stolen all the time," explains Manicas.

A SOCIALIST SPEAKER Mr. Giuseppe Saragat, former Italian ambassador to Paris, addresses a Socialist rally in Piazza XX Settembre. In his speech, Mr. Saragat discussed the question of the institutional form of government and declared that only a parliamentary and democratic republic can save Italy.

Italy Goes To The Polls To Determine Political Future

The President Pro Tempore will be elected by the delegates of the political party polling the largest number of votes. He will serve as President of Italy if the Republican form of government is chosen. Otherwise, he will only serve as President of the Cabinet. 

One of the principal functions of the Constituent Assembly in forming the constitution will be to determine a parliamentary system, either bicameral or unicameral. Another major task will be the formulation of economic policies to guide Italy during the period of contingency and to establish the economic system that will guide Italy in the future.

An analysis of political speeches and propaganda booklets issued by the parties reveals some pertinent factors of each. The Occupator presents a few highlights of the principal parties:

Democrat-Christian Party received more votes than any other single party in the local elections held during March and April. The party is composed of three groups: the right wing of clericals who favor the monarchy and the establishment of the Catholic religion as the state religion; the center group, the majority, which favors a democracy and a republic, and also favors the maintenance of the Concordat between Church and State; and the left wing, Christian Socialists or Christian Communists, who remain in the party favoring the religious program of one and the economic program of the other parties. The party favors a program of collectivism and industrial reform. They desire that representatives of labor be placed in the administrative council of industries and propose that workers share in industrial utilities and prepare for future joint-property ownership. The party is extremely flexible, consistently receiving strong support from the Catholic Church.

Communist Party is the strongest political organization in Italy. It maintains constant control over members with no factions in the group. During the Fascist regime, they were more active than other parties in the underground fight and hence they had more men and women sent to prison and places of confinement than the others. They draw their total support from the factory workers and farm laborers. The party believes in the nationalization of all land, banks, factories, and utilities and strongly favors the unicameral system of legislation. They are one hundred percent anti-monarchist. Their leader, Togliatti, lived in exile in Russia. The present Communist program criticizes the political activity of the Catholic Church but favors the freedom of religion. Embarrassed by Russia's demand for Trieste for Jugoslavia as reparations for Russia, they advocate Trieste for Italy. They probably favor complete autonomy to the local administrative government. Their platform calls for extreme social and educational reforms. Policy is not known due to Russian favoritism towards Jugoslavia and France, which seek reparations from Italy.

Socialist Party was at one time the largest party as far as membership in Italy is concerned. This party won an important victory in Milan during administrative elections by defeating the Christian Democrats and the Communist Party. Weakness lies in the different factions, which constantly split their strength. In the majority of local elections, they combined lists with the Communist Party. Another group sees international alliances with other European Socialist parties. The third group, under the leadership of Saragat, proposes a foreign policy permitting relationships with all foreign countries. Basically, this is a working-man's party with leadership in the hands of professional men and intellectuals. The party strongly favors adoption of reforms rather than radical changes and favors the nationalization of financial organizations and large industries. The party opposes the division of land programs and favors freedom of religion but opposes the Catholic religion as the State religion.

National Democratic Union is composed of the Liberal Party and Democratic Labor Party. It favors constitutional monarchy and can be compared to the Churchill Conservative Party of England. Strength lies in the fact that the group is composed of landowners, industrialists, bankers, and other large entrepreneurs. They favor private enterprise but oppose monopolies and support the maintenance of the present Concordat between Church and State. They are strong proponents of two houses by different electoral systems. The group favors the decentralization of the duties of the State to local authorities.

L'Uomo Qualunque Party (Common Man) is an outgrowth of a newspaper devoted to criticism of Italian political parties and professional politicians. The publication was conceived by a successful dramatic playwright. Main criticism is leveled against Socialists and Communists. Members are mainly composed of diehard Fascists, university students, and lower middle-income groups who fear the possible power of the proletariat. They are heavily financed by small businessmen. It is considered the most dangerous movement in Italy today due to continued clashes between Qualunquists and members of the left parties. They favor the inauguration of an Administrative State where technically trained men are elected without political affiliation to serve the general well-being of the masses, a program which political analysts compare with the Fascist doctrine which "rejects the doctrine of popular sovereignty for state sovereignty. For government by the whole people, it substitutes government by the chosen few, who are asserted to be capable of ignoring their own private interests in favor of the higher demands of society."

Blocco della Mena is composed of four parties: Italian Democratic Party, Monarchial Union, Democratic Center, and Liberal Democratic Concentration. It favors a Constitutional Monarchy and bases its foreign policy on the Atlantic Charter, seeking a representative system based on division and balance of powers.

Republican Alliance is a local party, Democratic-Republican Movement, that favors the American form of government, specifically a Presidential Republic. Its program contains the creation of a government with guarantees and respect for Provincial Rights, promotion of friendly relations between England, France, America, and Italy; and social and economic reforms against large industries and large land estates.

Republican Party derives its origin from Giuseppe Mazzini, who founded the Republican Party in 1828 in order to unite the different states of Italy. It favors the decentralization of political power, meaning the full autonomy of the regions and communities.

Foggia Army Air Base Chooses Its Queen For 1946

Silvana Cioni is crowned Miss Foggia Army Air Base of 1946 as 150 soldiers and civilians in the FAAB gym cheered. Six judges chose her Queen over three other contestants at Monday night's dance, and MC Gene Cohen put the crown on the head of the loveliest of them all. The proudest person in the hall was Silvana's mother as she held the white lily bouquet while the Queen danced.

Aida Dal Cim and the other contestants made it obvious that the judges' job was not easy. Aida, with Lt. Paul Kirby as her escort, walked past the AES mike where Sgt. Lou Cook was describing the happenings to the Foggia radio audience. The broadcast lasted half an hour.

Pina Regenersto, wearing a pink evening gown with delicate roses around the neckline, came down Judges Row with FO Floyd Garrison. The music for the ceremony came from Fred De Grazia's Orchestra, which played all evening to the packed gymnasium.

Lina Vinelli, smallest of them all, held on to Lt. Phil Polito as civilians and GIs passed judgment on the pair. After the decision, all of the couples marched to the throne and congratulated the Queen. Lt. Kirby, who also escorted Miss Cioni, danced the first dance with her; and after the formalities, none of the girls could sit out a dance until the end of the evening.

Nights 'Round Foggia By Eddie M. Dunaj

SO THE PEOPLE MAY KNOW: ON WHAT BASIS ARE THE OFFICERS AND ENLISTED MEN'S CLUBS BEING RUN? IS IT THE PURPOSE OF THE CLUBS TO GIVE EACH INDIVIDUAL THE MAXIMUM OF ENTERTAINMENT AND THE BEST QUALITY IN HIS DRINKS, OR IS THE INTENTION OF THESE CLUBS TO OPERATE ON THE PROFIT SYSTEM TO MAKE AN EARNING ON EACH INDIVIDUAL SOLDIER?

Blindfolds Revealed

Late comers to dinner at the Officers' club miss out on dessert, but this same commodity of food may be purchased for a nominal fee later in the evening at the Snack Bar. At certain Enlisted Men's Clubs, as much as five dollars profit is being made on a single loaf of bread. The soldier is charged thirty lire for a sandwich. Such a price is obtained on approximately fifteen sandwiches from a loaf of bread that originally cost the club EIGHT CENTS. The men at the bakery confirm our convictions, stating that, "Too much money is being paid by the G.I.'s for a bite to eat."

Why was there no explanation offered in the sudden drop of the monthly beer rations? Surprising, that as much as sixteen cans of beer are allotted monthly at the corner P.X., and this while the month is young. The remainder of the G.I.'s favorite drink is obtainable at the squadron clubs, which in itself is doubtful, as there are nights when the clubs run a "NO BEER TONIGHT" sign. Who drinks these precious rations at a price higher than the P.X. sells them for? What did happen to the original case of twenty-four cans of beer?

The Pay Off

In a few brief weeks, after a change of management and constant drawbacks, an Enlisted Men's club opened its doors to an ever-increasing turnout, but the fatal blight of monopoly hindered as well as destroyed all hopes of a fair enterprise. Working on the American exchange, a two dollar bar book may be purchased for four hundred and fifty lire. This puts a coke, the pause that refreshes and as far as we know the best-selling beverage, in the ten cent category or approximately twenty-two lire. An amount that doubles the price charged by any of the clubs in the town.

Such information reaches our ears, yet it is taken to be understood that these clubs are running on a non-profit basis. This method may be fashionable elsewhere, but we desire to serve notice upon these establishments that it will not go in Foggia. If such WHEELS are to run their clubs in such a fashion, then we will force the issue in denouncing these various deeds.

Static From Your AES by Ken Eill

Ah, yes, there's good news today because a bunch of swell guys are on their way home at last. By the time you read this, four of our most stalwarts will have left us. Joe Peale of Lawrence, Don Mietzman, a native of Dubuque, Iowa, John Gallagher, who will be very happy to see Detroit, Michigan, again, and of course Calvin Bourgeault, who is going to keep Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, awake with an occasional "Hello Ladies." And so the boresome foursome is leaving us, and speaking for everyone that knows and has worked with them, the best of everything to you guys, and don't let civilian life change you. Remember, we knew you when you were only sergeants.

And with tears streaming down our sallow cheeks, we hear of something else that makes us sad. Anita O'Day has left the music business for a housewife's job. Anita set the country on fire five and a half years ago when she made her debut with the Gene Krupa Band, and the fire hasn't gone out yet. She left the Krupa Band because of illness, returned with the Herman Herd for a short time, was with Stan Kenton's band for a wonderful period, and then went back to the Krupa Fold. I was lucky enough to see Anita the first night she hit New York with the Gene Krupa Band. It was a great band—Sammy Danahue, Sammy Musiker, Milt Raskin, Roy Eldridge—and Anita, an unknown, unheralded, redhead, stole the show from all these great musicians. She sang blues, jump, teamed up with Roy for a few unforgettable numbers, and with tears in her eyes had to beg off because the Krupa Band didn't have any more arrangements with her singing. The Krupa Band at that time was very fine. Anita and Roy made it one of the greatest of all time. Even the notoriously un-hip public at that time took Anita to their hearts.

All good things must come to an end, so Anita had to retire because of illness. She returned with the Herman Band and couldn't quite seem to find herself with it. Left to join the Kenton outfit and hit her stride again. She was really great. Stan wrote some fine stuff for her, and I think Anita was happy, but again she got the wandering bug and left to rejoin the Krupa Band. For a while it was great and then something happened to Mr. Krupa. He began displaying some very poor taste, having Anita sing such inane stuff as "Chickory Chick" and "Jose Gonzales." Having his name mentioned in the lyrics of a song whenever it was possible and even a few times when it wasn't possible. Maybe it wasn't Gene's idea, but still, it was his band, and he could have put a stop to it if he wanted to. A lot of people are bemoaning the fact that Anita quit. Knowing how much Anita loves to sing, I don't think she wanted to quit. I think she was disgusted, fed up, maybe even tired of wandering about trying to find the right place, so she's cooking bacon and eggs. I hope she tires of that soon and comes back. We jazz fans need her, the greatest jazz vocalist of this age—Anita O'Day.

Talking about greatest things of the age, every Thursday evening at 11:00, you can hear some of the most popular songs of all time done in new light symphonic arrangements by such wonderful musicians as Kostalanetz, Gould, Paige, and so on. It's "Reflections In Music," a relaxing half-hour of the finest in soft, lilting music with some choice words given by Roy Arndt. It's really a lovely show, so don't forget to tune in. Thursday evening at 11:00—Reflections In Music.

With tears of farewell to the boys streaming down our cheeks, we wrap up this week's issue and say goodbye till next week.
