Calling 'Em From The Bench By Eddie M. Dunaj

There was a mile-high stack of plates at the farewell banquet for the Rebel coach, Lt. Antonio Farina, and shortstop, Bob Caley, Sunday evening at the 779 Air Material Sqdn. At this surprise party, eighteen Rebel teammates feasted in an atmosphere that reflected gay youth without the intrusion of some silly, asinine military courtesy and old WHEELS dismal taboos. Here are friendships that are life-lasting and familiarity that does not breed contempt. "We presented Tony with a baseball, one of those hard-to-get items from Special Service," smiled third baseman Steve Enright, "autographed by all the team members." And what did Lt. Farina have to say as he gripped our hand in a firm handshake? "It was wonderful, the little baseball particularly. I'll keep it on top of my mantelpiece when I get married." What really struck home was this simple, creative verse composed by catcher Red Rummel as the teammates presented their coach with a wild, yellow print necktie: 

"Lt. Farina, oh noble Cha Chu, This beer, food is all for you. A grand fellow and all that you know, We bow our heads for home you go. In our pocket for Lire, we dip A present, one hundred poker chips." 

Hit hard by the recent shipment of men to the states is the Special Service team. Among those who departed stateside: Mel Burgess, Lou Avila, Jesse Hannon, and Joe Accardo. In the last game played, the Specials sent their boys home with their first victory of the season against the 779 Rebels, 8-7. 

It was close to dusk as the sun began a base lead for the horizon, in the twilight game between the 803 MP's Reds and the Specials. At the time of the fifth inning, Burgess's Specials were in the lead, 7-5, and Mel, confident of victory, attempted to quiet down the Reds' sideline hooters. "Do you guys want me to schedule a game for you with the Red Cross girls?" "We heard you," they shouted, "that's what we want!" Then came the eventful sixth inning, with the Reds trailing by three runs, 8-5. Specials hurler, Accardo, fanned two, and here we stop to consider whether the following throws were strikes or walks. Umpire Schwartz carried three men to bases on called walks. Poor visibility or threats could be blamed for the decision. Needless to say, the Reds gained four unearned runs and won the game, 9-8. Why is it that the teams in the American League must play in the absence of official umpires?

Lt. H. R. Griffen, Special Service officer, returned from Stuttgart, Germany, where he attended the Athletic School for the E.T.O. Among the many dignitaries in the sports world that appeared at Stuttgart were: Mercer Beasley, big-time tennis coach at the U. of Michigan, Len Lercy Malory, golf pro from Bridgeport, Conn, George Nilan, boxing coach at the U. of N.C., George Sportsman, Track and Field from Texas, and Charlie Foster, top softball expert, now recreational director at Lakewood, Ohio. Griffen, who was the only Air Corps man present at the Athletic School, graduated from Western Carolina Teachers, and intends to take up high school coaching, working his way to the Junior College position. 

Griffen gave us the dope on a ladder tournament for the tennis-minded as soon as the new court will be completed, now being constructed near the swimming pool, to replace the one at the 955 Engr., which is making way for the Italian Housing project.

Italy Votes For Republic

Italy is a Republic today. In a free vote in which over eighty percent of eligible voters cast their ballots on June 2nd and 3rd to make their choice of a Republic or Monarchy, fifty-four percent of the people chose the Republic. Simultaneously the people of Italy voted for delegates for the Constituent Assembly where the new constitution will be drafted.

In national voting, the final count gave the Christian Democrats 35% of the votes, Socialists 21%, and Communists 19%. Locally, however, the balloting was more in line with Southern Italy’s traditionally conservative vote. Foggia voted a 66% majority for the Monarchy, and the Christian Democrat Party got a 41% plurality. (See Page 4 for complete tabulations)

Close Republic Win

The close referendum vote (54% to 46%) came as a surprise to foreign observers who had gone out on a limb before election time to predict an overwhelming defeat for the House of Savoy. Stateside press opinion had been that the Monarchy had only a “slim chance”. Christian Democrats votes apparently surprised the people when, after having decided by a large majority at the D. C. party convention to oppose the Monarchy, they shifted heavily to the King’s side. If leftist votes went Republican, then only about one third of the D. C. votes were for the Republic.

Yesterday, after final results had been announced and the man on the street was hearing wild rumors that Sicily was thinking of secession because of the King’s defeat, four major parties entered a plea to the people to accept the results and maintain order. Until this time there have been no reports of serious violence.

115 Go Home

Under the latest redeployment requirements issued to Foggia Army Air Base, by MTOUSA Headquarters ninety-four Enlisted Men and twenty Officers left Foggia last week for the Replacement Depot in Leghorn on their way to the United States. The requirements necessary for redeployment under the latest regulations are: Enlisted Men, 43 points or 28 months of service; Officers' 66 points or 44 months of service.

In addition to the 114 soldiers who were redeployed, Captain Frank Voightmann, Commanding Officer of the 955 Aviation Engineering Squadron, returned to the United States for 45 days on temporary duty orders.

Foggia Food Cut Averted

Contradictory to a previous order by the Foggia Province Food Office which announced a food ration cut, it was revealed this week that the arrival of the freighter, USS Northwestern Victory, with a load of 8500 tons of UNNRA flour had averted the impending cut in ration and food crisis. The foodcargo of the American ship was delivered almost totally to the Puglia province, which is the heel of the boot of Italy, and it is now expected that the food situation in this geographical area will be secure until the harvesting of the local wheat crop in a few weeks.

Complete facilities are available, including track shoes, uniforms, and hot showers.

FAAB Transferred To Ninth Air Force Service Command

Few Noticeable Changes Expected

Official announcement of the transfer of the Foggia Army Air Base from the 40th Bomb Wing Command to the Ninth Air Force Service Command was made this week by Colonel Robert K. Martin, FAAB Commanding Officer. Colonel Martin further explained that the shift of command was necessitated by the fact that the Foggia Army Air Base consists of mainly a service group and had consequently lost its tactical statis. Like the 40th Bomb Wing, the Ninth Air Force Service Command maintains its headquarters in Erlangen, Germany.

Colonel Martin commented that the reorganization will have little effect on the working and training schedules of the base. Flying schedules will also be continued on the same basis as they have in the past months, and whatever couriers have been running will be mainteined.

Applicants Outnumber Openings In Regular Army

An officer applying for a commission in the ground forces of the Regular Army has one chance in ten of being appointed. In the Air Forces he has one chance in fifteen, a cable received here from M’TOUSA Headquarters stated recently.

In addition, certain officers now in the Army will be released, Colonel Robert K. Martin stated, even though they are in waiver categories and may have applied for the RA. These will include officers over age in grade, limited service officers, and officers with low efficiency ratings.

A total of 108,582 applications for the RA have been received by the WD. After rejections, and withdrawals, 97,550 remain. Of approximatly 23,000 applicants for Ground Arms, there are 4,000 vacancies, but 50,000 applicants for them. In technical and administrative forces there are 27,000 applications for 2,400 vacancies.

Provided the Senate confirms nominations, the WD proposes to announce successful applicants on or about July 1st. The men remaining on the eligible list after that will be utilized if Congress authorizes increases in the RA. If this happens there will be another opportunity to apply for the Regular Army.

Redeployment Change

It was added, however, that the change may effect redeployment, in that the group will be able to get rid of some surplus personnel, the Colonel said. Classifications of surplus personnel, he added, have remained the same. The list of surplus officers was published over a month ago.

"We are trying also," Colonel Martin concluded, "to return home all Class V category officers as soon as possible."

Last Big Shipment of Wives Leaves Soon

Rome — In the most recent Red Cross Family Service conference held here this week, and attended by Misses Helen Andren and Sandy Kalajinski of the Foggia office, latest plans for the shipment of wives were formulated for Italy. In the Foggia quotas the last large shipment of Italian wives to the United States will leave Foggia on June 19 for Naples. From there the wives will sail on June 29.

In this last big shipment, Foggia has been allotted a quota of 26 wives, which Miss Andren advised, will be filled without difficulty.

Mel

Charles Melvin Warrall, the youngest American in Foggia, waved to us from his high-chair in the officers' mess recently, and we took it as an invitation to have dinner with him.

Mel was pretty busy wacking at a custard cruller to take much notice of us after we sat down, so his mother Katherine, wife of Lt. Charles Warrall (955 AES), offered to act as Mel's press agent. She said that two year old Mel was very satisfied with Foggia after being here a week. His room had been freshly painted by Pop Warrall, and after Mel got used to taking his food from foreign-speaking waiters, he found that it tasted fine. Mel mumbled agreement through a mouthful of cruller, and winked good-naturedly at us.

Mel Vs. Mike

There had been only one personality clash for Mel since his arrival, his mother explained. It seems that Mike (Pop Warrall's pet dog who had been there before Mel came overseas) and Mel have diplomatic troubles. All amiable blond-haired Mel wants to do is love the dog, but Mike refuses to have the little guy climb on his back and hang on to his tail as he slides off. Mel, in turn, is deeply insulted when he throws a stick for the dog - just like Pop Warrall showed him to do - and Mike returns the stick to Pop. Luckily though, Mike knows his place, and every so often he runs off to Foggia Main. After he has thought things over for a few days, he returns.

Besides mixing custard crullers with vegetable soup, Mel has other hobbies. Free-style painting struck his fancy recently. He found a can of blue paint that was being used to decorate the apartment - probably left by Fate for talented hands - and he sloshed around inspirationally for quite a few minutes before the painter noticed the clash of colors in the brown bedroom. His mother nipped the project before too much damage was done, but not until Mel had begun swapping his shoes blue.

Two Laps Around

At this point in the interview, Mel sat upright and announced to the dinning room at large that he had had enough, and was now ready for his after-dinner constitutional. His mother patiently helped him out of his high-chair, and he took two quick laps around the dinning-room before he rejoined us. He arrived with a cigar-band around his thumb, and Pop Warrall, smoking a cigar across the table from us, gave him another band.

Mel, his father said, has probably seen as much of the world as any one of two years. Born in Champaign, Illinois, Mel went with his folks to Boca Raton Field, Florida, then to visit his father's home in Philedelphia, to his mother's home in Terre Haute, Indiana, and then overseas. He really enjoyed that boat ride to Italy. Every one on the ship made friends with him, and when they docked at Naples he refused to get off.

The biggest problem, his mother explained as Mel did a few acrobatics under the table, is finding healthy playground space. He misses his back-home yards where he could be turned loose and would play all day. Otherwise, he's happy here. As we said goodbye to Mel, he blew a little foam at us from his father's can of beer, and laughed happily.

Red Eye

When the Second Bomb Group moved from the old airfield into Foggia last October and November, the officers were billeted in order of rank, and when the Group filled up the BOQ they discovered that the flight officers were left out in the cold, so to speak. Apologetically, the FO's were pushed into the Sarti Hotel, a place for transient officers, and only from time to time were their cries heard.

In common misery, a sort of fraternity was established, an amiable group that never excluded friendly lieutenants. Thus, the hybrid rank, not commissioned officers and still forbidden to fraternize with enlisted men, made the Sarti their not-so-quiet castle. Transient officers marveled at the comraderie that existed at the Sarti, and USO troops who billeted there met the boys and left to spread the story of their parties and celebrations all over Europe.

A Fraternal Bar

Recently, during an idle discussion about court martials, some of the more energetic FO's decided to organize a club. It was agreed that the organization would take the shape of a bar—a healthful place, they planned, in the open where one could drink and sun himself at the same time. It was set up on the patio on the third floor, walls sternly whitewashed, decorations colored a fiery red, and an imposing bloodshot eye painted on the yellow bar. Everything was done by the FO's personally, and the Red Eye members (a self-styled clique that welcomes only Sarti residents) decided that it was to be a before-meal (every meal) cocktail lounge. Red Eye was opened officially on March 16th, timed for the arrival of the USO Show "Washington Slept Here". But testing and tasting by specialists of the fraternity began two weeks prior to the arrival of the show.

Visitors who came to gaze on the tranquillity of the fraternal brothers were received by a cool nod, much like that given by combat veterans to quartermaster soldiers. The FO's lived happily, idly, and put on shirts only for the arrival of a USO party, all members of which have officio standing in the Red Eye.

Tradition Disputed

But more staid members of the USO - stage hands probably - and officials in Theater Specials Services do not smile at the tradition of the Red Eye. The Sarti Hotel's reputation is to them one of wild parties, trumpeteers playing through the windows all night, and a place where bad girls go worse. Recently an embittered USO directive changed the Camps Shows' billets in Foggia to the more moral 55th Station Hospital, and they wondered about one of their girls who deserted the show in Leghorn to revisit one of the Sarti boys.

Red Eye's latest blow came when a number of their tribe was transferred to the 1898th Engineers, "to work", the boys say horrified. The Red Eye is a sad place today. Over their cokes the FO's talk of the good old days, and as a member pours himself another drink, they say, without the former brotherliness, "Mark it on the books, Jack. You're going to have to pay for drinks from now on."

New Ribbon

We've been looking for a Commendation Ribbon (new peace-time award) owner in Foggia, and thus we found Captain Fritz Bluhm of the 55th Station Hospital with two. Just over from the States, Captain Bluhm got his first award for excellence of command while CO of Fitzsimons General Hospital in Denver, Colorado (July 1942 to June 1944), and the cluster for meritorious service as Chief of Military Personnel at the same hospital (September, 1945 to March, 1946).

"I'm a master sergeant," said the Captain with a smile. In the Regular Army, of course. Actually, I am a master sergeant in the RA and a Captain in the Reserve (since 1935) at the same time. A little awed, we asked how long he had been in service. "Twenty years on the 19th of this month," he answered. As we started to ask the ne question he said, "And I'll probably be a thirty-year man before I quit." We think the man deserves another ribbon.

A Prayer
Once more is plunder done; the world doth lie
Prostrate, as if by Hell's own vampire stung.
Bled waxen white, whilst through her wounds the cry,
Accusing, soars to the blood red sky o'erhung.

Oh pray for us who perpetrate this rape
Of Earth, whereon the Lord's own Eden bloomed.
Inciting wrath from which there's no escape.
No road, save one, and thereon walk the doomed,

Yet still we do naught but to shed dry tears
That clouded mem'ries soon dispel.
While as we view our banal crime with speechless fears
Our hearts applaud greed's rise to some new dias.

Ah, pity us whose right hand begs God's bliss
And whose left trails behind for Satan's kiss.

Flo Ted Kissen

No More Clubmobile

Of all the people who are sorry to see the Red Cross Clubmobile come to an end, (and there are many) little Jean Copp is, perhaps, one of the sorriest. She looked glum sitting there in the ARC, chin tucked deeply between her palms.

"Tell us about the last ride of the Clubmobile," we asked. Jean straightened up.

"There they were!" she began whimsically. "With tears streaming down their faces, and — oh". She stopped and wrinkled her face into an expression of petulance as she tucked it back into her palms.

Yes, Clubmobile is gone and although it might not sound like anything worrisome, from an easy-chair in the Red Cross of Foggia proper, there has already been many a cry of anguish from the less fortunate in the areas surrounding the town. The move, it seems, has sprung from a War Department directive, and isn’t the ARC’s idea.

“It’s a disappointment to a lot of men,” says Jean who already is reminiscing about the ‘good old days’. “As soon as we’d drive up they’d drop everything and tear over to the place where we serve the doughnuts and coffee and lemonade. Whenever we were a little late there would be a line formed and they’d make cracks.”

Jean sighed a remorseful little sigh, for now as acting directoress of the officers’ section of the RC Club, life will be infinitely less exciting. Less exciting for Peg Starring and Ann Starbuck too, the other intrepids of the Clubmobile route.

There were two trips daily totaling some eighty miles around Foggia and toward Manfredonia. Between a thousand and thirteen hundred doughnuts were consumed every day. and ‘gallons’ of lemonade and coffee. Then there were also the incidental jobs like bringing airplane models and magazines to the boys who asked for them.

“It was very satisfying work,” states Jean, “And fun too, I loved it, even when we got caught in Healthy in the rain.” (see cut) Jean’s face became a shade more melancholy.

“I hope it’ll come back,” she said sadly. “Maybe, if there’s enough requests…”

Mosquito Fighter

We walked into BOQ 20 the other day and came into a mild fit of sneezing when we entered a hallway foggy with DDT. Further on were three Italians with spraying units strapped to their backs, and close by, his head in a mist of DDT, was Lt. Paul Nighswonger, Foggia's inexorable mosquito fighter.

He looked a little weary and we thought that perhaps all that DDT was wearing him down.
Let me know if you need any further assistance!

Wives Object

"No," he explained, "DDT doesn't hurt people. I've done everything but swim in it and I feel okay. The worst of it is all the trouble it seems to cause. A lot of the wives don't like us to spray their rooms. It does make a big mess."

One of the two-man spray teams prepared to spray an officer's room. Lt. Nighswonger covered the exposed clothes with a blanket, arranged the man's raincoat over some toilet articles and then motioned the laborers to begin. One started plumping and in a few moments the room was enveloped in an artificial fog of the insect-killing solution.

"We only spray it on the walls and ceilings. But of course it gets on everything," he said wearily, "It's just a big mess and I make enemies. It'll evaporate soon though and they'll forget about it. At least I hope so. I don't want so many lasting enemies."

The sprayers finished the room and opened the windows. Then they retired to spray a bathroom.

"Some wives have even refused to let us spray their apartments," he continued, "They don't realize that they're in the middle of Italy. I wish they'd all be like Mrs. Palmer and Mrs. Sadler. They were very nice about it and we had to do their apartments twice."

Biggest Part Over

The spraying of BOQ 20, we learned, is one more in the long list of places that the anti-malarial team has cleansed. Eventually every military establishment in Foggia will be in insect-proofed by the spray, even offices. The biggest job, that of spraying all the farmhouses around Foggia has already been largely completed. The teams ran into very little opposition there.

"They welcomed us, said Lt. Nighswonger, "Remembered from last year. The foreman of the sprayers would approach the houses and yell 'Ho Fleet' (We have Flit) and they'd come out smiling."

A squad of sprayers emerged damply from the ping-pong room. Lt. Nighswonger opened a door and looked into an officer's bedroom, then entered and started the preparations.

"Hope he's not much bigger than I am," he said as the sprayers began to pump their apparatus.

Foggians voted last Sunday and Monday in the first free election here in over twenty years — for men under forty-five and for all women, it was the first time in their lives to have cast a ballot. The 30,000 people crowded the polls, and many, like the man and woman above had to wait on lines all day to exercise their newly won right.

Italy's Fourth King Is Its Last

Umberto II, fourth king of an Italy unified in 1861, became this week the last member of the House of Savoy to rule this country. In 1848 Victor Emanuel I, from the ruling family of the state of Sardinia-Piedmont, gained popular support of a confused Italian people when he offered his father’s “Statuto” to Italians, which provided for a king, two-chamber parliament, and council of deputies. With the aid of the fiery Garibaldi, and (indirectly) even the help of the king-hating Mazzini, the House of Savoy ruled all of Italy, except Venice, by 1870.

The House of Savoy, associated with the unification of Italy, went on to make its reign far from distinguished in the annals of social or political progress. When the men about the King (Mazzini, Cavour, Garibaldi) died or left public life, the nation floundered externally and developed a case of social sea-sickness internally. King Umberto I, successor to Victor Emanuel, was assinated in 1900 after many attempts at his life.

Internationally, Italy was having trouble with France and its territorial ambitions. Bitter at the French acquisition of Tunis, Italy turned to Germany, and consented to sign the Triple Alliance with Austria, traditional enemy of Italy, as the third signatory. At the turn of the century, Italy tried to invade Albania and was repulsed, but when she went into Lybia in 1911 the country in left one year.

King Powerless

In World War I, Italy dissolved the Triple Alliance when Austria attacked, then accepted England's offer of Trieste and African colonies, and entered the war against Germany and Austria. The end of the war left Italy weak; that and the fact that England could not live up to her promises to Italy left the way open for Mussolini. Victor Emanuel III did little to resist the dictator, and eventually the king found himself powerless.

With the defeat of the Axis, a Provisional Committee was established and with the support of the Allies, decided to let the people choose the form of government they desired, Monarchy or Republic. Victor Emanuel III abdicated after fourty-five years in power, in a political move designed to strenthen the position of the Monarchy. His son, Umberto II took over with the humble statement: "I further confirm my pledge to respect, as any other Italian, the free decision of the coming referendum which I am sure will be inspired in the best interests of the country."

The nation voted, but the Communists and Socialists opposed the monarchy, as did the Republican Party tradionally anti-king and great champions of Mazzini. By a 54% majority, the Republic won.

Memorial Day was observed on the 31st of May. In Italy, three days later, the people went to the polls and chose their form of government and their leaders. Women voted for the first time on a large scale in the country's history. In all, more than eighty per cent of the people cast their ballots.

Following so closely upon the day that we choose to pay tribute to the memory of our men who died fighting for these freedoms, we cannot help but observe that 'they have not died in vain!'

Nights 'Round Foggia
By Eddie M. Dunaj

SO THE PEOPLE MAY KNOW WHAT THE CLUB MANAGERS HAVE TO SAY ON LAST WEEK'S APPEARANCE OF "NIGHTS 'ROUND FOGGIA"

In this series of articles, we are attempting to portray both sides of the question. Playing no favorites and having always in mind that it is our duty to serve the community in reporting everyone's viewpoint, we presented last week the G.I.'s story, the story of patrons and dwellers in our Night Clubs, the ones to whom such statements are made as, "The customer is always right."

This week, the various Club Managements presented their story to us and we print it with what hopes of an understanding it has to offer in bringing a concise and clear picture of the existing situation. Each of the managers who called on us, was anxious to bring to light many events unknown to the average G.I. A few still remain unknown. This is their story and their problems.

One of the Club Administrators proposed lowering the price of Coca Cola to five cents. This, as a special feature between the hours of two and five in the afternoon, as arrangement for the crowd at the beach which makes its appearance there for the relaxation and comfort a few hours in the afternoon offers under a sunny sky and in the refreshing Adriatic breeze.

The management claimed that they would be operating at a loss of one cent per bottle, stating that the Coca Cola is a hard item to get and what stock is available is used for mixed drinks. However this loss can be made up, with both parties happy. As an added attraction, they proposed a huge Pig Roast, a picnic for all the Enlisted Men, with food and drinks on the house. The Club Representative suggested the near future as the date for this occasion. Nights 'Round Foggia is desirous to announce this day and hope the Manager's statement, "So everyone can get a hunk of it," will soon become a reality.

The administrators at the Officers' Club, took it upon themselves to brief the soldiers (including EM and Officers) on the fact that the clubs must operate on a profit basis. A fund is necessary to provide the patrons with an abundance of liquor, such as American whiskey. Expenses must be met for entertainment bands, free Snack Bar nights and parties. Military personnel attached to such clubs are paid fifty percent of their base pay out of the Club fund. The biggest headache at the Officers' Club is the restocking of 1200 glasses, at thirty lire each, per month. "Just where they go no one knows," the management explained.

With a personal attitude towards the late comers, who miss their dessert at dinner, the Club Officer wishes to state, that the food commodities are supplied by the club and prepared for the Snack Bar by their own cook and baker. To their knowledge, every officer should receive his dessert at meal times, unless some of them get seconds, using the scheme of changing tables, "The Club has nothing to do with the Mess Hall," stated the management.

Static From Your A.E.S.
by Ken Eill

Ahhhh Yes, there's bad news today for by the time you read this our CO, Lt. Charles Meuche will be on his way to the land of the living. The man's going home, that is. And a lot of good wishes from the gang up here go with him because he's been such a swell guy both on and off the job.

While we are on the subject of being on the job, there is a guy up here who is really on said job, Pfc. James Luman Rock, of Flint, Michigan. James has had fifteen months of service so far, five of them overseas. As a civilian Jim graduated from high school and came right into the Army. He went to sheet metal school and then learned all about kitchens the hard way. He came to the A.E.S. and has been working as an engineer ever since. The man's simply mad about bowling and baseball and when he gets out of the Army, he wants to go to the General Motors technical school.

And now we present the golden trumpet of Randy Brooks... and surprise, surprise! ... it really sounds like a golden trumpet, for Randy Brooks plays a really wonderful horn. Randy is no newcomer to the band business. He was with the old Ray Herbeck band for a short time, the pre-war Claude Thornhill band, and the Les Brown outfit where he received a great deal of attention and comment. Then Randy left to form his own outfit. The band has been in existence now for about sixteen months and is definitely on the way to the top of the musical heap. There was a little tough sledding at first, but it looks like the Brooks style of music has finally caught on. He has a pair of good vocalists in Dorie Vincent and Billy Usher; Willie Baker's tenor sax in the outstanding instrumental feature, and the arrangements of Johnny Brooks (no relation) are really fine on both ballads and jump. Of course, Randy himself is terrific on anything he plays... his tone is clear and brilliant with lovely phrasing and hard driving on the frantic antics. He has some new ideas both for the band and on his trumpet, and he isn't afraid to use them. He has one of the finest ranges in the country, both upper and lower register and has the good taste not to overdo his high-note stuff the way a great many other trumpet men of the day are doing. An MTOUSA cable received by the Red Cross Family Service has stated that no further shipments of babies under six months old will be permitted to leave Europe for the United States. Foggia VD Rate Triples June 14 - The venereal disease rate in Foggia's Army installations during May has tripled over rates in recent months, according to a statement made today by Lt. Franklin N. Crider of the FAAB Dispensary. April's five cases (making the rate 53.5 cases per thousand men per annum) were considered high, although compared to cases in ETO, it was not above the overseas average. In May, however, the VD rate jumped to 160.9 cases per thousand per annum, with 19 new infections treated, and reached a very serious high. The alarming jump in the number of infections was attributed by Lt. Crider to the influx of new men into Foggia last month. "It seems as though the men who were new in Foggia attempted to make their arrival one big fling and this has been the result," Dr. Crider reported.

Polio Scare Subsides Possible Epidemic Thought To Be Isolated Case The poliomyelitis scare which developed after a German prisoner here died of the disease is believed to be no more than an isolated case, Lt. Elrie Rodgers, 55th Station Hospital medical officer said this week. The polio that attacked the PW was an acute, rapid-action type, and the man died four days after reporting sick. Following the diagnosis of the sickness as poliomyelitis (also called infantile paralysis), the 55th Station Hospital issued orders eliminating close contact among people in congested places. Along with this came the Air Corps directives placing beaches and swimming pools off-limits. These measures, Lt. Rodgers specified, are only the usual precautionary steps taken by the Army when any contagious disease breaks out. There have been no other cases of polio thus far, which indicates that the one that did occur was isolated, a not uncommon occurrence with poliomyelitis. The 55th Hospital orders have already been lifted and close seating is again permissible in the Flagella Theater. The ban on swimming stands, however, at least until the completion of tests on the water, and possibly until stagnant sewage deposits (discovered in streams emptying into the beaches) are cleared out.

Testa, come one asked us what the festa had been Tuesday night that got all those civilians out in a truck, yelling viva something-or-other. On Being Nine

It's hard to remember what it was like when we were nine years old. About all we can recall was that we were in the fourth grade, learning the multiplication tables and spending most of our idle hours wishing we could fly like "Lindy" — the exemplification of flying in those days. Just recently, we went to visit a young fellow who is nine years old (who was in the hospital recuperating from a case of measles) and who also wants to fly. Only he wants to fly like his Dad, Archie McCasland.

Jerry McCasland was sitting up in bed, a pair of earphones on his head (listening to the 55th Station Hospital's Earphone Radio) and sucking on a sour ball. He greeted us shyly and went back to listening to Baby Snooks on the air. Betty McCasland, as blond as her son and with intelligent blue eyes, politely asked Jerry to treat us like guests, and we could remember being nine years old again and wondering why the devil everyone was always visiting us when our favorite program was on the radio. Jerry chewed meditatively on his sour ball and said hello.

Many Friends

How old? "Nine; be ten in August." Weight? "Sixty-eight pounds before I caught the measles." Height? "Four foot, five." From what we remembered of our ninth year, friends were one of the most important things in life. "I went to school in Dallas," said Jerry, "and I had lots of friends there, but I got lots here too. And Johnny and I go to the beach and play together a lot." "Johnny," said Jerry's mother, "is the little Foggia boy who Sergeant Shuey takes care of at the 529th Headquarters."

As Jerry ate another sour ball and went back to listening to Baby Snooks, Betty McCasland told us a little more about her son. Her biggest worry was how to provide for his education for the one year that they expect to be in Italy. She will teach Jerry the few subjects that the teacher advised before they left Dallas, but in the main, most of his education will have to be what he can learn by seeing Europe and make up the formal education by the art, culture, and travel he gets in Europe.

No Harness

"I'd like to see Rome," said Jerry, rejoining the conversation. "And I'd like to fly there. Dad was going to take me flying to Naples, but first, they couldn't get a chute harness small enough for me, and then I got the measles." He offered us a sour ball. "The nurse gave me these," he said, "When Mother gives me candy, she rations me to one bar a day. These are small anyhow."

"How do you like it here?" we asked.

We still think being nine years old is a wonderful thing. And education here in Italy? Why, he'll really be able to tell those kids back home some stories.

DeGrazia, the floor of the office was littered with sheet music, and tools for the repair of reed instruments were lined in a rack on his desk. But being the maestro of the FAAB Band entails more than leading musicians through their cadenzas, and Frenck De Grazia was busy in some of his administrative duties when we disturbed him. After he returned the telephone to its cradle, Sergeant DeGrazia turned to us suddenly, exclaiming, "Well, I don't know, one of these days I'll get these concerts going without any trouble." He smiled as though he had said something rash. The bandmaster was preparing a series of band programs to be given in the city of Foggia for both the soldiers and the civilians. "I'd like to give one every week in one of the open squares. We'll probably wind up getting a flatbed and parking it in the middle of some big street."

Civilians Like Band

The idea of giving public concerts came to the FAAB bandmaster after, oddly enough, he had received several compliments on his band's work from several Foggians. "Oh, they like the band all right, but I can tell that they don't think we can play anything but swing and marches. Now I've been working with these boys for months and I don't think there's another army band that's putting out as much. They're really getting good. They have to, to give out with some of the things, like a fifteen-minute piece from Bizet's Carmen that we have on the book."

Frenck De Grazia can talk about musical organizations with authority after spending fifteen years in the music business. After playing his way through Arizona University, Frenck hit the road with several bands and for a while taught music classes at the exclusive Arizona Desert School for Boys. Then, when army service came, DeGrazia went to Italy where he conducted the famous Twelfth Air Force Band, which, after the war, he later brought here to Foggia. Of the original crew, Frenck is the only remaining member. "But I can't get over these new boys. They're really coming along."

Reed Man Out

The FAAB Band has been having its troubles lately. George Keeley, ace reed man, vocalist, and drum major, has been in the hospital, and DeGrazia is still busy making allowances for instrument shortages, but most of all he is kept busy with administrative detail and wishing someone else would take the red tape off his hands.

O, Captain

We said goodbye to Sergeant Milton Hoffman on Monday morning. As Editor of the Foggia Occupator since its inception eight months ago, he was responsible for the newspaper as it stands today, for the good and the bad, for the pleasant and the bitter. He was the Editor, and three officers, two enlisted men, and a whole civilian staff took orders from him in the truest military style, accomplishing his idea of a newspaper that was not "in the truest military style" in unit newspapers.

Milton Hoffman, as a man, was an outspoken liberal and confident that soldiers from America and civilians from Italy could live together peacefully and happily; and as an editor, he pressed that belief with a zeal that often annoyed less confident soldiers and civilians. Truth was an obsession for Milton Hoffman, and he let no preconceived prejudices or staff recommendations color his newspaper. Under him, the Occupator tried to be free of libelous stories about civilians as well as soldiers.

We were sorry to see Milton Hoffman go.

Army: The Doolittle "gripe board," appointed by the War Department to investigate Army personnel relationships, recently offered the following suggestions:

1) Eliminate off-duty saluting except on Army posts and in occupied areas. 2) The system of promoting officers by seniority be discarded for a merit system. Officers should serve one year in the ranks. 3) In courts-martial, the higher the rank, the higher should be the penalty. 4) Wholesale distribution of decorations be stopped. The higher a man's rank, the more difficult it should be to get an award. 5) Identical allowances for food, travel, and quarters be given to all ranks. 6) Rules against social fraternization of ranks be wiped out. 7) Army pay be increased to attract high-caliber men from civilian jobs.

The War Department said that some steps have already been taken (ordering of identical uniforms for all ranks, abolition of "off-limits to enlisted men" areas) and others will be taken as may be indicated and possible.

A man I beheld through the streets of darkness; a man whose sight left him when the first bombs, their sibilant sorrowful dirge, chanted on... Foggia. He told me he saw unending spaces of brilliant lights when he fell: colors and shadows... colors followed by complete darkness. His face was wet, for blood and sweat and terror were moistening the stones, the rubbish, the mortar that crushed his body. Then, while the world was quaking, a maddening untold pain terrified the blind man: for he saw that under that debris was lying he... and all Humanity. Later his thoughts abandoned him. He scrabbles and gropes now, along the bullet-scarred walls, the empty spaces, Paolo, the blind man... and all Humanity.

Victory parade in celebration of the new republican government in Italy winds through the streets of Foggia (Tuesday). Although Foggia voted heavily monarchist, republican celebrations occurred entirely without incident. Photos by Bufalo

Foggians Mark Republic With Large Parade

June 11 — Taking cognizance of a national holiday declared in Rome to mark the victory of the Republic in the recent elections, leftist party members of Foggia marched through the streets tonight in a large victory demonstration. Previous to the parade, several units of Carabinieri were placed in strategic locations throughout the city in the event of disorders. Although in the national election Foggia Province voted for the monarchy by a majority of more than two to one, the parade wound through the streets of Foggia and into the Piazza XX Settembre without incident. 

The parade, led by a placard-covered truck in which workers from Foggia's paper plant were riding, organized near the railroad station and from there began its march through the streets. Several of the demonstrators carried signs reading "Viva La Repubblica" and the Italian tricolors. Demonstrators in the truck threw flowers into the streets and cheered loudly as the parade passed the American Headquarters in the city.

Lauds Republican Choice

At the conclusion of the peaceful demonstration, a crowd of several thousand Foggians gathered in the Piazza XX Settembre to hear speeches in commemoration of the victory of the Republic. 

In the featured speech, given by Domenico Fioritti, head of Foggia's Socialist party, the victory of the Republic was evaluated as a victory over fear. "It was claimed by the Monarchists," Fioritti said, "that the Republic would lead to chaos... just as the monarchy conquered Italy through the fear of separation of provinces and later the fear of Bolshevism. But at last, fear has disappeared, and the people have received their freedom and unity."

On the importance of the victory, Fioritti remarked, "Now that we have given to the whole world this great example of a historical revolution without bloodshed, we can confirm that a people of these moral principles reach out for high destinies."

King Leaves Italy In Unrest

Rome, June 14—Umberto II, former King of Italy, left his homeland today for Lisbon, Portugal, ending the three-century reign of the House of Savoy. Behind him, he left a proclamation that only increased the agitation which has beset the country since Umberto first indicated that he suspected election fraud in the recent national referendum.

In his final proclamation, Umberto stated that he was forced to leave Italy because of the illegal action of his government, which "with a revolutionary gesture" assumed arbitrary power.

Compromised With Fascists

Today Christian Democrat head, Alcide De Gasperi, answered Umberto's charge in a national radio address, in which he stated that the Italian people are determined to defend their own holy right to the future. By leaving Italy, De Gasperi declared, "Umberto expiated the past faults and mistakes of his House, which once compromised with the fascist dictatorship."

After adding in his proclamation that he hoped the Supreme Court will express "its free opinion on electoral irregularities," the former king stated, "I am sure that we may still continue that cooperation and maintain what is truly required: the unity of Italy."

Italy This Week

Governor Thomas E. Dewey of New York addressed a large crowd in Madison Square Garden this week on the occasion of the proclamation of the Italian Republic. Mr. Dewey called for a quick signing of a peace treaty with Italy and the acceptance of Italy into the United Nations. UNRRA chief Fiorello La Guardia and Charles Poletti, former American military governor of Italy, also spoke at the rally.

General Mark Clark was this week awarded a citizenship ad honorem by Sorrento. The award was granted, it was stated by Italian officials, because General Clark has shown his friendship for the picturesque Italian town and also the friendship of the American people to an Italy that is on its way to democracy.

Guglielmo Giannini, head of the Uomo Qualunque, an extreme rightist political party, was converted to Catholicism on Wednesday in Rome. Giannini visited Foggia several weeks ago in connection with the national elections.

All-important grain harvesting is now taking place in Foggia Province and will be completed within a week. It is expected that the harvested crop will come close to pre-war yields. Last year's crop of 600,000 quintiles was bad because of the summer drought. Pre-war levels for the grain harvest have been from three to three and a half million quintiles.

Election results in Foggia Province will send the following proportional representation to the Constituent Assembly in Rome next month: 7 Christian Democrats, 4 Communists, 2 Socialists, and 4 Qualunquists.

In Taranto, a large southern Italian seaport, last Tuesday's demonstration marking the proclamation of the Republic was broken up by monarchist members of the San Marco battalion (Italian commandos) who threw hand grenades into the crowds of demonstrators. Thirty-six persons were injured. The battalion has been moved out of Taranto.

Amici d'America (Friends of America), an Italian non-political organization, is opening up an educational and recreational institution in San Ferdinando for the town's young children. San Ferdinando has long been known as a center for black market activities. Food for the institution will be provided by the Italian government and UNRRA.

The Italian Youth Movement, organized on lines similar to the Boy Scouts, is opening several summer camps throughout Italy, the largest of which will be situated at the east end of the Italian spur, near Manfredonia. A total of 400 hungry youngsters fed by UNRRA will attend the camp during the summer season.

Rioting at the Bari-Milan soccer match last Sunday broke out after the referee refused to call a penalty against the Milan team. The crowd poured onto the field and chased the referee out of the grounds. Milan won the game 3-1 after the crowd was dispersed by the police. As an aftermath, no more soccer matches will be played in the Bari Stadium for an indefinite period.

Nights 'Round Foggia (In the absence of Ed Dunaj, our regular club reporter, now vacationing in Switzerland, here is the account of the grand opening of the Castle Bar, the new officers' nightclub in Foggia.) 

The floor show was to begin at 10:30, and at 8:30, there were plenty of people climbing the double flight of stone steps leading to the Castle Bar. They reached the door, and that was as far as some ever got. There were two guards there: cute girls in orange and blue doublets, one blonde, the other brunette. They snapped to attention at the appearance of each new guest. 

Once past the guards, there was a choice: right, the Grand Ballroom; left, the Castle itself. We chose the Castle first, the place that named the club. 

Den, Cave, Cavern 

There it was, a den, a cave, a cavern. The soft couches and easy chairs are placed in shadows along the walls and in recesses where a visitor can toy with the animal feeling of being in a private lair. Not so, however, at the big 'J' shaped bar. Too many people vied for the swivel seats. But there are 'decorations': three tipsy-looking ghosts peering from a balcony, a gleaming-eyed spider clinging to a web that covers the ceiling, a flame-licked red devil. That devil! It made people flinch every time they ordered another drink. 

A speaker somewhere in the wall spread soft music throughout the room when French De Grazia's 'Occupators' played in the Ballroom. 

When the music began, we congregated with the rest of the life in the Grand Ballroom. Here, the stress is on 'glamour'. The dominating color is a soft, feminine, cotton candy pink. Immediately inside was one of those florid filigreed food displays. Miniature sandwiches and meal delicacies abounded but were dimmed in the light of the pastries and cakes. Even the nice bit of 'edible' sugar statuary didn't compare with these. The icing seemed to taste like lemon. 

Occupators Were Hot 

The Grand Ballroom is made in a strictly modern scheme. There are some four main rooms, with rich decorations denoting future times. Lighting is indirect, of course. The 'Occupators' looked cute. They were perched up in a sky-blue orchestra nacelle with twinkling silver stars pasted above their heads. The acoustics were fine. Someone asked, "How do you like it up there?" 

"It's hot," was the reply. 

Shortly before 10:30, showtime, French De Grazia began exercising his clarinet with 'The Bee' and selections from the Scheherazade. He had drummed up quite a little interest by the time Foggia's Johnny 'In the Spot' Bowman hopped upon the circular stage to announce the beginning of the floor show. 

It was a better than average Italian show. There was some pleasant dancing, not too laborious, and a few highlights like the little man who looked more like Charlie Chaplin than the great comedian himself did in his last two pictures. A magician with plenty of aplomb produced a few tricks that not anybody could explain. This was unusual. His high spot came when he put a flight officer's head in a midget guillotine. The machine had just severed a cucumber neatly. There was an air of disappointment in the crowd when the flight officer's head didn't drop into the wooden tub. MC Bowman did his bit with Dave Finch. 

Dave did imitations, and in one, Bowman became 'Itchy', a bug-ridden little boy demonstrating the wholesome qualities of 'Septic Scotch'. As he stood on the stage in side bangs and maroon garters, someone said, "Bowman, you're a character." 

The show ended, and then there was a plate of ravioli for everyone. It left a nice taste in our mouths, and we went away that evening feeling kindly toward T/Sgt. Vincens Siano, manager of the Castle Bar.

Static from Your A.E.S. by Ken Eill

First off, we go to C.B., meaning, of course, Charlie Barnet, the Mad Mab of the saxophone. Charlie has gone on for years being one of the most consistently underrated musicians I know of. The guy plays alto and tenor like mad and is one of the very few that can make the soprano saxophone really sound good. Charlie has quite a few unorthodox ideas on how said saxes should be played. Not afraid to try them out, he's always experimenting—trying to get different effects by blending the tones of various instruments or by off tones on the sax. He has always been a great admirer of Ellington and it shows up very often in his music. He uses a lot of Ellington tunes and a great many more Ellington moods, but he doesn't copy lavishly or imitate Ellington, as a great deal of the public seems to believe. Charlie puts his own phrasings into anything he plays, at times so subtly as to be almost unnoticeable unless you're listening really closely. As far as his band goes, Barnet has always had a great one. He's had several, and none of them have ever been bad or even mediocre. He's an amazing organizer and can have a brand new band sounding good in less time than most other bandleaders would allow theirs to be heard. He is also a great discoverer of talent and has always recognized good musicianship and surrounded himself with it.

And to prove it, here are some of the men who have either been discovered by or played with the Mab: Cootie Williams, Howard McGhee, Al Killian, Peanuts Holland, Bobby Burnet, Dizzy Gillespie, Bernie Privin, and many others on trumpet; the wonderful Eddie Bert, Trummy Young, Tommy Peterson, Ford Leary, and more on trombone; Buddy DeFranco and Ray DeGeer played in his reed section; the late Bus Etri, Chubby Jackson, Oscar Pettiford, Chickie Fromm, Cliff Leemans, Bill Miller, Dodo Marmarosa, Ralph Burns were at one time in his rhythm section; Frances Wayne, Gwen Tynes, Lena Horne first sang with Barnet. There are even more great artists than these, but there's no more room. Just one more thing—you'll notice that many of these wonderful musicians are Negro, and it's another thing to the guy's credit that he has courage enough to fight for the music and the way of life he believes in, in that music. So more power to Charlie Barnet and men like him. I wish there were more.

Foggia-Bari Enter MTO Ping Pong

A Foggia-Bari Zone Table Tennis Tournament to be played on the 1st and 2nd of July at the FAAB gymnasium will decide the zone team which will journey to Rome on the 12th of July for the MTO Table Tennis Championships. The Theater Championships will be held at the Rome Rest Center, and each of the four zones of Italy will be represented by a team of twelve contestants. Zuccaroni Takes Unpopular Decision In Fortress Card

June 10 — In spite of a cut forehead that caused blood to stream down the side of his face and obscure his vision, Zoupa Zuccaroni outpunched the shifty, steady jabbing Vincenzo Affatato tonight at the Fortress Club to take a booed decision in the feature match of the eight-bout boxing card.

Affatato won the sympathy of the fans with his fast footwork and agile maneuvering, and early in the second round, he opened a cut above Zuccaroni's eye with a sharp left jab. Zuccaroni outpunched his opponent throughout the round but was unable to land a knockout blow. Zuccaroni weighed in at 170; Affatato at 168. Both fighters are from Foggia.

Refuses Shake

In the semi-final match, Nick Tamalio, a San Severo slugger who lost a close decision last week, decisioned Russo Vincente of Foggia in another unpopular ruling that had the fans howling. After the fight, Vincente refused to shake Tamalio's hand, claiming that the decision should have been his. He climbed out of the ring and raised his hands over his head in the accustomed sign of victory, receiving the plaudits of the crowd. Matchmakers are attempting to arrange a return grudge fight.

Reds Take Third In Row June 9 -- Displaying a powerful hitting attack along with "Smokey" Joe Bagacki's three-hit pitching, the 803rd Red swamped a hapless 345th Ranger nine, 14-4 this afternoon at the Foggia Stadium. Bogacki was rarely in trouble as he struck out nine of the thirty-one hitters that faced him. His fine pitching was obscured by the fact that his teammates pounded two Ranger pitchers at random. Twelve of the Red tallies came in the third, fourth, and fifth innings. Twenty-five batters paraded to the plate in these three stanzas as they garnered all but two of their runs and ten of their thirteen hits. Ranger Defense Weak The Rangers were as futile on the defense as they were on the offense. Committing eight costly errors at critical times cost them nine runs. Tom McCorkell, Red third sacker, came within inches of the only home run of the day when he drove a hard smash down the left field line. Umpire Warehime ruled the drive to be a foul ball, and McCorkell returned to the plate. He subsequently drew a walk. Ray Moore and Don Wilmont, Red sluggers, accounted for eight runs batted in with a double and a single apiece. In the fifth inning Bogacki showed the fans his stuff as he retired three straight batters on strikeouts. The win marked the third straight for the MPs and the second loss in a row for the Rangers.

ZUCCARONE TAKES ONE IN STOMACH Vic Affatata pushes a hard one into Tony Zuccarone's midsection in the third round of their featured five-round bout in the regular Monday evening boxing card at the Officers Club. Zuccarone took the punishment and went on to a victory by decision.

Sport Shots By the Sports Staff

As American League play goes on, it looks as though Mike Demato will continue to show himself as the finest ball player on the local hardball lots. Mike not only is the league-leading Barons' pilot, but has put in some sterling pitching performances as well as being one of the league-leading batsmen. On the mound, Demato has struck out twenty-three men in nineteen innings of pitching and has allowed twelve hits. At the plate, the laconic Barons' mentor is hitting a hot .545, with four doubles and three home runs on his batting string.

John Russel of the FAAB Gymnasium just let us know that from this time on all ball games in the Foggia Leagues will begin at the scheduled times, and that forfeitures of games will be imposed against teams that show up late. This means that the ball clubs will have to get to the Stadium at least a half hour before game time if they expect to get in that pre-game workout.

Probably the team that needs the workout most is the 779 Rebels, who have at this writing dropped five games in a row. Tabbed before the season (by this red-faced columnist, for one) as a favorite, the Rebels got off to a good start in the Spring season and whipped all comers. In the inaugural league play, the Rebels began in fine style by taking the first two games as expected. Then they unexpectedly dropped from first to eighth place in the standings as a result of five straight setbacks.

When the Softball season opened this past Monday, Foggia at last got its two major leagues working, and the competition for the National and American League pennants will be keen. In the American League, Security has shown the smoothest playing and the best hitting in the loop. However, the loss of Austinson, their flashy third baseman who was hitting .692 when he left for the Stateside circuits, might make a difference in the pinches. The 955 Sparkplugs, who are making it a hot race in the American loop, have exhibited good pitching and team play, but their hitting has been constantly on the weak side. Red Cooke, hard-hitting manager of the Sparkplugs, has been in a slump, and in the first four contests was batting a pallid .272.

In the two-month softball race, Foggia ball fans expect a lot of surprises. Most of the teams are untested, and little is known about their prowess. From what we gather, the 955 Turbos should be the team to beat. Their big worries, the 1585 Eagles, have been riddled by redeployment and of the starting lineup, only three remain. Fireballer Johnny Tothe and his battery mate, Jim Potzner, have both left the Eagles' team with bigger plans. Now the Turbos are wondering about the two 529 teams. In spring practice, Johnny Smarelli's 529 club upset them three times.

The opening of the track season brought to our attention some of the flashy equipment Special Services has gathered together for Foggia's harriers. Aside from the uniforms and spikes that are prerequisite to any track team, there is some good weight equipment and an aluminum pole for the pole vaulting event. We're wondering if anyone on the local scene can break a two-minute half mile or a four and a half minute mile.

Sparks Lead League After Crucial Week, June 14 — The 955 Sparkplugs were the hottest team in the league this past week as they took the league lead by trouncing the 779 Rebels and the Security Barons. 27 Wives Leave; ARC Service Ending

Twenty-seven wives of soldiers in the Foggia-Bari area left Wednesday morning for the June 29th sailing of the Vulcania from Naples. This makes a total of approximately 300 wives to have left Foggia in the past year, according to Miss Helen Andren of ARC Family Service, and constitutes the next to the last shipment from this area.

"ARC Family Service in Foggia and Bari," said Miss Andren, "will end in the middle of next month with one more shipment of wives. After that time, wives en route to the States will be processed by the Army and will leave from Naples in small units of ten or twenty."

(Miss Andren added Friday that 15 wives will leave Foggia on June 29th to sail on the SS Bari from Naples.)

"Black, Brown, and Beige" Played on AES The Duke Ellington work, "Black, Brown, and Beige," was played over AES Foggia last Thursday as the main part of an all-Ellington program. The six movements of Black, Brown, and Beige, with interpretations by Ken Eill narrated by Dave Fenton, were described as "a tone parallel of the negro's life in America from the days of his slavery until he gained his freedom through the Emancipation Proclamation." Aside from Ellington's great experiment in serious composing, Eill's program introduced six of the Duke's popular recordings and a poem by William Blake.

130 Surplus Officers Leave In Year's Largest Shipment

The bulk of Foggia Army Air Base's surplus officers, approximately 130 men, started leaving for Leghorn by air Thursday in the largest officer Stateside shipment this year. Ninth Air Force Service Command's sudden call for the redeployment of the officers (with 37 months or more service as of August 31st) was attributed by Colonel Robert Martin, Commanding Officer of FAAB, to "the pressure that has been put on higher headquarters by FAAB for the past months."

Clarifying another redeployment situation, Captain J. W. Harrison, Base Personnel Officer, added, "Enlisted men whose wives left Foggia Wednesday and who are eligible for redeployment will be flown to the port of debarkation as soon as the movement of these officers is completed."

9th Service Level

Officer redeployment rates here are now at the same level as those in Ninth Service Command Headquarters, and there are only approximately thirty-three officers left who will be eligible for redeployment, under the present system, by August 31st. Six high-ranking officers, however, are expected to leave before the end of this month because of maximum age requirements as stated in a recent War Department letter.

Although the shipment of surplus officers left few gaps in staff or other key positions, there was a serious loss of flying personnel. "We have only fifty-five flying officers left," said Captain Henry M. Rollins of the S-3 Office, "and only nineteen of these are first pilots. These men will have to do a great deal more flying to keep up the courier runs, and they will have to share the clearance officer and tower officer jobs besides."

Local Items

About two weeks ago, part of the 442nd Infantry Regiment moved into Foggia to give the 1898th Engineers a hand. When we spoke to some of the Nisei boys recently, their biggest question was, "Why in the devil are we infantrymen here in an engineer outfit?" and they left no doubt that they did not like some things here. We spoke at length to some of them, officers and enlisted men, and saw how and where they are living. They have some pretty good gripes, too.

The story goes back to their occupation duty in Leghorn. After one of the finest and cleanest combat records in the European theater, they took their hitch in Leghorn, "which wasn't bad, considering..." They were led to believe that they were going home, but it turned out that only a token force went to the zone of the Interior, and the rest ended up in Foggia.

Valley Forge

In the Dust Bowl, in the midst of the old airfields area (which is affectionately called Valley Forge), the 442nd boys were set up in tents. In all fairness to living in tents in that sandy wasteland, we have to say that it is no worse than conditions combat troops endured out there during the war. But the war is over, and while the 442nd never shied away from combat, they can see little reason for living like that now. They look at the sweet condition of the troops living in town: clean and comfortable rooms, good plumbing, clean mess halls, plenty of nightclubs and theaters, and good access to the ARC. Then they see their own quarters: tents, hot and barely furnished, with five men sharing one tent. Drinking and washing water comes from the mess hall or the latrine. Their supply room, where they are to draw clean sheets, is a weak-looking shack with plenty of holes for ventilation and dirt, and the floor is a dusty mass of white chalk that makes it impossible to keep fresh sheets clean.

Mess Too Small

One of their officers, pointing to the condition of the small mess, said, "The place is too little for feeding over 150 men, and the POWs eat there too. It is impossible to keep clean, and I'm worried about dysentery starting. I tried to build a new mess hall, but I was refused materials and laborers. One reason is that they don't want any permanent building." He went on to explain that lumber for other projects was "on requisition," but not available yet. The men have built themselves a fine club, and they wait to be able to work on their tents, but they have not been able to. Said one of the boys, "The German POWs on the field have modern conveniences, running water and all. I saw a Special Service radio in one of those tents, and when I took it away, they made me return it. Special Service refused to give me a radio, however." PBS Special Service has not authorized FAAB to give them equipment.

18 to 24 Months

442nd men claim to be sticklers for organization, and as they laugh at the way things are being run, they point out another fallacy that no one seems to notice. "All our boys," said a sergeant, "are in the 18 to 24-month category. Now they're taking riflemen and training them to be desk clerks and interior pool attendants. By the time they are trained in these new jobs, they'll go home and we'll have to start all over again."

All of the discontent explains some of the flare-ups that have occurred in town, surprising in view of their spotless conduct record in Italy. A few civilians, surprised to see boys of oriental descent, have passed some pretty nasty remarks on the spur of the moment. The boys, who take a fierce pride in their Americanism, have tried whipping a few of the hecklers.

We've called too many outfits Lost Battalions to tag the 442nd with that, but the Front Office would do well to look out their way once in a while.

Ice

Our pipes gleaming with hoar frost in the interior of Foggia's ice plant prove that the place is operating if the whirring of the electric motor and the swish-flap of the spinning fly-wheel belt leave any doubt. When we visited the factory this week, we entered gingerly, sniffing at the air for ammonia fumes. When we had come three months before, we were wet-eyed and choking after five minutes inside.

Big Repair Job

"We cleaned every valve and tightened every gasket," said Cpl. Alvin Lanier, the man who has been in charge of the ice plant for four months and who has been repairing it for most of the last three. When he started the repairs, almost everything was broken down. The electric engine and compressor were worn out; half of the parts had to be discarded. The ice cans leaked. The eight-inch, fifty-foot-long driving belts were cracked and almost useless. Now, everything is fixed but the belts. These are simply spliced every time there is a break.

"One snapped into three pieces Sunday," said Cpl. Lanier, "and broke seven times in the week prior to that. Listen to the splice wallop every time it goes around," he said illustrating.

Simple Process

The ice-making equipment is fairly simple and neatly centered in the little plant. In the middle of the room is the ammonia compressor, a large horizontal cylinder with the nine-foot flywheel some twenty feet away. On each side of the room is a freezing vat. Ammonia is fed into the cylinder, compressed, and led through pipes to the vats. These are the pipes that grow white with frost when the machine operates. At the vats, the ammonia expands and cools, going into a labyrinth of smaller pipes which are immersed in the salt water of the vats. The salt water is cooled and circulates around the cans of fresh water which turns to ice. Then the ammonia returns to the compressor and begins the cycle again. The capacity is over 12 thousand pounds at one time at present, although this isn't the maximum capacity when everything is operating normally.

Every Thirty Hours

"Some of the cans still leak, and we haven't got enough RPMs. We ought to be able to turn out a batch every twenty-four hours, but the best we can do right now is one every thirty." The ice goes to mess halls all over Foggia for storage purposes. It doesn't go into drinks, however.

"The medics declared it inedible," said Lanier, showing us the storeroom. He indicated the stacks of sixty-pound blocks. "It looks clean," he said, "but you know you can't judge anything by that. The medics said it's inedible, so I guess it is."

Justice

We were walking home from the office pretty late one night this week, and as we rounded the corner near the Red Cross, we saw a large civilian truck and trailer halted in front of the MP station. The MP's objection was that the truck was going the wrong way on a one-way street. Although the driver objected that the only one-way sign had been pointing the other way, he was made to back his truck and trailer up the main street.

Three blocks further on, we saw—as we had seen often before—a couple of drunken soldiers staggering down the street, making passes at every civilian who got near them. But here there were no MPs. We suggest that the MPs step out of their station more often at night.

Merger: Unofficial reports from Washington take a dim view of the possibility of an Army-Navy-Air Force merger in the near future. Hottest objections have been coming from influential Naval personnel, whose chief objection has recently been 'the independence of the Air Force on a merger agreement. Secretary of War Patterson has been insisting on a true merger, while Secretary of the Navy Forrestal would concede only to a Minister of Common Defense with vague powers to "co-ordinate" the effort of the War and Navy Departments. Washington reporters state that the merger bill cannot be passed through the divided Congress while the chairmen of the House and Senate Naval Affairs Committees put the spikes into all bills on the subject. If a bill passes at all, they predict, it will be on the Navy's watery concession.

ANS

Business: Advice to veterans planning to start small businesses is given in a new book by Sidney Margolius, "A Fresh Start." The ex-GI, who is an expert in his field, says that two main factors in the failure of small businesses are (1) lack of adequate financing and (2) lack of technical knowledge. The big question is not how much it costs to go into business, but "how much does it take to stay there". Funds are needed not only to buy property and equipment but to pay the overhead and promotion costs while a trade is being built up. Says the author, the 3,000 and 5,000 dollars of which many ex-GIs speak when planning businesses are barely enough to cover initial operating funds of most businesses. As an example, the author gives several typical minimum investments (all in dollars): Restaurants, 300 per seat; Clothing Shops, 5,000 to 8,500; Hardware Stores, 6,000; Furniture Store, 8,000 to 12,000; Drug Stores (with fountains) 7,500; Food Markets, 5,000 to 12,000; Cleaning-Pressing, 3,000 to 5,000; Filling Stations (leased) 2,500 to 6,000. One important financial aid under the GI Bill provides self-employed veterans who are not earning 100 dollars monthly the difference between that and what they are earning (for up to 52 weeks).

Employment: The Supreme Court ruled that the Selective Service Act does not confer superseniority on veterans over non-veterans who held jobs while the vets were away. Justice William O. Douglas ruled that the veteran had the same status he would have held if he had not been drafted (time in service counting as time on the job), but that he could not claim greater seniority than a man who had been on the job a longer time than the vet's employment time plus his service time.
