EDUCATION

The following institutions have been approved by the Veterans Administration for study under the GI Bill of Rights, according to the American Embassy in Rome, Italy: Universities of Bari, Bologna, Catania, Firenze, Genova, Milano, Napoli, Padova, Palermo, Parma, Pavia, Perugia, Pisa, Roma, Siena, Torino, Trieste, and the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore di Milano.

Academies of Fine Arts of Torino, Bologna, Florence, Milano, Roma, Venezia. Conservatories of Music of Milan, Turin, Florence, Naples, Rome, and the American Academy at Rome.

The following are partial lists of institutions of other foreign countries approved by the Veterans Administration:

Switzerland: Federal Institute of Technology at Zurich. Universities of Basel, Bern, Zurich, Fribourg, Geneva, Lausanne, and Neuchatel.

France: The National Conservatory of Music at Paris, the National School of Fine Arts at Paris, and the American School of Art at Fontainebleau.

Czechoslovakia: The School of Fine Arts at Prague.

Service men or veterans desiring to enroll in a foreign institution (whether it's listed above or not) should request complete information from the Veterans Administration, Washington 25, D.C. as to whether it is an approved school. Men desiring entry in approved organizations must make all arrangements directly with the school, and must arrange with the State Department for necessary visas and passports.

The student is entitled to the same benefits granted men studying in American schools, but the Veterans Administration will not pay any additional costs, such as travel expenses. For further information see the Information and Education Officer of FAAB or write to the Veterans Administration, Washington, 25, D.C.

ITALY

Umberto II left Italy last week, and in spite of his charges of fraud in the elections and his hints that he had not given up hope of regaining the throne, Italy remained quiet. The Italian Supreme Court announced a Republican victory by nearly 2,000,000 votes, and Premier De Gasperi broadcast to the nation his shame in "the tragedy of that man" Umberto "as part of the national catastrophe," and asked the nation for unity.

UNRRA announced its plan for Italy in the second half of 1946. According to Harlan Stone, vice president of UNRRA in Italy, they will try to meet a schedule of 750,000 tons of wheat, 700,000 tons of coal monthly, and gasoline costing 18 million dollars. He bemoaned the fact that the world price of grain has climbed from 71 to 90 dollars a ton, and that the Italian Government, which is paying for all that, will have to make up the deficit in exports. Mr. Stone also assured the Italians that he was attempting to speed shipments of sugar, dry legumes, fish, evaporated milk, fertilizer, and insecticides. In addition, he said, Allied military material in Italy will be available for the purchase of the Italian Government. F. H. La Guardia, new Director General of UNRRA, will be at a Paris conference in August, and he is planning to visit Rome, "if possible."

Constituent Assembly members, the men who will draft Italy's new constitution, lined up as follows after the final votes were tabulated: extreme left — Communists and Socialists: 125 seats, moderate left — Socialists, Actionists, and Democratic Christians: 160, center — Democratic Union and Uomo Qualunque: 80.

Lucera had a courthouse fire last week when a man, Angelo Pavone, on a charge of theft, was bribed by other people under indictment to burn the records. He was paid one hundred thousand lire to destroy the evidence, and after Italian and American military firefighters extinguished the blaze, damage was estimated at three million lire.

Fiorello H. LaGuardia, former mayor of New York City and UNRRA chief, expects to be in Paris two months hence, and the director of the Italian mission, Harlan Stone, says that LaGuardia will try to visit Rome. (See UNRRA above)

CARTOON DIVIDEND AND FAREWELL TO LACE

One of the saddest jobs in the Army is saying goodbye to old friends, and this week we say it to Miss Lace, that bosom buddy of GIs throughout the war years. Her creator, Milton Caniff (a civilian during the war because he was too old for service) who gave his all for the little guy, decided to accept his ruptured duck, and along with him went Lace. Above you see how she took her farewell, quiet and humble as always, and the big spread is a couple of her favorite poses for the boys over here. We wish her all the best, and (to anyone else who leaves this place) we hope she doesn't have to come back again.

Dreams are made of fluffy stuff like light meringue and misty moonbeams. They are woven with spider silk, soft and shining, and colored iridescently from the sparkling fountains of fine spray; as fragile as a fairy's wings or a flower in May. Dreams are fond memories of forgotten days; they are flitting fantasies of the present and hopes and fears of the future. They are mirages of life, fitfully fleeting and reappearing. Dreams are the courageous deeds of cowards, the luxury of the impoverished, the happiness of the wretched, and the fairy princess of youth's first love. Dreams are the achievements of the great; the Psyche of the Poet, the vision of the Saint, and the audacity of conquerors. Dreams are the castles in the air that suddenly disintegrate, and the sculptures on the sands that silently slide to the sea. They are the languid longings of loneliness and lust of love-starved youth. Yes, dreams are made of fluffy stuff. They almost are and are no more and, having vanished, are forever lost. "Oh! I'll bet I know what you're wishing!" "Haven't I seen you somewhere before?" Sanford Golding

Static From Your AES by Ken Eill

Greetings (what again) this time to our new C.O., Captain Stewart G. Scull, of Philadelphia. Captain Scull has had quite an army career, spending about seven and a half years in the army since his first enlistment in 1931. As a civilian (yes, he remembers) he was a commercial artist and a sheet metal draftsman, leaving the Navy Yard in 1942 to come back in the army to serve with the 19th Tactical Air Command with General Patton's Third Army, and the 29th Tactical Air Command with General Simpson's 9th Army, as a combat intelligence officer. He was one of the people that really knew what was getting on.

Four Times Over

The Captain wears the bronze star, the A.T.O. ribbon, the E.T.O. ribbon with six battle stars, the Occupation ribbon, the Victory medal, and the Belgium fourragère and two citations awarded to him for the Battle of the Bulge. He also participated in the air invasion of Europe and the Normandy campaign. Captain Scull has been overseas four times. He's been to Hawaii, Panama, and this is his second trip to Europe. Altogether, he has spent twenty-two months overseas. Quite a record.

From C.O. to C.V., standing for the new star award winner for tenor saxophone, Charlie Ventura. Charlie, as far as I know, is still with the Gene Krupa band but has been talking about forming his own outfit. The guy has a wonderfully frantic, wild raspy style, jumping around the upper register quite a bit. He seems to be able to do just about everything he wants to with the horn from great section work to inspired, brilliant solo work both on fast or slow stuff. He doesn't need to copy anyone, as he has a very fine style of his own.

Trying To Copy

There is a little of Gillespie in his work but a lot more of Ventura, and there are a lot of young tenor men who are trying vainly to get that Ventura in their own horns. Charlie is fine both in big band stuff or small band work. His fine work with the Krupa Trio continually amazes everyone. Without a doubt, he is a musician to watch. His amazing speed, technique, and ideas make him one of the outstanding musicians of the day. A comparative newcomer to the music business, Ventura is already a capable and natural musician. If he ever steps out with his own group, there's going to be a lot more good jazz music to be heard. So hats off to Charlie Ventura and let's hear more of him.

Another guy you're going to hear more of is David Fenton, one of our announcers, who has already taken over such favorites as the Make Believe Ballroom, every afternoon at 4:30, and Reflections In Music every Saturday evening from 9:30 to 10:00. So keep listening for two newcomers to their trade, and they're both good too: Charlie Ventura, tenor sax; David Fenton, announcer.

That's all for this week, gang. See you next.

New Currency Control, QM Books To Be Issued Soon USFET Attempts To Nip Black Markets By Tightening Up On Transmitted Funds

June 28 — Two new finance developments were to be put into effect in Foggia Army Air Base within the next two weeks. The first, according to a USFET circular 82, announced a new Currency Control Book that would impose stricter controls on the transmission of funds to the States and would make deductions for purchases made in government stores. The second, concerning dependents of men stationed here, was the announcement of the proposed opening of the Quartermaster Sales Store (commissary) in the Foggia area early next month.

Few Changes The new Currency Control Books are expected to be issued to FAAB personnel before the middle of July. Chief changes from the old book will be that it is now designed to be a permanent "bank book" and that purchases made in government theaters, post exchanges, commissaries, and clothing stores of five dollars or more will be entered in the book. Men with dependents will not be issued additional books, and the entry of money will only be made to the nearest dollar. Large scale black market operations in Germany were suggested by finance officials here as the main reason behind the change. Entries of the number of the book owned by each man will be made on his AGO 66-2, and spot checks will be ordered regularly to ascertain if a man is using his properly issued book when transmitting funds.

Sales Books "The new QM Sales Books will be available to all US military or civilian personnel who get the approval of the Commanding Officer," said Lt. Joseph Metzler, FAAB Finance Officer. "Rationing of purchases made," he said, "will be as strict as they..." (See QM Sales, Page 4)

Red Cross Combines Clubs and Cuts Snack Bar Hours

June 27 — The American Red Cross Clubs in town combined this week on an officer-enlisted men basis, and at the same time the new club was preparing to comply with a Rome order to close the Snack Bar, except on special occasions.

Closed On Orders

Foggia's 'Uncle Joe' Hamilton, ARC Director, will close the refreshment counter on orders from ARC Headquarters in Rome, which cited the "general world food shortages and greatly reduced appropriated funds" as the reason for the closure. However, an open letter to local ARC directors from Washington in May had hinted at a cut in food dispensing since the Army, which is now paying for civilian labor in Red Cross clubs, is attempting to nip expenses. The local Theater command, in turn, had refused to pay the wages of snack bar employees.

In spite of Mr. Hamilton's persistent efforts in the past month to change the snack bar ruling for the Foggia area, the cut will go into effect. Local military personnel were taking a pessimistic view of the end of this incentive to visit the ARC, and Mr. Hamilton quoted a Military Police officer as predicting that drunkenness in the Foggia area would rise 10%.

Ceremony Saturday

The Red Cross people were planning to make an ironic ceremony of the snack bar closing Saturday night when they will hold a mock Irish Wake. At nine PM Saturday, the Christiana Maria Band is to march through the streets to the Red Cross Club playing Chopin's funeral march and carrying a coffin marked "Old Man Snack Bar."

Last of Austrian POWs Leave On July 3rd, 1946, according to orders received early in June, 118 Austrian POWs will leave the 55th Station Hospital, going by train on the first leg of a long-awaited return to their homes in Austria. Stationed at the hospital since October 1945, they have proven their efficiency and capability in the various duties assigned to them. Maintaining their own hospital with two of their own doctors, they also worked in the American hospital as ward boys, mess attendants, cooks, and in various other capacities. Originally a company of 220 men, half of them left Foggia, homeward bound, five months ago.

LOCAL ITEMS Executive title of the longest titles we've discovered in Foggia is attached to Pfc. (S/Sgt.) Ben D. James: "Medical Administrative Non-Commissioned Officer In Charge." Remarked a Medical Technician: "He just sits there and shuffles the papers like a deck of cards."

Befanatrofio

Around Easter time, the 55th Station Hospital "adopted" the Befanatrofio Orphanage in Manfredonia. The orphanage is more accurately a foundling home (the only one in the area since Foggia's was bombed out), housing children from two weeks to fourteen years, many of whom are illegitimate children of American fathers. "We chose to adopt this orphanage in particular," said Elizabeth Thornton, ARC Director at the hospital, "because we felt a responsibility for these babies whose American fathers had deserted them."

Some of the staff of the 55th visited Befanatrofio during Easter, and they reported on the situation of the children. "Conditions are truly tragic," said Miss Thornton. "Some of the babies are just pale, pasty-looking things, and they just lie there. They have come from various sources - many of them were brought in by people who found them in the fields or by the shore, where their mothers had deserted them. Some had been lying unattended for days. There were a few who would not live." During Easter, the staff of the 55th Station Hospital donated approximately 448 dollars to Befanatrofio.

EM Give 15,000

Chaplain Myles McGowan had originally requested the 55th to help the home, and after Easter he asked them to take it as a permanent benefice. Thus, the staff of the hospital made the home's charity their responsibility. The enlisted men's club at the 55th donated 15,000 lire immediately, and the doctors, nurses, and other officers added 10,000 lire more. Two of the doctors wrote home about the state of the orphanage, and their wives contacted pharmaceutical companies. Lt. Elrie Rodgers' wife got answers from many, and she mailed him 1500 cc's of vitamin A and D concentrate (enough to feed 100 children for three months) from the Walker Vitamin Products Company. E. R. Squibb and Son promised to send many forms of vitamins and minerals, and Mead Johnson and Company sent an eight-ounce bottle of Cod Liver Oil.

Other donations have come in. Chaplain McGowan's collection box at church services has gathered thousands of lire for Befanatrofio. The Fortress club decided to donate all the money thrown into the ring during the weekly boxing matches at the club (amounting to between 5,000 and 10,000 lire), and the boxers will be paid directly by the club instead. Men who have been going home have left a great deal of food and clothing, and some have even given money for the home.

Progress Made

Since Easter, Befanatrofio numbers have grown from 157 to 174 children. Says Miss Thornton, "People who visit the home now for the first time are shocked at the sight of such poverty in children, but now that I've seen some of the children grow, I can tell of the progress made in some of them. Those tiny starving things have grown, and although they are still pale and small, they sit up now and play around a bit."

Handle

"You have to roll your tongue to pronounce his name," Cpl. Robert Worthen explained when he demonstrated, through the rigid calisthenics on his vocal cords, the name of Cpl. Uville Ogle.

Humanity

The Geneva Convention occupied the busy medics at the Base Dispensary during the last few days, and such a diversion of interest prompted us to pay them a call to satisfy our curiosity. Thrusting a hypodermic needle with a sweeping curve into his victim's arm, Cpl. Freeman Wilmer, Medical Technician, greeted us, "I'll be with you in a minute." We snapped our eyes back into their sockets and entertained our attention to the umpteen V.D. posters that decorated the walls of the Dispensary. A rather sinister smile came from Cpl. Wilmer as he advanced towards us, weapon in hand, "Sweating it out I see, well you should have thought it over before."

Breaking Glasses

We explained our presence and managed to hold off this aspiring Medical Doctor before he had the opportunity to practice on us. The Corporal retreated to his desk, picked up a couple of small glass containers, and began the process of destruction, using a pair of scissors for a hammer. We wasted no time and made a quick departure.

As we stepped into the waiting room, Pfc. Ed Booth, Assistant Base Sanitation Inspector, with that grin (after effects of extreme indulgence in that potent stuff) shouted, "The Geneva Convention stated so." We knew then that our man was found.

Ed Booth, one of the remaining Pfc's on the Base, recognized us. Perhaps it was our magnetic personality that convinced him to inform us about the drastic measures certain people have taken in violating the Geneva Convention according to the Medic's claim. 

Guard Duty

Ed poured his lamentations on us, and with him were his fellow Angels of Mercy. An injustice was done to them, so they claimed when they were notified to stand guard duty at the Headquarters and Base Squadron gate. The Medics felt that they were not called for extracurricular activity of such a nature where firearms were involved.

These ex-gunners and mechanics, now attached to the Base Dispensary, received approximately a hundred and ten hours of basic instructions in the Medical Department from Lt. Frank Crider, Assistant Base Surgeon. The boys are proud and happy in this new venture of theirs in Medicine, be it Sanitation, Malaria Control, First Aid, or Pro Stations.

We learned to our amusement what the Geneva Convention was all about, as far as the Medics were concerned.

Allergic 71. T C Allergic To Combat, was what Corporal Foster Kelley told us in reference to the outfit he was attached to for twenty-three months in Africa. He was with a crash crew on the line, and we wondered if the corporal treated any of those casualties resulting from air mishaps. "All we got out were either dead or all right," Kelley stated.

A GI Returns

We said hello to a guy in a neat civilian suit with a Ruptured Duck in his buttonhole. McConnell Staley had come back to Foggia to marry Miss Margaretta Tizzano. Mac had come to Foggia originally in February 1944 with the 31st Depot Supply and was stationed at Foggia Main airfield. He met Margaretta later that year, and although he wanted to get married soon after, the future father-in-law objected on the grounds that the war was still on and he did not want his daughter to end up a widow. STATESIDE  
Washington: Secretary of War Robert Patterson approved nine out of 14 recommendations by the Doolittle "Gripe" Board. Among those are 1) Equitable distribution of allowances for officers and enlisted personnel for food, clothing, quarters, and travel pay. 2) Enlisted men will be able to accumulate leave or furlough time and will receive terminal leave. 3) The hand salute will be abandoned outside Army Posts except in specific conditions. 4) Promotion sheets will be completely reviewed.

Aviation: One of the newest Army bombers to have some of the hood of secrecy removed is Northrop's XB-35, "the flying wing." Shaped like a huge boomerang with no fuselage or exposed engine nacelles, the plane spans 172 feet (span of a B-17 is 104 feet); the crew, engines, fuel, and armament are housed inside the wing. From a center width of 37 feet and 10 inches, the wing tapers to a mere 1 foot and 4 inches, and the empty weight of the plane is 89,000 pounds. It can carry from 73,000 to 120,000 pounds of useful load. The Army Air Forces has ordered 15 of the huge wings, the first of which will cost 13,000,000 dollars to build. The first ones will have pusher-type gasoline engines, but it is expected that later models will be jet-propelled.

Boxing: Joe Louis beat Billy Conn Thursday night to retain his championship of heavyweight boxing. The win occurred in the eighth round, and Conn was knocked completely unconscious. The fight may have been dull, but the after-effects were noisy enough. Representative Donald O'Toole (D., NY) demanded that the purses be held up until the fight, which he called a "stinkeroo," be investigated. He wanted an investigation of the arrangements made between Promoter Mike Jacobs and the fighters, the splitting of the purses, and the existence of any debts of the fighters to Jacobs. Assistant US Attorney General Wendell Berge said that the Justice Department would look into Jacobs, boxing, and baseball. Then a spokesman for the Justice Department denied it. According to O'Toole, Jacobs said, "O'Toole was trying to shake me down for fight tickets." And on the strength of that remark, O'Toole is attempting to sue Jacobs for 100,000 dollars.

Jobs: According to Sidney Hillman's Amalgamated Clothing Workers, CIO, there is room for more than 100,000 returning servicemen in the clothing industry. A recent program was inaugurated by the union to train and absorb into the needle trades these vets who had never held jobs before, including many with amputations and major disabilities. A New York specialty store head says that better apparel supply cannot improve materially until more men go into the needle trades field. In some factories, he points out, the workers' average age is as high as 60 because for several years few skilled hands have entered the field during the war. Shortages became more acute.

Housing: President Truman recently signed the emergency housing bill, intended to provide 2,700,000 homes for veterans in two years through private construction. The "heart" of the program provides 400,000,000 dollars for subsidies to spur production of bottleneck materials.

POWER FORE AND AFT XP-81, one of the hottest of the Army's new fighters, is shown diagrammatically above. Built by Consolidated Vultee, it is the first plane ever to fly with a gas turbine engine designed for propeller drive. Powered by a General Electric gas turbine engine in the nose and a jet engine in the tail, the trim fighter will fly at a speed of more than 500 mph.

"I Love The People! The Assistant American Town Major is Foggia's own Poet Laureate. Lt. Fiorentino A. De Marzo spoke with us for a while after he deposited another poem on our desk; and as he spoke he seemed to be speaking as the American historian of the people of Foggia—and all humanity.

"Nature does not appeal to me as much as human beings do," he said. "I love to watch people and write about people, and I try to describe what I see in humanity. And there is a tint of pessimism in my work."

His work, with its pessimism and with its beauty, has been popular. It might be explained in one respect that he not only writes in English of the people of Italy, but he writes in Italian as well. Some of his works have been published in Italian language magazines in the States.

Jet of Feelings "Poetry is a jet of feelings," he went on. "I write free verse because I think that one sacrifices meaning for rhyme."

Fiorentino De Marzo's experience shows why he knows the Italian people. He lived nineteen years in Italy; then he taught Italian (and French) in America. During the war he came back to this country with the Army to act as an interrogator and censor of POW documents with a section of AFFIQ.

He is a lover of Rooseveltian doctrines and he writes of Freedom:

"The cheer of Freedom from fear is an echo today resounding from our dead heroes, whose sacrifice before the Altar of Humanity whose glorious deeds shall make it live eternally."

From "Freedom from Fear" by Lt. F. A. De Marzo

STRUGGLE

I saw a fight yesterday. Two young lads in rags, in tears, with rage. Their fists, their tender bodies fought with blood and cries that puffed their veins, their eyes. They pushed and hit and scratched and bit at each other as at Hunger, Privation, Destitution: all that is Misery of life. Some men stood by and watched but did not move, for their faces were lowered and their bodies stood still like statues and looked at the little ones in whom they saw the Struggle, the Bitterness of life, bloodless. One pale man, alone, moved his jaw and a shiny tear, resembling a falling star, furrowed his cheek and spread on the ground upon the tumid blood shed by the two little beings in a Foggia alley.

F. A. De Marzo

The Water You Drink

The first of a series of four articles by the Town Major's Office.

Did you know you were drinking water out of the longest aqueduct system in the world? Or that the direction of a mountain stream had been changed in order to get good water here at all? These and other interesting facts came to light recently in discussing the coming water reduction with the Italian water engineers.

Government Subsidized

The Ente Autonomo per l'Acquedotto Pugliese is the government-subsidized company that supplies water not only to Foggia Province but also to the other four provinces of the Puglia Region (Bari, Brindisi, Taranto, and Lecce), with a total population of 2,524,000 (in 1940) distributed in over 300 towns. The water for most of these Pugliesi all comes from the same place: an underground source in the mountains at Caposele, 48 miles south-southwest of Foggia, which provides an excellent brand of H2O at the rate of—take a good breath—from 3 to 6 tons a second. (The way it all happens, why, and how the rate varies is described in an article quoted below.)

Started in 1902

The Acquedotto company first started its activities in 1902, utilizing the more easily harnessed springs. It was not until 1915 that the main source at Caposele was captured—a procedure that involved some smart engineering because the water, while plentiful, was all running out the wrong side of the mountain. Since it would have taken considerable time and effort to turn the mountain around, the engineers decided to cheat nature in another way and made the water come out on the Puglia side of the mountain. Having taken most of nature's trumps with that trick, they went on to a grand slam by piping this vast supply hither and yon through all of Puglia right down to the base of the heel.

But that wasn't easy. From Caposele to Villa Castelli (10 miles east of Taranto), a total of 152 miles of the main had to be laid, branching north and southeast at Venosa (40 miles south-southeast of Foggia). The main trunk from Caposele passes through 99 tunnels, one of which, near Spinazzola, is 12 miles long and 675 feet underground, 93 bridges, and 6 siphons. The next most important line runs northward, passing Foggia about 10 miles west and supplying Foggia's reservoir by means of a smaller branch line. Some U.S. systems carry more water, but none, the Acquedotto says, is as long as that right here in Puglia, which is 1,196 miles long. (Catskill, N.Y. 92 miles; Los Angeles 240 miles; Coolgardie, W. Australia 350 miles).

ITALY THIS WEEK

International Paris Conference saw Italy caught between disagreements in which she had little to say. The Four Powers did not seem likely to resolve their differences in time to give Italy her requests for control of Trieste and no war reparations. Russia has been insisting on Yugoslavian control of the Trieste area and also for payments from the Italian government for war damages: 100,000,000 dollars. The Americans and British are taking the Italian side.

Britain has agreed to credit Italy for expenses of quartering and moving British troops by writing off an equivalent amount from the debt owed by Italy. The agreement was written into the Italian armistice terms.

American officials plan to start negotiations this week to buy fruit from Italy to offset shortages in the States. Liberty ships, fifty in all, will be sold to Italy at a cost of 25,000,000 dollars. An Italian maritime commission is at present touring US shipyards to choose the ships, which will be sold to the Italian government after American shippers had first choice.

National Giuseppe Saragat was proclaimed President of the Constituent Assembly in Rome this week. One of the heads of the Socialist Party and former Italian Ambassador to France, Saragat was elected by an overwhelming majority of 401 out of 466 votes. (Saragat visited Foggia late in May during the political campaign).

The Assembly, consisting of 468 delegates who are to draft Italy's new constitution, opened sessions Tuesday as Vittorio Emanuele Orlando, senior statesman of the group, addressed his colleagues. He appealed for reconstruction and peace all over the country and said that Italy would be unable to accept impossible decisions from the Paris Conference. Twenty women listened to his speech. They were among the newly elected members, sitting in a democratic assembly.

Amnesty was granted to thousands of Italian political prisoners in the first act of the new Council of Ministers. The action granted complete amnesty for political prisoners convicted between the day of Italian Liberation up to June 18 of this year. Death sentences were commuted to life imprisonment and life sentences to 30 years. Many men were released entirely. The act was the first in line to solidify the nation on the eve of a new government.

Food demonstrations were held in Bari and Brindisi Province last week in protest against local authorities for the high prices and the unemployment of ex-soldiers. Local newspapers reported few acts of violence, none serious.

Italian Committee for Supply in Rome has requested UNRRA to increase the bread ration to 250 grams per day. (Now it is 200 grams.) This year the total grain production is expected to be 57 million quintiles, but the number of calories for Italian consumers is still inferior to most European countries. UNRRA has not answered the request yet.

Foggia 50 tons of grain were contributed by farmers to local warehouses (Grani del Popolo) by June 23rd, the Corriere di Foggia reported. The fine results of the first part of the harvest—increased production and good quality grain—has resulted in shipments to Naples and Bari to increase supplies there.

Weather recently—the high temperatures followed by stiff breezes—were described by Professor Redia, a famous Italian meteorologist, as characteristic of June and determined by Atlantic sea currents. Next summer, however, he predicts it will be "scorching."

FAAB employees report good progress in their club. Their own dispensary in Headquarters Building, organized in May by a civilian doctor Rossi, functions for the aid of any of the 1,664 members that need medical aid. A food cooperative has also been set up recently in order to bring food to members at a lower cost than sold at the markets, and the Civilian Mess has proven popular with the employees who like American-style food at a low cost.

The club's entertainment and educational section has been one of its most active with the weekly issue of Il Portavoce, a mimeographed poop sheet on civilian employee affairs, and with the dance committee that puts on weekly affairs, including excursions to the suburbs. Say the directors: "Attendance at the affairs is multiplying geometrically."

An American gun was cited as the weapon that killed a farmer in Foggia this week. The farmer presumably caught a thief trying to steal fruit from his tree, and the thief shot and killed him. Another farmer was killed when he surprised some people trying to steal wheat from his fields.

Dear Editor,

New Swimming Pool To Open Saturday

After a month and a half of hard work chasing down elusive equipment, Foggia's new swimming pool is practically completed and will open Saturday, June 29. Thanks to the efforts of S/Sgt. John Russel, aided by Cpl. Ed Lencowski and Pfc. Skelly, swimming enthusiasts no longer need to make the long trek to Manfredonia to indulge in their favorite sport. Located directly across the street from 803 M.P.'s, five minutes' walk from town, the pool is easily accessible to all and sundry. 

Housed in a building which was severely bombed during the war, the pool was unrecognizable as such when the boys started to work on it. A pile of steel girders and other debris outside of the building is mute testimony of the labor involved in resurrecting the place. A scarcity of necessary materials added to the difficulties of the job.

70 By 35 Feet

Holding approximately 3,000 gallons of water, the pool is 70 feet long, 35 feet wide, and is 10 feet at the deep end, 3 feet at the shallow end. The water is pumped in from the same source the Foggia drinking water comes from, but due to the former sabotage of the chlorinating system, chlorination has to be attended to after the water is in the pool. Water will be changed once a week, probably the latter part of the week to ensure fresh water over the weekend when the biggest crowds are expected.

At the present time, the pool will be open from 10 A.M. until 6 P.M. As soon as nylon netting is obtained for screening to comply with Malaria Control regulations, the hours will be extended to 10 P.M.

Cpl. Lencowski hopes to install a three-meter diving board and possibly have diving exhibitions in the near future. If there are any good divers in the crowd, he'd like to hear from you.

June 24 — Foggia pugilists, under the management of Alfredo Russo, dealt out terrific punishment to the boys from Giovinazzo as they took eight of the nine bouts at the Fortress Club tonight.

The main bout of the evening was a bloody, slugging affair with Sammy Sabotini winning over Kid Caccoco by a technical knockout in the second round. The aggressive Sabotini was slamming hard lefts and rights to Caccoco's face and body when the Giovinazzo boy threw up his arms in a gesture of defeat while the crowd booed him and cheered Sabotini.

Two More Quit

In the seventh and eighth bouts, the fans almost brought the house down with jeering. Zucco Zuccaroni and Rocky Fiore TKO'd Bonserio and Mastrandrea in that order. Foggian Zuccaroni had a slight edge on Bonserio going into the second round when Bonserio folded up and quit. Zuccaroni was proclaimed the victor by a TKO. The circumstances in the eighth bout between Fiore and Mastradrea were a little different. After Mastradrea had floored Fiore with a terrific uppercut to the jaw, he retired to his neutral corner while Fiore was being counted. As Fiore was struggling to one knee, Mastradrea lunged across the ring and battered Fiore with hard lefts and rights. Fiore rallied and made a valiant comeback by standing toe to toe with the Giovinazzo husky and trading punches. Disgustedly, Mastradrea turned his back on Fiore and walked out of the ring. The fight was awarded to Fiore on another TKO. These three bouts had the fans howling and booing the angry Giovinazzo fighters.

More Civilian Employees To Be Fired; Security Sqdn., Officer Mess To Move 700 To 800 Employees To Be Dismissed As Budget Is Slashed

July 5 — Between seven and eight hundred civilian employees of Foggia Army Air Base will be fired early next week, according to Lt. Paul F. Kirby, Civilian Personnel Officer. The cut, which had been anticipated early last month, will leave less than one thousand people employed here and came as a result of a reduced budget for the months of July, August, and September. "FAAB has requested an appropriation of 165 thousand dollars for the next three months," said Lt. Kirby, "15 thousand dollars of which is earmarked for American War Department employees. That leaves 50 thousand dollars per month for other civilian help."

Cutting 30,000 Dollars

"Our present number of employees is 1700, and we paid them 40 thousand dollars during the last pay period (2 weeks). If our present rate of expenditures is maintained, we will be spending 30 thousand dollars over our budget."

The new budget request is an emergency one caused by a mix-up during the transfer of Foggia units from MTOUSA to the 40th Bomb Wing and then to the Ninth Air Force Service Command. In the process of transfer, MTOUSA notified Washington to cancel proposed funds for Foggia, but ETO heads did not take over the request. Although the 40th Bomb Wing, when notified of the error, began emergency measures for Foggia funds, Ninth Air Force did not continue them.

Security Moving To 529th Area

July 3 — Colonel Robert K. Martin, Commanding Officer of Foggia Army Air Base, announced today two scheduled changes in FAAB organization that were brought about in part by the reduction of civilian employees to take place early next week. Security Squadron, the Colonel said, will be moved into the 529th Headquarters area, and the Officers' Mess will leave the Fortress Club and move into the smaller Castle Bar Building.

The date of Security's move was not yet announced, but according to Tech-Sergeant Vincent Siano, the Officers' Mess should move before July 9th. The new mess, formerly used by 529th Headquarters and Staff officers the first part of the year, has been completely redecorated by Sgt. Siano's men. When the Fortress Club leaves the building, the enlisted men's club, The Embassy, will open under the management of Sergeant Ed Cahill and Pfc. Robert Moeller of the 955th Squadron. The club, said the Colonel, will be open to all enlisted men and their guests, since new regulations forbid women to enter 779th AMS and 955th AES clubrooms in the Squadron areas.

Major Berg Receives RA Nomination

Major William W. Berg, Executive Officer of Foggia Army Air Base, was included in the list of those nominated for appointment to the Regular Army by President Truman last Friday. Major Berg is the only officer in the Foggia area to receive the nomination, one of thirty-eight in the Mediterranean Theater.

Major Berg served first as an enlisted man with the 11th Infantry at Fort Benjamin Harrison, Indiana, from 1936 until 1939. After two years as a civilian, he re-enlisted in January 1942, and in March 1943, with the rating of M/Sgt, he was sent to the Adjutant General OCS. After graduating in June, Lieutenant Berg was assigned to the newly activated 455th Bomb Group at Fort Washington, Maryland, and five months later he was transferred, with the 455th, to the Mediterranean Theater. Stationed at Cerignola for 18 months, the major has been in Foggia for the past year.

Food Campaign Starts in FAAB

The critical food shortage prevalent throughout the world inaugurated an intensive drive on food conservation in the Foggia area this week. All mess sergeants have been instructed to institute a program for the elimination of waste, and every effort is being made to save food for the starving people of the world.

In order to give an incentive to individuals to increase their efforts, competitive actions will be taken to credit those messes which have achieved success and to bring failures to the attention of those messes which have failed in developing the spirit of this program.

Comparison Of Rations

The general scheme for organizing this competition will be to have all messes compute the monetary value of rations authorized in comparison to those consumed. Mess sergeants at the squadron mess hall were interviewed on the effect this drive would have in changing the quantities and qualities of food.

T/Sgt. Vince Ciano, Officers Mess: "In regulating the amount..."

EM Fathers, Men With 20 Months To Be Home September

The following cable on redeployment procedures from the Adjutant General, War Department was published by FAAB this week:

"Effective immediately, the following will govern demobilization of the Army. a) All volunteer enlisted fathers, regardless of length of service, will be separated from the service by 30 September 1946. b) All enlisted men, except volunteers, with 20 months service as of 30 September 1946 will be separated from the Army by that date. c) Beginning 1 October 1946, all enlisted men, except volunteers, with 18 months as of 30 November 1946 will be eligible for discharge and will be separated from the Army by 30 November. d) All enlisted men, except volunteers, who accumulate 18 months service in any month subsequent to November will be separated from the Army by the last day of the month in which they accumulate 18 months service.

"Previously announced discharge criteria remains unchanged for officers...

Home September 20

"The above constitutes the War Department program for demobilization of enlisted personnel. Theater commanders will schedule the release of personnel affected by this criteria in order to ensure that all personnel eligible by 30 September and 30 November arrive in the Zone of Interior not later than 20 September and 20 November respectively...

July 5... The Foggia VD rate climbed again in army installations to a peak of 174.48 for the year. Capt. Louis Diaz (medics), who is organizing a drive to stamp out VD, said, "Through the medium of orientations, movies, and posters we hope to stop the dangerous rise." LOCAL ITEMS

Frustration

We walked into the I and E Library recently and found Wally Cole and George Jonesckies (Sergeants both) trying to find out what to do with a fistful of good money orders—seventy dollars worth in all. Their story was: back in March and April, the Information and Education Section inaugurated courses for the United States Armed Forces Institute. The deposit was two dollars in money orders for each subject, and by the middle of April, they had collected ninety-two dollars. It later turned out that the money was not needed, and they sent letters to all of the subscribers informing them of their refund. Only twenty-two dollars worth was picked up, and thus they have seventy dollars worth of money orders uncashed. They would appreciate it if the claimants would appear; or maybe someone has a bunch of blank dog-tags?

APO

After spending our entire army career envying the lot of the mail clerk ("All he ever does is hand out mail"), we finally got around to delving into the mysteries of what makes an Army Postal Unit tick and we emerged with a definitely changed attitude on the situation. The boys have a lot of work to do, put in a lot of hours to accomplish it, and the result is a very efficient job. The FAAB Army Postal Unit, with Lt. A. F. McCasland, Postal Officer; T-5 Bill Bigley, non-com in charge; and a staff of nine men, handles mail for 12 separate units, including two in Bari.

Starts At 6 AM

Starting as early as 6 AM with the task of loading the outgoing mail on the Naples plane, they settle down to routine chores at 9 AM when the Post Office opens for business. Until 4 PM they are kept busy handling money orders, stamps, distributing the mail, and taking care of the packages that are brought in for mailing. A word about the packages: they cannot be accepted unless they are properly wrapped and packed securely enough that they won't rattle, and the boys would appreciate it if you would make sure that these conditions are complied with before bringing your packages in.

The Post Office closes at 4 PM but the work is not quite finished. The money collected for money orders remains to be counted and then, after 5 PM, the mail plane arrives from Naples. In order to facilitate early delivery and keep up our morale, the mail is sorted immediately so it will be ready for delivery the following morning. The boys generally finish sorting the mail by 8 or 9 PM and decide to call it a day, and from where we sit it looks like a fair day's work.

Speeding

The Military Police are enforcing the speed limits in town, and it is giving rise to many gripes by the local drivers. But in spite of the fact that our Editor got one of the first Traffic Violation Tickets handed out this week, we think the tightening up of traffic controls is a good thing. Our friend, to be known here as Shorty, tells us a beauty however, that we must pass on. The charge against him was "accelerating at forty miles per hour," and he is particularly broken up because he had gotten his driver's permit only a few hours before and he swears he was in second gear behind a truck.

Shots We walked into our Base Dispensary the other day for our tenth of a CC skin test inoculation, the commencement of a series of four diphtheria toxoids. A freshly painted sign decorated the doors, "Open For Business." We laughed at the medics' sense of humor and entered the dispensary in gaiety. The angels of mercy picked up our scent and assailed us. Twisting our arms, they marched us to a partitioned area where we caught a glimpse of a giant-sized hypodermic needle (actually a spinal injection needle as we were later informed) attached to a sign:

Get Your Shots Here  
Free Of Charge  
Plenty For All

We sweated it out as a medical technician toyed with his hypodermic, "Notice the hook on this one," he explained with gleeful pleasure. An electrical shock paralyzed our arm. We knew then that the medics' deed was done. Assisting us to a nearby chair, the technician prepared for his next victim, "Step right up gentlemen; all the shots you want, free of charge."

The sense of humor of our medics touched us. It did more than that, it penetrated us. "And what do we get out of this," they questioned their patient, pointing to a lonely stripe on their arm.

The Water You Drink (Second of a series of three articles by the Town Major, Captain David Ives. In last week's article, the author told of the building of the Acquedotto Pugliese and the sources of its water.) The water, being tapped underground, is kept that way (subsidiary reservoirs also being subterranean) until it reaches the user, so that in normal times the Italians have used chlorine only when a break or other mishap has made contamination possible. U.S. Army policies, however, call for chlorine in any case, just to be safe either in the main supply or at the point of consumption.

(There are certain areas, such as for the time being that to the northeast of Foggia, which are supplied from wells. Such water should always be chlorinated, and that in the area mentioned has always been so treated ever since Allied troops first settled there.) The Acquedotto engineers are justly proud of their achievements. And why not? Do you know how Foggia got water before the Acquedotto? By train, from near Naples. There used to be a saying in southeastern Italy that what it needed was water and justice. To date, they figure, they've got the water.

Why Water Cuts Now, for those relentlessly logical minds which have been wondering why, with so much good water, there has to be a reduction, here's a translation of an article which appeared last Sunday in the "Gazzetta del Mezzogiorno" ("Southern Gazette") of Bari, one of the best newspapers in Southern Italy (after that plug, we hope they won't mind our lifting their stuff):

The reduced quantity of water and the recommendation to avoid waste, which may bring a still further limitation, has caused many consumers to ask: Why is there a lack of water after a rather rainy winter season? "We must go back a little to the origins of the springs of the Acquedotto and to the subsoil phenomena which bring about these variations, in order to explain the present shortage."

"The mountain mass which feeds the springs of Caposele consists of large banks of limestone, sometimes fissured, sometimes compact, and almost entirely surrounded by impermeable rock, so as to create a huge reservoir into which the complex network of underground streams pours their waters. The fissured rocks at the surface absorb the rain and the melting snow and thus furnish abundant water to this natural reservoir, from which the overflow leaks out of the mountain where the permeable layers come in contact with the impermeable ones. This is the origin of our springs (so-called outcrop springs). The case is similar for the acqueducts of Naples and Palermo and the 'Acqua Marcia' of Rome."

ITALY THIS WEEK International Paris Foreign Ministers Conference agreed on French demands for the Tenda and Briga area on the French-Italian border, with the stipulation that Italy continue to receive hydroelectric power from plants in the area. The Italian press greeted the news bitterly and as a unit condemned the proposal. Arturo Toscanini, scheduled for a concert performance in Paris on July 8th, canceled the program in protest of the agreement. Norway signed a trade agreement with Italy involving the exchange of three billion lire in commodities. Italy also agreed to build four ships of 9,000 tons each for Norway.

ITALY THIS WEEK

National Enrico De Nicola was proclaimed provisional President of the Italian Republic. The 68-year-old lawyer was credited as "figuring un-importantly in several pre-fascist governments" by the American press but was greeted warmly by most of the Italian newspapers. His Naples birthplace figured largely in his nomination, as the Italian government needed a strong inducement to appease the monarchistic South. In 1913 (under Giolitti), he was Undersecretary of the Ministry of Colonies, and in 1919 (Under Orlando), he served as Undersecretary of the Treasury.

Production in Italy has been going up according to recent reports on silk and electric power. This year's production of natural silk in Calabria amounted to 509,300 pounds (pre-war world production was 135 million pounds), and in the first four months of this year, 4,328 million kilowatts were produced in Italy in comparison to last year's corresponding production of 3,329 million kilowatts.

Shipping services between Italy and America are to be increased in July. The reason given is "the increasing commercial and passenger traffic between Naples and New York."

Trieste saw serious rioting that resulted in the deaths of several civilians and the wounding of nine Allied soldiers. The fighting broke out when members of the Giro d'Italia (Tour of Italy) 2,000-mile bicycle race were attacked south of Trieste. Immediately after, gang wars began in Trieste between pro-Italian and pro-Slovene groups. A general strike paralyzed the city (the Italians called a work stoppage protesting the attack on the cyclists, and the Yugoslavs struck because of the riots that followed). By Wednesday, the city had quieted down.

The population of Italy was announced unofficially by ANSA Agency as 45,769,000, which constituted an increase of 780,000 since 1940, despite war losses.

Lire values fluctuated this week ranging (on the Rome Black Market) from 400 to 440 lire to the dollar. The reason given by the American press was the anxiety over cabinet troubles in the new government.

A general strike of one half-hour duration has been called by the Italian General Confederation of Labor for Monday. The strike will protest the anti-Italian decisions of the Big Four Foreign Ministers at Paris this week.

American cows, 300 in all, were scheduled to arrive in Naples this week. They are a gift from the Protestant Church of America and were shipped to Italy by "The American Relief For Italy Inc."

Exports from Italy planned for the last half of this year were listed in a recent report as amounting to 100 thousand tons of vegetables and fruit and canned food worth from 30 to 40 million dollars.

ITALY THIS WEEK

Foggia

Elio Longo, an Italian soldier, was killed last Tuesday when an Italian Army jeep hit a bus on the Foggia-Manfredonia road. An Italian Army officer was also seriously injured.

Manfredonia wheat farms belonging to the Cetonza Brothers were invaded by about seven hundred people with two hundred carts coming from Barletta, Canosa, and Andria. The pillaging was halted peacefully by Carabinieri, police, and Finanza Guards who arrested four people.

STATESIDE Mail: A P-80 jet plane carried a letter to President Truman from Schenectady, NY to the White House (350 miles) in little over an hour, in the first flight of its kind. But mail to the Mediterranean Theater was breaking no records as the Army's C-54 planes were withdrawn from Italy runs for inspections and maintenance checks. MTOUSA officials are studying methods for obtaining temporary air services to replace the grounded planes.

Rome American Jobs: The United States Employment Service is optimistic about the latest figures on veteran employment. At the latest Census Bureau report, it was estimated that only 930,000 veterans were still unemployed out of the 11,400,000 that have been thus far discharged. Their optimism is based on the gloomy predictions by some government agencies that 8,000,000 men might be looking for work this summer, and that in the past three months employment of veterans had increased about 2,600,000.

Food: America's export goal of six million tons of grain for overseas relief for the first six months of 1946 will be met in July, according to Chester C. Davis, chairman of the Famine Emergency Committee. Davis praised Canada's aid and the "excellent cooperation of the Latin American Republics, who have made available 2,120,000 tons of grain. He cited a survey by a private firm which showed that seven out of ten US housewives polled had changed their menus to meet world shortage requirements.

US Embassy Sacred Cow: The name of President Truman's plane, "The Sacred Cow," which received publicity when a picture of M/Sgt. Freddie Winslow was shown with the insignia on his jacket, was attacked by the New Jersey Council of Christian Churches. The Council suggested changing the name to American Eagle or Chariot of Freedom.

Rome American Bonus: The Illinois Legislature voted the nation's largest state bonus for veterans: averaging 400 dollars each. The bill, signed by Governor Green, will be presented to the voters at a referendum next November. Next largest state bonus thus far is New York's: 250 dollars for each man.

ANS Sports: American League managers are practically conceding the AL pennant to the Boston Red Sox whose blazing record of 41 victories in 50 starts is unequaled since the turn of the century. Only in 1928 and 1939 did any team come even close to that mark (the powerful Yankee clubs). Only manager to refuse comment on the Boston chances is Joe Cronin. He is keeping his fingers crossed.

ANS Religion: Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini became the first American citizen ever elevated to sainthood in the Roman Catholic Church. Born in San Angelo, Italy in 1850, Mother Cabrini performed most of her works in America. She founded her own religious order after she was refused admittance to an established one because she was too frail and she established a school, hospital, or orphanage for each of the sixty-seven years of her life. Her canonization (27 years after her death) is the shortest in the history of the papal courts. ANS

Freedom From Fear

Freedom from fear! A voice yelled in the darkness of horrors in war. Freedom from the whip and the chain, from the devilish means of attack and spoils. Freedom from the sword of Damocles that hung with blood and tears above the necks of humanity. Freedom, the gallant people shouted at the Hun hordes that trampled over the skeletons and the scorched soil of the trembling neighbor. And the Word was heard, or the Word was taught by a fight the world will never forget. The cheer of Freedom from fear is an echo today, resounding from our dead heroes, whose sacrifice before the Altar of Humanity, whose glorious deeds shall make it live eternally. Freedom from fear! Shout we at the meetings and treaties, at the man of the street, at the new armies, at God, Freedom itself.

Lt. F. A. De Marzo

MAIL CALL (This letter comes from John Caldwell, one of the original staff of Occupator, who went home to Oregon the first part of this year. We reprint the letter in part for the interest of our readers.) 

Dear Editor,

At last I feel like a real veteran. Over ninety days have gone by since my discharge and no longer am I being deluged with propaganda that says "Re-Enlist in Grade." Maybe that idea of going back in sounds a little funny to you fellows who are still overseas, but a surprising number of men get fed up with this new civilian life. They don't like scarcities or responsibilities, so they head back for OD's just as soon as they've had a turn in civvies.

The food shortage is undoubtedly the problem that causes the most civilian gripes. Bread has been cut, butter is still hard to find, meat is scarce, and some bakeries close up a week in every month due to the sugar shortage. A majority of the people take it very well. They feel that Europeans have as much right to eat as they do, which is quite a concession for an American. The majority of the yelping comes from a minority that doesn't see why we should feed "the treacherous Japs, the filthy Germans, and the lazy Wops" and thinks that we make "too damn much fuss about the Frogs." When I hear that sort of thing, I just wish they could see a bunch of Foggia kids.

John Caldwell

ANN GIRL ABOUT TOWN Encore gab and gossip from the tired old pen of Miss Crisco of Foggia. The death of Old Man Snack Bar has made the tongues not only wag but also hang out. Saturday night's good old wake was final. Midst roaring laughter, the wailing and weeping Red Cross bags, all draped in black, and Deacon Hamilton, looking like Fu Man Chu's twin brother, were led by the boys of Maria Christiana to the candlelit death chamber to the tune of Chopin's funeral march. The most important character of the procession was Old Man Snack Bar himself, who lay dead in a black coffin, which was hoisted and borne by solemn G.I.s and escorted by Buck, Jerry, and others carrying signs reading: "So Long Battery Acid, Buona Sera Gelati, Goodbye Stinkin' Sinkers," and a huge donut pompously draped with the inscription, "Here Lies Indigestion." Ceremonies proceeded with Cooke reading the epitaph, composed by Jock "5000-words-on-any-subject" Jordan, and the bags and congregation chanting a farewell dirge. Delivered then by Leo Coletta was a telegram in the form of a small will, with the request that the boys be given at least some coffee and donuts three times a week. The request being granted, the band plunged into the Stein song and all but blew everyone out on their ear. The finale was Mrs. Joyce Steinke playing "Happy Days Are Here Again" and on to a Community Sing.

Static From Your AES  
by Ken Eill

Today we render, as to tear apart, the story of each character: George Waine McClain. Late of Weidman, Michigan, George has been in slavery for 16 months, 5 of which have been spent in dear old Foggia. His Army training was for B-29 sheet-metal worker, but as usual, things went astray, and he is now an engineer at AES. Before coming into the Army, George Wayne spent six or seven years playing on the basketball team of, and trying to get out of, Weidman High School. Since his entrance into the Army, George has gained valuable experience at such interesting things as KP and guard duty, and proudly states that he can clean a latrine with the best of us. Once his thirty years are up, he wants to go to the General Motors tech school and later sell automobiles. 

"Siugei Woohoo"

He does not believe the airplane is here to stay. His chief occupation at present is engineering, but in his spare time, he plays around with photography and thinks of stupid sounds to make at inopportune moments. And so, with a "brighiee" and a "siugei whoohoo" from George, we end this tale of woe.

Having no connection at all with McClain, the band of Johnny Moris comes up next. Johnny's band has been together about a year and a half, and for a guy that made his name playing something like "Paradiddle Joe," Morris has a remarkably hip band. He personally has been in the business for a long time but wasn't brought to the attention of the public until he started playing drums with Tommy Pastor about four years ago. He left Pastor and formed his own band, getting a group of young serious musicians. The two outstanding men in the band are Martin Dane, trombone, and Georgie Cirillo, trumpet. Georgie had his own band for a while, and Mario is definitely one of the finer of the young musicians. He's got some fine ideas and an exceptionally high range. There's a lot of power and invention in his style, and he keeps getting better.

Out Of This World

Georgie Cirillo is just out of this world. He's only nineteen and one of the finest lead trumpeters in the business. His tone is brilliant and powerful. His range is very fine, and he's always on the head. He plays a fine jazz horn too, with a terrific beat and lots of drive. The future of jazz is in the horns of men like Georgie. Keep an ear out for him. The band is about the same: a bunch of sincere musicians who like to play and can, and won't stop trying or hearing.

Remember fellows, for programs designed the American way... stay tuned to your AES throughout the day. That's all for this week, so until next... arrivederci... aroovde... ahhh nuts. Goodbye.

Leghorn Boxers To Fight In Foggia Wednesday  
New Inter-City Bouts Planned  

July 4 — Arrangements were concluded today by FAAB Special Services with Leghorn and Pescara to have an inter-city contest at the Flagella Theater Wednesday. This was the first move in a plan to bring the top ring men from South Italy to challenge Foggia's favorite sons, and at the same time, it opened the Flagella to handle the big audiences that have been turning out the past weeks.  

On top of the card Wednesday will be 170-pounders Zucco Ilucearone from Foggia and Bruno Questa from Leghorn. Zuccarone, former middleweight champion of Italy, has won seven and lost none in the Fortress Club fighting to date. A hard hitter and fairly fast, he concentrates on killer punches rather than boxing technique, and it has stood him in good stead thus far. Questa, however, promises to give Zuccarone the toughest competition to date, since he has years of boxing experience behind him and is a slugger like Zucco.  

Sabatini vs. Altino  

Also from Leghorn is Posi Altino, who will match Foggia's favorite Sammy Sabatini. Sabatini, 153 pounds, is one of the gamest fighters to be seen in the Foggia ring this season, and he is fond of close-in fighting. Leghorn's Altino, who weighs in at 152, has a long amateur record behind him and has just recently turned pro.  

Other Leghorn men to arrive will be Piero Scardino, 128 pounds and contender for the Italian Featherweight; Vincenzo Carbonici, 129-pound professional; and Mario Rosellini, 130-pound professional. Against them, FAAB is pitting Tony Fiore, Vince Russo, and Parlo Rossetti, all in the 130 weight bracket.  

Pescara men will be from among those who fight Friday night at the Fortress Club.

Torchies Swamp 779th Five, 60-29 The Summer Basketball League opened last Tuesday night as the Fire Department "Torchies," led by Jenkins and Wolff, routed the 779 quintet 60-29. Rated as one of the pre-season favorites to win the tournament, the "Torchies" presented a powerful squad as they completely outclassed the 779 five. Other teams that will bear plenty of watching are the 1898th 'Dozers, Security, and possibly the Plugs from 955. All games take place at the local gymnasium at 1900 hours.

Zucco Takes Seventh Win

July 1 — Zucco Zuccarone, Foggia's own undefeated champion, added another victim to his long string of victories by decisioning Romeo Milite, Amateur Champion of Italy from Pescara, in the five-round main bout at the Fortress Club this evening. Milite weighed in at 142 pounds, while the husky Zuccarone tipped the scales at 178. Zuccarone kept the smaller Milite from landing many solid punches but could do little better as the Pescara Mighty Mite continually tied the big Foggian up in the clinches. The crowd yelled mightily for Milite, the popular favorite, but Zuccarone was too powerful for the loser. The win was Zuccarone's seventh straight in the Fortress Club.

The semi-final match was a free-swinging, bloody thriller in which Mickey Montanani took a close decision from Foggian Sammy Sabatini. Montanani drew blood from Sabatini in the first round with a flurry of lefts and rights to the face. With his nose bleeding furiously, Sabatini made a great fight of it with the lightning-fast Montanani but the lad from Pescara dealt out terrific punishment to his slower but game opponent to win by a close but clear-cut decision.

Crowd Approves

In a one-sided but interesting fight, Frankie Franceschelli won over Russo Vincenzo in the first professional bout of the evening. Franceschelli pressed the fighting all the way and had the crowd roaring with approval at his skill in the ring. Foggian Vincenzo put up a nice fight but was clearly outclassed by the fast Franceschelli.

In the amateur bouts of the evening, Frank Scarano decisioned Bob Reese in a slugging affair, Fiore battered out a bloody victory over Carbane, and Riccuci won a popular decision over Rana. Proceeds of the night went to the Children's Orphanage in Manfredonia.

Vincenzo Russo (left) tries to slow down Frankie Franceschelli from Pescara Monday night at the Fortress Club. In the hottest fight of the evening, Pescara's man beat Foggia's Russo. Photo by Bajal.

Skelly Scores In Fifteen Seconds

June 28 — Twenty-year-old Hugh Skelly from Rye, NV, KO'ed his opponent Puccirossi in fifteen seconds, setting an all-time record in the Foggia area in the outstanding fight of the evening at the Fortress Club. Three left jabs with a right cross brought the Italian boxer down. It was so sudden that Skelly's opponent as well as the boxing fans were caught off guard when the knockout punch was delivered. The hundred sixty-two-pounder, Hugh Skelly, stands five feet eleven inches, with every pound of potential force backing his punches. Skelly ventured into the pugilistic engagements during basic training and continued training with exhibition bouts and workouts.

Cunningham Wins

Cunningham took the decision over his opponent, Ricucci, in a three, two-minute round bout. Tonight, nine bouts were divided into three classes: the boy exhibition, amateur, and professional. Shoeshine and Nease's boy slugged it out to a draw, while the Foggia boys split two wins apiece with S. Severo in the amateur contest. In the professional class, Foggia won both five-round bouts as Carbonaro defeated Papagno from S. Severo, with Zuccarone taking the decision over the Manfredonia boy, Rana.

Edd Lencowski and Doc Sabatini judged the bouts, with Vince Ciano refereeing. The Ripple Lounge management is the sponsor of these Friday night boxing matches.

Foggia Teams Challenge FAAB

July 4 — The City of Foggia and the Foggia Providence track and field teams announced that they would take on any American team in late July and early August, respectively, at the Foggia stadium. The events will include running, jumping, and throwing the javelin and the discus. Any team or individual interested should contact FAAB Special Services.

Damato Hurls One-Hitter  
July 2 — Making his initial appearance on the mound for the 779th, Mike Damato pitched a one-hit masterpiece while his teammates pounded out eleven hits to triumph over the Special Service Specials 11-0 at the Foggia Stadium this afternoon. Damato was invincible throughout the game as he struck out 14 Specials. The only hit off Mike was a scratch single into right field in the fifth inning by Gus Gustafson. His shutout was in danger only once when the Specials put men on second and third base with no outs. Pitching carefully and surely, he retired the next three hitters on strikes to work himself out of the tough situation.

The big hit of the day was Tony Slovik's two-run triple to right field in the big Rebel fifth inning when they tallied four times. Scoring in every frame, the attack was led by Bill Falk, who scored three runs on two singles and a walk in five appearances. The win marked the third straight for the Rebels, and it was the sixth defeat for the Specials in a row.

Negro, White Relationship Discussed At Flagella: July 10 — Three Negro soldiers, Sgt. Henry Connell, Cpl. Verlon Moore, and Cpl. R.L. Wilson, headed by Capt. Henry Jones, discussed better relationships between Negro and white troops with the assembled military personnel of Foggia Army Air Base at the Flagella Theatre Wednesday and Friday morning.

The discussion acted on the basis of a question received from Capt. Jones, C. C. 2042nd Trucking Co., who wanted to know from each individual speaker how better relationships and understanding could arise between the Negro and white troops. It was for this reason that the three Negro soldiers told their story. Sgt. Henry Connell, a member of the famous 332nd, 301st, and 100th Negro Fighter Groups, is the only man left out of these groups still in active service overseas. With twenty-six months of Army life behind him, Sgt. Connell concluded his speech, "A rather difficult question to answer but I believe that this discussion brings out some points in improving a better understanding for better relations between the Negro and white soldiers."

Fighting the battle of Italy in the front lines, Rifleman Cpl. Verlon Moore believes in human kindness towards each other. "We are in the same Army, serving our country and performing the same duties," spoke the 92nd Infantry Division veteran, who helped push the enemy back from below Leghorn to the Bologna front.

It was a race between the truck drivers on who could bring the greater quantity of bombs in the shortest length of time when Cpl. R.L. Wilson delivered his bomb loads in the Foggia area. "Sabotaged bombs occasionally lit up," said the corporal of the 2042nd Trucking Co., "Six of our boys went that way back in Africa."

Cpl. Wilson ended his talk in a frank and open session, "We misunderstand each other and then we'll be able to work together."

Foggia Loses 3 Out Of 5 To Leghorn At Flagella

July 10

Before the largest crowd yet to witness a boxing show this season, the Leghorn boxing team defeated the Foggia squad in three of the five bouts at the Flagella theatre this evening. It was a night of good and bad fighting that had the huge throng in an angry mood at the long delay between bouts.

The main event was between Foggian Zucco Zuccaroni and Bruno Questa, a rough and ready fighter from Leghorn. After delaying the match for 30 minutes, Zuccaroni finally put in an appearance and was promptly taken apart by the husky Questa. In the first four rounds, Questa seemed to be playing with Zuccaroni as he took everything the Foggia champ had to offer and laughed in his face. In the fifth and final round, he bore down and slammed the heavier Zuccaroni into the ropes and around the ring to earn a popular decision. Zucco was plainly afraid of Bruno as he tried to clinch with him at every chance.

The semi-final bout was a mismatch between the powerful 152-pound Terry Tosa from Leghorn and Kid Traversa, a local Foggia boy. Traversa was fighting in Sammy Sabatini's place, who was supposedly ill, and was sadly out of shape. Traversa put up a game fight but the ring-wise Tosa slammed him into semi-consciousness with a series of left jabs and powerful right uppercuts. Traversa's seconds threw in the towel in 1:32 minutes of the second round.

The best fight of the evening was between slugging Vince Russo of Foggia and lightning-fast Mincinco Carboncini from Leghorn. Russo stood steadfast as his opponent darted in and out with quick left jabs until the final round, when he opened up with long sweeping left blows that jarred Carboncini continually. The fans were begging for a knockout by the popular Russo but it wasn't in the books as the game lad from Leghorn hung on until the final bell. Russo was declared the winner by decision as the crowd gave both fighters a great hand.

In the other professional bouts, Scadino of Leghorn outpointed Fiore of Foggia, and Rossetti decisioned the other Leghorn entry, Rosellini.

Air-Sea Rescue Unit Planned

July 10... A new Air-Sea Rescue function is being planned for the near future, it was announced by Major Harold L. Thayer, S-3 Officer today. The unit will be attached to the 529th ASO and is to be operated under the supervision of S-3. At the present time, it is in the process of organization, stated Major Thayer, "and will be put into active use on the expected assignment of two new crash boats." 

At the present time, the newly organized outfit has but one boat at its command, a 35-foot Higgins J-boat.

Lt. Averill, Sgt. Harold Spruill NCO in charge, Cpl. George Erickson, and Cpl. Wilburn Perryman, with the aid of Italian laborers, reconstructed an empty hull into a rescue ship.

The arrival of the crash boats in addition to the homemade vessel will enable the air-sea rescue outfit to patrol the offshore waters in event of an air mishap over the Adriatic.

LOCAL ITEMS

Sentinel

We've heard a lot of discussion, pro and con, about the guard duty situation at the 529th Squadron, so we stopped in the guard room the other day and had a chat with the Commander of the Guard, S/Sgt. Ed Sabotka. Ed tells us that the temporary arrangement in effect since the first of June, of pulling men from the squadron for guard duty, will be terminated on the twelfth of July when the Security Squadron moves in. We figured that would make a lot of men very happy indeed, but when we were so bold as to mention the fact, Corporal James Miller, Corporal of the Guard, denied it most vehemently, "This guard duty out here is a good deal, we never had it so good" (we stand corrected). In fact, after we found out the schedule they work, we are inclined to agree. The boys work four hours on, eight hours off, four hours on, and a day off. Applicants please form a line to the left.

Billeting We were talking to Lt. John Cahir, Billeting Officer, the other day about the problems he has to contend with in finding living quarters for the men whose dependents are arriving in ever-increasing numbers these days, and it would appear that he is a very busy man indeed. The Lieutenant and his staff of two men, S/Sgt Don Pickett and Pfc Conrad Smith, have already provided living quarters for approximately thirty-eight families, and more are expected in the near future. The lack of furniture, cleaning supplies, etc., are tending to make the Lieutenant a potential client for some enterprising aspirin salesman. The early arrivals to the Foggia area were fortunate in that they inherited the furniture left by former American occupants, but that supply has been exhausted, and no other source has been discovered as yet. No natural gas is available at present in Foggia, and there are no cooking facilities, so most of the wives are bringing hot plates with them. Included among the many duties of the billeting department are fumigating the apartments before occupancy, redecorating and remodeling when necessary, and furnishing cleaning supplies.

Conditions in Italy aren't too bad, according to the Army wives now living in Foggia. They have nothing but praise for their living quarters, which are much better than they expected.

We asked the husbands, who had been waiting anxiously, lest their families declare conditions impossible, how they felt when they found that their wives and children were satisfied. To a man, they replied it was a great relief to know everything was all right.

The most serious problem is the lack of cooking facilities, although many of the wives brought electric cookers and hot plates along with them.

Mrs. H. S. Palmer, Phoenix, Ariz., an "Army" wife of long standing, is especially delighted with her 6-room apartment and the maid who keeps everything spic and span. "This is a great help," Mrs. Palmer said.

Mrs. Peter Pauluk, Detroit, Michigan, finds things better than she expected. "From the pictures I received from my husband, Lt. Peter Pauluk, I thought that I would have to rough it," she said. "I must say I'm delighted, although I only wish we had some hot water."

Mrs. Gene Cruce, Oklahoma, did not expect as much. "My husband, Lt. Gene Cruce, told me we would practically be living in tents," she said. "But here we have 4 rooms and a bath with maid service, which is very hard to get in the States."

Festivities

The enterprising family at the 55th Station Hospital took advantage of a sunny Fourth of July to hold a celebration at Penicillin Park. On meeting Miss Elizabeth Thornton, head of the hospital's ARC, the first thing she said was, "I'd like to thank all those connected with helping to make the party at Penicillin Park a success. Sgt. F. W. George and Sandy Kolazinski for their work in decorating the area; Lt. Kenneth Hrbden who contributed to the building of the barbecue pit; Doris Helsingren and Mess Sgt. Parisella for the fine meal, and Captain Zin who so appropriately named the park."

Food Served

The food served, as we got it from Miss Thornton, was built around two barbecued suckling pigs and fifty chickens. A variety of vegetables and fruits was procured right from the hospital's own garden. With a stomach full of good food, it is easy to see why such games as Croquet, ping pong, badminton, archery, and draught (a checker game played on an oversized board) could be played with such gusto. A potato race, she continued, was run by the local nurses as well as a jump relay.

The big prize of the day was a phone call home. "Tickets," said Miss Thornton, "were given out to each individual as they entered the park while the bed patients received their stubs on food trays. A box of tickets corresponding to those held by the guests was then drawn to determine the winner. T/4 William W. Charnoock, now on his way to the States, won the prize."

Washington: The Senate was expected to vote on the GI Leave Bill next week after it had been given a favorable endorsement by the Senate Military Affairs Committee. The House had passed the bill on June 7th, giving enlisted men terminal leave pay amounting to thirty days' pay per year.

The OPA was still on top of the American public's personal agenda. Labor as a body was behind renewal of the bill, and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that the cost of living had risen only one-third since 1939. Rome: The American 442nd Infantry Regimental Combat Team will be reviewed by President Truman on Monday in Washington. The ceremony would accord the Japanese-American veterans honors equaled by no other unit in World War II.

Rome: American Jobs: Returning veterans who have had experience with training pictures and projectors are expected to swell the ranks of more than 4,000 road showmen who were in the traveling motion picture business before the war. (Traveling showmen have become aware, during the past five years, of the increased interest shown in these small-scale movies by the major studios.
