Aviation: Capt. Miller, skipper of the Pan-American Constellation, zoomed off the runway at LaGuardia Field with a payload of 42 passengers, headed for Shannon, Eire. An hour later, the engine burned out of the wing and fell on a farm near Plainfield, Conn. Miller cut an engine on the other side to relieve the pressure on the weakened wing. Spotting a field at Willimantic, 25 miles out of Hartford, the pilot circled the field and came in against the wind. The fire damaged the hydraulic system, locking the landing gear as he belly-landed the plane with the engine still burning. Not a single passenger was hurt.

Sports: Going to Mexico to get away from the heat may not sound reasonable. But it may make sense in the case of Sam Breadon, owner of the St. Louis Cardinals, whose plans for a visit south of the border followed hard on the heels of the blasting he took in the press for rejecting the request of 100 disabled veterans for tickets to the Brooklyn-St. Louis game on June 12. The Water You Drink  
(Last of a series of three articles by the Town Major, Captain David Ives. In last week's article, the author told of the reasons for the reduced quantity of water.)

"Besides the fact that much of the water is due to the melting of the snow, the water circulates extremely slowly inside the mountain, with the result that the supply of the springs is about six months behind the rainy season. Hence the flow is maximum in the season of least rainfall, which is just when it is most needed. Also, as with all hydrologic phenomena, the quantity of water at the springs undergoes considerable variations stretching over cycles of tens of years.

Record Of 27 Years

"A better view of the phenomena can be obtained by citing data from the last 27 years of the Acquedotto's history. We notice first of all that the maximum volumes were consistently obtained during the season of least rainfall. During 1920-1930, the volume of water (per second) at the spring was initially about 4 tons; it dropped to slightly over 3 tons during the first quarter of 1921, and then rose again to about 6.5 tons during the second quarter of 1924. A year later, in June 1925, the volume had dropped again to 3.5 tons, and it remained practically constant, with small peaks of 4 tons, until June 1929; then it rose again to 5 tons per second in June 1930.

Recently: 3.2 Tons

"The lowest recorded volume was about 3 tons in December 1932, followed by slight increases and some contractions until 1938. 1939 starts with 3.7 tons, and in June 1941 a maximum of 6.2 tons is recorded. During the following years, it gradually dropped; for the last six months, it has kept rather steady at about 3.2 tons per second.

"These figures lead one to notice that the present volume is one of the lowest ever recorded. The fact is rendered even more severe by the steady increase of population, of water consumption, and of the number of localities supplied. One must also take into consideration the greater consumption—and often waste—which still goes on under the name of 'military needs', in order to understand the reasons which have brought about a reduced water supply.

Optimistic Estimates

"The slow reactivation of normal conditions and the legitimate expectation that the present exceptional drought at the source will not recur in the near future, lead us to be optimistic as to the supply during the coming summer months. Meanwhile, the supply from other sources may help to prevent the effects of future droughts. Should, however, the population still increase in Puglia at the present rate, then there would be nothing left but to start thinking about building another aqueduct."

One last word. Foggia, ever since the first days of its occupation, has received a priority rating in the distribution of water, despite the complaints of other cities in Puglia. Reductions here are made only as a last resort. It is hoped that the coming reduction will be only temporary; but if not, it should be borne in good spirit with the facts in mind.

ITALY

Trieste was the scene of soldier-civilian fighting this week, as according to the Associated Press, about one thousand British soldiers banded together and swung their heavy belts at civilians in the streets, breaking shop windows and injuring several people. British authorities in Trieste denied the violence reported and claimed that there "were no injuries or shop windows broken."

The University of Padua's big bell (the city is located 22 miles southwest of Venice) rang continuously for three days and nights as a token of national grief for the decisions of the Paris Foreign Minister's Conference on Trieste. Said the students: "The historical bell of the University, decorated with gold metal during the struggle of Liberation, will strike to express the sign and the cry of pain for the mutilations which the Four Foreign Ministers inflicted on Italy." The electric engine that usually runs the bell was out of order, so the students took shifts for the seventy-two hours.

The corn crop in Italy fulfilled original expectations of a poor quality and quantity, even though pre-season predictions of dryness were not the reason. Rain came in time, but so did early colds and insects (locust plague), and the crop was greatly weakened.

Francesca Saveria Cabrini (1850-1917, an American citizen, famous for her founding of schools and orphanages) was elevated to sainthood of the Roman Catholic Church in Saint Peter's (Rome) by the Pope. Members of the Daughters of Cabrini order and Bishop Sheil of Chicago were among those present for the ceremony, during which an airplane circled Saint Peter's and scattered pictures over the people in the square.

Cerignola's mayor, Professor Antonio Bonito, resigned his post last week. Reasons for his resignation are obscure.

Gino Bartali won the Tour of Italy. The 29th annual bicycle race took him from Milan to Turin, from Genoa to Rome, from Naples to Florence, and from Trieste to Trento: a total of 3,300 kilometers (2,050.5 miles). It took him twenty-two days in all, and his actual "bike-time" was 95 hours.

Foggia Carabiniere caught one of the notorious Sacco gang. The man known as Salvatore was from San Nicandro Garganico and had six warrants out for him on charges of homicide, rape, and thefts. Three other men were arrested as accomplices.

SWIMMING MEETS SLATED FOR ROME

July 9 -- A Foggia AAB swimming team will leave for Rome on the 27th of July to compete in the open theater swimming championships to be held at the Rome Rest Center on the 2nd and 3rd of August, it was learned today. Cpl Ed Lencowski, Base swimming pool manager, announced that swimming practices for the coming event will begin at 6:45 PM, Monday, July 15th, at the FAAB pool. Applications will be taken at the local Gymnasium and swimming pool and must be entered on or before the 20th of July.

Competitive Races

There will be the usual races in the meet, such as the freestyle, backstroke, individual medley, relays, and diving events. There will be plenty of good competition as most of the outfits in Italy shall be represented. Cpl Lencowski stated, "With a good turnout, the FAABs would stand a very good chance of bringing home a Mediterranean championship."

Boxing Bouts Turn Into Dance Routine

July 5 - The main event of tonight's bouts at the Fortress Club was a waltzing, loving cup sort of a fight, with Romeo Milite finally decisioning Sammy Sabatini in the dull five-round affair. The usually hard-hitting Sabatini failed to connect with his potent right or, for that fact, with his left. Milite, who fought a great fight against Zuccaroni two weeks ago, was content to get in enough body blows to decision Sabatini.

Most interesting bout of the evening was the bout between middle-aged "Pop" Mario and Peppy Pastorella. Introducing a new and different style never before seen at the Fortress Club, "Pop" weaved, bobbed, and fought his way to a five-round draw with his confused opponent. Mario would stand still while Pastorella would pepper his face with left jabs, then suddenly duck and send a looping left to his opponent's baffled countenance. He was undoubtedly the most popular fighter on the card as he won his audience over with his tricky and interesting style.

In the other bouts, Scarano decisioned Imperatore, Ricucci won a popular decision over Rana, Oatto took a close one from Fiore, and Maiello won from Risi.

By the Sports Staff

A Foggia-Bari track and field team will be organized to compete in the Mediterranean Theatre Championships, which will be held at the Yankee Stadium, Leghorn, Italy, on July 20th and 21st. It has been announced that there will be eight running events, four jumping events, two relays, and four weight contests. All competition will be governed by the International Olympic Rules.

The one bright spot in the 529 Yankee lineup is quiet Ron Schaber, pitcher and infielder of the in-and-out Yankee nine. Ron, at this writing, is leading the team in batting averages with a cool .363. Schaber is one of those silent ball players who does his job well and usually goes unnoticed by the fans in the stands but definitely is noticed by his teammates and his opponents. His deceptive sidearm pitching looks easy to hit until the time comes to hit it. A slow tantalizing curve and good control are his main assets.

In a brief look at the various hitting, pitching, and base running records, we find that although the 955 Sparkplugs are the league leaders, the hitting and base path honors are mostly sewed up by the lower-standing teams, such as the 779 Rebels and the 345th Rangers. At this writing, the first four in batting averages are Keysor and Greiner of the Rangers, and Damato and Janovick of the Rebels. Mike Damato of the Rebs is still pacing the league in homers with three, and Pete Janovick of the same team is far away the leader in "runs driven in" with 14 to his credit. 

Tommy Thompson, stellar second sacker of the Sparkplug nine, is the leader in runs scored with 18 tallies. Ed Greiner of the Rangers has lined out seven doubles to lead in that department, and we again find Damato in the runner-up spot with five. Three base hits are evenly distributed with no player having more than one. The stolen base column finds Rebel speed merchant Tony Slovick with seven thefts, Tony Ruzich, and "Tex" Childs of Special Service close behind with six apiece.

In the pitching department, we find that Ranger Ed Greiner is the strikeout king with 63 to his credit in six games. Damato is again in the second slot with 51 whiffs in five games. The Sparkplugs show their superiority in the won and lost column. Big "Moose" Varga with a 2-0 record and "Red" Cooke with four wins and one defeat are pacing the circuit. The best-pitched games of the season belong to Cooke and his no-hitter and the Varga-Cooke combination that so effectively whitewashed the 779 team with four safeties.

Red Cooke Hurls Yankee's Second Shut Out

July 11 — Red Cooke, 955 Sparkplug mound ace, continued his mastery over the 529 Yankees as he shut them out for the second straight time, allowing but three hits and striking out 13 as his teammates pounded out a 12-0 decision at the Foggia Stadium today.

Victims of Cooke's no-hitter three weeks ago, the Yankees could do little with his pitching slants while the 955 lads, with the aid of eight 529 errors, blasted two Yankee pitchers for their eighth victory in eleven starts.

Nick Ingenito, "Plug" third baseman, again led the hitting attack with two safeties in three official trips to the plate. The big blow of the afternoon was Al Levick's double down the right field line that drove home two runners. Cooke helped his own cause along by lining out a single in two official appearances and scoring three runs.

First Contingent of 838th Eng. Arrives Outfit Boasts Own Baseball Team, Band, Newspaper July 12 -- Sixty Negro troops arrived by truck transportation in the Foggia area today, as an advance contingent of the 838th Engineers Aviation Battalion, stationed at present at Camp Marcinasi on the outskirts of Caserta. The remainder of the Battalion is expected to arrive in the near future. The majority of the men are reenlistees and arrived in Italy in April of this year. A large number of them have had overseas service previous to their re-enlistment and many of them are familiar with Foggia. The battalion will take over the old 345th Aviation Engineers duties and will be stationed near Manfredonia. Entertainment The outfit boasts its own baseball team, swing band, and weekly newspaper. According to T/4 Harry A. Bell, Special Service NCO, the baseball team, known as the 838th Bulldozers, has lost only one league game the entire season and is a top-notch team, possessing a southpaw pitcher of reputed major league caliber. The swing band has won great popularity in the outfit and has been called on for numerous outside engagements. A military band is in the process of formation.

Mess Hall Fire Caused by Defective Stove

July 17 -- A fire at the 529th Air Service Group mess hall Wednesday morning sent Second Cook Corporal Bennett to the hospital with second-degree burns and caused slight injuries to Corporal Rodney Crabb and two Italian employees. Caused by a defective stove, the fire was confined to a small area in the kitchen. The damage was slight.

Captain Robert W. Clark, the new Commanding Officer of the 529th ASG, who entered the kitchen as the fire started, aided in extinguishing the blaze.

Trapped In Storeroom

Corporal Bennett and the two Italian employees, trapped in the storeroom when fire engulfed the doors, were forced to escape through the flames. Bennett suffered second-degree burns and was taken to the hospital where his condition is described as "good."

Corporal Crabb, while removing smoldering boards from the door frame after the fire had been extinguished, inadvertently touched a hot wire and was thrown to the floor. Examination at the dispensary disclosed bruises and pulled ligaments in his left arm.

Bulldozers Take League Lead Shimizu Blanks Sparks on Two Hits

July 16 — The 1898th Bulldozers moved into a half-game lead for first place, as George Shimizu held the 955 Sparkplugs to two hits, handing them an 8-0 shutout at the Foggia Stadium this afternoon.

The Sparkplugs, who have been the league leaders for exactly a month, were held completely in check by Shimizu's steady and business-like hurling. "Red" Cooke and Nick Ingenito were the only "Sparks" to touch home for safeties. Even though the Sparkplugs managed to get five runners on base during the game, not one got past second base.

The Bulldozers tallied in the first frame as "Slats" Omiya worked "Moose" Varga for a pass and promptly stole second and third. Jim Fitzpatrick went down swinging, as catcher Reese dropped the pitch while throwing Fitzpatrick out, Omiya scored. Retiring in order in the second inning, the "Dozers" started a rally in the third that didn't stop until five runs had crossed the plate and every man on the team had made an appearance at the plate.

The big blow of the inning was Jim Fitzpatrick's scorching single through the box with the bases loaded that drove home two runs. The final two runs were scored on successive singles by "Bulldog" Drummond and George Shimizu, a walk to Omiya, and Fitzpatrick's second hit of the afternoon.

LOCAL ITEMS

Vocabulary While sipping a Coke at the American Red Cross the other day, we overheard this tidbit. "I'm taking a course in basic English and already I know two hundred of the basiest words." Let it be known that Pfc. Charles Goodenough is accredited with this statement.

Musical

Before an estimated crowd of fifteen hundred G.I.'s, we were told, Lawrence Tibbett, the American operatic and concert baritone, accompanied by the Foggia Army Air Base Band, especially flown up for the event, gave a concert at the old Seventh Repple Depot in Naples. The Foggia lads were chosen in preference to the Caserta Band by the Caserta Special Service.

"It was about 9 o'clock Thursday morning when we took off for Naples," said Frenck De Grazia, bandmaster. "Being a usual trip, I won't bore you with details, but the fellas seemed to enjoy themselves," he continued. "After landing at Naples, the immediate problem that confronted us consisted in finding a place to rehearse. (How many of you khaki-clad lads remember the theater where we saw such chillers as The Isle of the Dead or laughed with Danny Kaye in Up in Arms?) This perplexing question was solved by going through our numbers in that very same theater, and later in the evening, we gave the real thing there."

Concert A Success

"The concert," Frenck poured forth, "was a great success. Our program wasn't all longhaired stuff; as a matter of fact, we played a good bit of light classical and some groovy music. Lawrence Tibbett, a regular joe, was well received by the audience. He's a terrific singer," Frenck added.

Tibbett, we were informed, will not give another concert in this theater. He'll be going to Germany and then home. We shouldn't feel bad, however, as we all can buy tickets upon reaching New York and delve into the finer things of life.

Commissary

Because of the fact that paint can't be secured and the lack of one good refrigerator, the new Commissary at the 779 Air Material Squadron, under the direction of Lt. Thomas Witek, isn't quite ready to do business. When asked about the situation, Corporal Victor Crabtree, accountant clerk, replied, "To the best of my knowledge there is no paint of any sort available for us. Utilities at 529 Air Service Group has a beat-up icebox," explained the corporal, "but a want of aluminum and glass is holding up repairs." He added, however, that the commissary is expected to open in the immediate future.

Busily at work fingering papers, Vic kept up an amiable conversation. "We've been working for the past two weeks and a bit of business has come our way. The clubs, for instance, buy supplies through us while Quartermaster does the actual issuing. Once we're open to the individual, of course, the store will be similar to A&P or National T back home, namely self-service."

Variety Of Goods

A wide variety of goods will be carried, to include everything, as the proverbial saying goes, from soup to nuts. A staff of seven men is employed to make buying more convenient for the purchaser, although as Corporal Crabtree puts it, "we're minus a butcher."

Departure

J.G. Local boy went up to Leghorn this week for his return trip to America. During his stay in Italy, FO Eugene S. Cohen expressed a deep affection for the people of FAAB and the people of Foggia. He left firmly convinced that the two can live together.

The Managing Editor of the Foggia Occupator began his journalistic activities on the paper as a sports writer. Cohen wrote his first story for the number one edition of this army publication nine months ago. "Just enough time to have a baby," chuckled Gene with a sense of humor that developed the Local Items style.

Important Contribution

Perhaps the most important contribution to the news-hungry people of the world from this newspaper were the photo releases of the food riots in Foggia by the Associated Press. Papers in all parts of the United States had access to them, and clippings from Chicago, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Indiana, and several New York papers have already been received with the pictures of Foggia. These photographs were taken on the day of the riot by FO Eugene S. Cohen.

Four years of college under the G.I. Bill of Rights await the one-time editor of the Foggia Occupator. One of them he expects to spend in the Italian Universities. "You can say I'm going back as a professional student on the Army payroll," spoke the enthusiastic ex-managing editor.

Liquor

Anywhere in Italy - Surveys have concluded that the American of World War Two is more sober than his father, but failed to state the fact that he also has the world's toughest stomach. No one here seems to give the slightest thought to the potency of Italian liquor. It is very seldom that you see the enticing labels of VO, Old Grandad, or other U.S. favorites. Therefore, everyone is falling into the habit of Italian whiskies, rums, and wines that have been dreamed up by the Italian distillers.

There was the story of a sergeant who favored Genuine Scotch Whiskies over everything. He said every time he got looped on it he had visions of being in charge of a chorus of girls teaching them how to "take it off." Having such an effect, the demand soon exceeded the supply. Then fake Genuine Scotch Whiskies, those which produced no visions, soon filled the shelves of the liquor stores.

Italian "booze" at its worst does not hurt the user as much as the liquor brewed by the GI himself. Such concoctions as straight alcohol and juice, aftershave lotion, and distilled potato peelings are guaranteed to make anyone take off into a world of their own.

Herm was driving a weapons carrier in the vicinity of the tar pits at Foggia Main and was unfortunate enough to have a flat tire, but that was only the beginning of his troubles. Tours Around Foggia  
(This is the first of a series of articles exploring Foggia and its vicinity)  

The church of Monte Calvario on the San Severo road is about the best place to begin. Not only does it offer a wide variety of camera shots, but it is also a pleasurable tour. The Church of Monte Calvario, better known as the Church of the Crosses, was built around 1600 by the Spanish Padre, De Olivada. The name, Church of the Crosses, was later given to the church as it was built around a huge wooden cross carried there by pilgrims from the villages close by Foggia. These crusades demonstrated the religious belief of enduring hardships for Christ.  

Chapels in the Garden  
Upon entering the gardens surrounding the main chapel, it becomes evident that even this beautiful edifice did not escape the ravages of war, for barbed wire and shells are abundant. The buildings, however, are being repaired, and they will soon regain their natural beauty. In the center of the garden stand five chapels, utilized as burial places since in that era the modern cemetery was not known, and members of that religious order were interred in vaults underneath each chapel. Later, the relics were transferred to a crypt located in the basement of the main chapel.  

When we began our exploration, the caretaker almost fell over backwards in his desire to help us. He quickly ushered us inside the building where the beautiful frescoes of Tintoretto (1518-1594), a Venetian painter of the Renaissance period, can plainly be seen. The building still retains some of its natural beauty, and one can easily imagine the charm of such a setting.  

Weird Things  
Leading us down to the cellar, which was dark and stumbling with old age, he began to talk of the weird things we would see. Little did we know of the truth in this old character's words, but after groping around in the dark, we finally found a light bulb that managed to flicker every second or so, and there before us was a small grotto filled almost to the top with human skulls and remnants of skeletons. He spoke quickly in mixed Italian and English, telling us that these were the remains of priests and nuns transferred from the chapels in the garden.  

The Flight of Stairs  
Coming up from the dark we saw another set of stairs leading off into nowhere, so we tagged along. The stairs led us on a merry chase, going around corners so sharply we almost met ourselves coming back. When we reached the top, there was Foggia in the distance, and we were standing in an ancient belfry.  

After that, it was "Chow," and the old caretaker wobbled over to a shady spot to sit and reminisce.

ITALY

The Constituent Assembly met at the Montecitorio Palace in Rome Monday, where President Saragat of the Constituent Assembly read the speech of Mr. De Nicola, Provisional President of the Italian Republic. In his declaration, Mr. De Nicola stated, "The Republican form of Government will assure to future generations a climate of true democracy." He concluded his message with "God grant Italian Resurrection."

President of Ministers, Mr. De Gasperi, submitted the list of new ministers of the first government of the Italian Republic and stated, "The all-important problem is still that of foreign policy." With regard to the Trieste situation, Mr. De Gasperi said, "The Italian people want that country which is Italian." He also gave thanks to the countries of Latin America who made a common approach to the "Big Four" in favor of a right and just peace with Italy.

The government allotted four million lire for the reconstruction of the Foggia and Bari area. The grant will cover public works, including roads, government buildings, and railroads.

Two riders were killed and five more wounded when a group of gangsters, armed with guns, hand grenades, and daggers, attacked a civilian truck near Cassino on the Rome-Naples road.

Why I Washed  
by Pfc. Robert G. Hoyt

Dear Jack:

I suppose you've heard that I'm no longer a cadet, and naturally, you'll wonder why I was eliminated. Well, it actually didn't have anything to do with the way I fly. They can always find something even if you fly circles around them.

What really happened was, I got PO'd at the Major. I was a little high in the Cadet Club on open-post night, and he was in there and saw me and said something about my blouse being unbuttoned. There was one button loose.

"Listen," I said, "Why don't you take that Boy-Scout stuff and put it where it belongs?" I really told him. He said something about 'impudence' and I said, "Why don't you go back to flying balloons, jerk? It'll go with your stomach!"

So he called the MPs. He wanted to court-martial me, but of course, he knew I had too much on him. Everybody knows he's drunk most of the time.

So they washed me. I'm just as glad. A man's got to keep his self-respect. Well, Jack, give 'em hell in the Infantry, and let's hear from you.

Be seeing you,  
Phil

Dear Sally:

The real reason I washed out, sweetest, had lots to do with you, just like everything else in my young life.

You see, darling, an awful lot of what happens in cadets depends on how your instructor likes you. My instructor liked me okay at first, I guess, but something happened.

The way it was, I met him in town one time, and his wife and sister were with him. We all had a drink together. It seems like his sister kind of fell for me, though I didn't say two words to her, and the next day my instructor tells me she wants a date and how about it? Naturally, I thought of you right away. I said no, I couldn't as I was practically engaged.

He was pretty insistent about it, but I wouldn't give in. Finally, he got sore. The very next day I got a check ride, and they washed me. It's too bad in a way because I did want to fly, but as I've said to you before, honey, I don't think the kind of love that can't stand a test is worth much.

By the way, don't say anything about this to the others—they might think I was silly.

All my love,  
Phil

Dear Uncle Fred:

Uncle Fred, I think I can tell you the real reason I washed out, but please don't tell Dad and Mom, as they'd just worry about it. I was washed out for what they call 'Flying accident due to pilot error'. I could have set them straight on that, but it wasn't worth it to me.

The way it happened was this. I took my ship up the other day for practice acrobatics—solo, of course—and was about to come out of a spin when the controls caught. I got her down all right, but she was pretty well smashed up. I found out the mechanic was drunk during the pre-flight check and had left a wrench in the fuselage. It had caught in the control cables.

I could have reported it that way, of course, but I happened to know the mechanic and what it would mean to him. He has a wife and three kids. If I reported him, he'd get a prison sentence for sure.

So I let it go. As I said, it wasn't worth it to me. He has promised he'll never touch another drop, and that's reward enough for me.

By the way, could you let me have a fiver? I had to bribe the crew chief not to report the mechanic, and am a little short.

All my love,  
Phil (Yank Magazine)

Foggia Boxing Team Takes On Pescara Huskies

July 18 --- When the Foggia boxing team takes on the Pescara Huskies at the Flagella Theatre this Tuesday, July 23rd, it will mark the second in the series of inter-city boxing matches now in progress.

One of the featured fighters of the evening will be 19-year-old Stewart Evans. Stew is a tall, well-built lad from Newton, Massachusetts, who loves to get in and "mix it up." The 172-pound GI recently slugged his way into a three-round decision over a badly beaten Carbonara and immediately won his way into the fans' hearts with his aggressiveness and boxing skill.

Another personality on Tuesday's fight card is "Pop" Mario, a middle-aged pugilist who keeps the audience roaring at his peculiar style. Mario, a short stocky fighter, bobs, weaves, and laughs his way through the bout, all of which tends to highly agitate his adversary. His best punch is a right jab delivered from behind the back during "close-in" fighting.

Joe DiGuart is a newcomer to fight fans in Foggia and was discovered while working in the 529 mess hall. Boxing promoters at the local gymnasium were impressed by his muscular build and persuaded Joe to work out at the gym. He showed up so well that they decided to put him against Pescara's best.

Outstanding fighters from Pescara will include Romeo Milete, Amateur Champion of Italy, and Frankie Franceschelli. Milete is a lad with lightning footwork and a darting left jab. He made a lasting impression on FAAB fans when he fought the 40 pounds heavier Zucco Zuccaroni to a standstill for five rounds, only to lose the decision by a hair. Franceschelli left an equally impressive record behind him in his only appearance in Foggia by defeating the popular Vince Russo decisively in five rounds.

By Jim Boyle  

Due to the deactivation of the 345th Engineers, the team known as the 345th Rangers was forced to withdraw from the Foggia American League. The Rangers, at the time of their withdrawal, had won four and lost six while holding down the fourth spot in team standings. With the 345th team now out of the league, there are only five teams left of the original nine squads that opened the season.  

"Watch out for the Special Service Specials" rings the cry from the watching baseball world. With the acquisition of "Tex" Childs, "Lefty" Elliot, Wilson Welker, and others from the once powerful Security Barons, the team has improved overnight into a team that should get the title of "giant-killers" if they live up to this writer's predictions. Although definitely out of the running for the pennant, the Specials have no pressure on them during the games as those fighting for the flag. Proof of this was provided in the 1898th game. The Specials battled the new league leaders down the line and were finally nosed out in the late innings.  

Let us not forget the big swimming meet to be held in Rome on the 2nd and 3rd of August. At the present time, there are eight swimmers and divers trying out for the team, and Cpl Lencowski would like to see at least twelve more spirited contestants come out and make the tournament a successful one for the Foggia entry.  

Special Service announced that there will be a Theater Tennis Championship tourney at Caserta to be held from the 7th to the 10th of August inclusive. Also to be held in the near future are badminton, baseball, and softball tournaments. The elimination process will take place in the Foggia-Bari area, and the outstanding team of the sector will enter the finals.

French Whitewashes Specials, 3-0

July 13 — "Bulldog" Drummond's timely double that drove home two runs in the sixth inning broke up a tight pitchers' battle between Bob French and the Specials' Lefty Elliot, as the 1898th Bulldozers triumphed over the Special Service nine 3-0, at the Foggia Stadium this afternoon.

Both pitchers hurled shutout ball until the eventful sixth inning when the Bulldozers scored three times to clinch the contest. Drummond's two-base blow scored Johnson and French with the winning runs.

French kept five Special Service singles well scattered in achieving his first shutout of the season. He displayed good control by striking out seven while walking none. Elliot whiffed eleven 'Dozers and gave up three walks.

First Contingent of 838th Eng. Arrives Outfit Boasts Own Baseball Team, Band, Newspaper

July 12 -- Sixty Negro troops arrived by truck transportation in the Foggia area today as an advance contingent of the 838th Engineers Aviation Battalion, stationed at present at Camp Marcinasi on the outskirts of Caserta. The remainder of the battalion is expected to arrive in the near future. The majority of the men are reenlistees and arrived in Italy in April of this year. A large number of them have had overseas service previous to their re-enlistment, and many of them are familiar with Foggia. The battalion will take over the old 345th Aviation Engineers duties and will be stationed near Manfredonia.

Entertainment

The outfit boasts its own baseball team, swing band, and weekly newspaper. According to T/4 Harry A. Bell, Special Service NCO, the baseball team, known as the 838th Bulldozers, has lost only one league game the entire season and is a top-notch team, possessing a southpaw pitcher of reputed major league caliber. The swing band has won great popularity in the outfit and has been called on for numerous outside engagements. A military band is in the process of formation.

Mess Hall Fire Caused by Defective Stove

July 17 -- A fire at the 529th Air Service Group mess hall Wednesday morning sent Second Cook, Corporal Bennett, to the hospital with second-degree burns and caused slight injuries to Corporal Rodney Crabb and two Italian employees. Caused by a defective stove, the fire was confined to a small area in the kitchen. The damage was slight.

Captain Robert W. Clark, new Commanding Officer of the 529th ASG, who entered the kitchen as the fire started, aided in extinguishing the blaze.

Trapped In Storeroom

Corporal Bennett and the two Italian employees, trapped in the storeroom when fire engulfed the doors, were forced to escape through the flames. Bennett suffered second-degree burns and was taken to the hospital where his condition is described as "good."

Corporal Crabb, while removing smoldering boards from the doorframe after the fire had been extinguished, inadvertently touched a hot wire and was thrown to the floor. Examination at the dispensary disclosed bruises and pulled ligaments in his left arm.

Bulldozers Take League Lead Shimizu Blanks Sparks on Two Hits

July 16 — The 1898th Bulldozers moved into a half-game lead for first place, as George Shimizu held the 955 Sparkplugs to two hits, handing them an 8-0 shutout at the Foggia Stadium this afternoon.

The Sparkplugs, who have been the league leaders for exactly a month, were held completely in check by Shimizu's steady and business-like hurling. "Red" Cooke and Nick Ingenito were the only "Sparks" to touch home for safeties. Even though the Sparkplugs managed to get five runners on base during the game, not one got past second base.

The Bulldozers tallied in the first frame as "Slats" Omiya worked "Moose" Varga for a pass and promptly stole second and third. Jim Fitzpatrick went down swinging, as catcher Reese dropped the pitch while throwing Fitzpatrick out, allowing Omiya to score. Retiring in order in the second inning, the "Dozers" started a rally in the third that didn't stop until five runs had crossed the plate and every man on the team had made an appearance at the plate.

The big blow of the inning was Jim Fitzpatrick's scorching single through the box with the bases loaded that drove home two runs. The final two runs were scored on successive singles by "Bulldog" Drummond and George Shimizu, a walk to Omiya, and Fitzpatrick's second hit of the afternoon.

Saturday mornings will be utilized as training periods for FAAB personnel, it was learned today. Educational films, Articles of War, drill periods, and I & E programs will be attended by all men, in compliance with military regulations.

All clubs in and around Bari are off limits to FAAB personnel, it was announced today by Colonel Robert K. Martin.

The new hotel at Siponto, although completed except for necessary mess arrangements, will not be opened until Manfredonia bay has been declared fit for swimming purposes. There is no swimming in the bay at the present time due to the presence of mustard gas in the water.

The hotel, when opened, will be utilized as a rest center for personnel in the Foggia area but will be unable to accommodate women guests, due to the lack of private sanitary facilities. 

In order to meet the civilian employees payroll, guests will be required to pay a small cover charge.

Colonel Robert K. Martin recommends that all personnel interested in applying for a direct commission as a Second Lieutenant make application in the Unit Personnel Office at their earliest possible convenience in order to expedite the necessary paperwork when the commissions are made available.

Vocabulary While sipping a Coke at the American Red Cross the other day, we overheard this tidbit: "I'm taking a course in basic English and already I know two hundred of the basiest words." Let it be known that Pfc. Charles Goodenough is accredited with this statement.

Musical

Before an estimated crowd of fifteen hundred G.I.'s, we were told, Lawrence Tibbett, the American operatic and concert baritone, accompanied by the Foggia Army Air Base Band especially flown up for the event, gave a concert at the old Seventh Repple Depot in Naples. The Foggia lads were chosen in preference to the Caserta Band by the Caserta Special Service.

"It was about 9:00 o'clock Thursday morning when we took off for Naples," said Frenck De Grazia, bandmaster. "Being a usual trip I won't bore you with details, but the fellas seemed to enjoy themselves," he continued. "After landing at Naples, the immediate problem that confronted us consisted in finding a place to rehearse. (How many of you khaki-clad lads remember the theater where we saw such chillers as The Isle of the Dead or laughed with Danny Kaye in Up in Arms?) This perplexing question was solved by going through our numbers in that very same theater and later in the evening we gave the real thing there."

Concert A Success

"The concert," Frenck poured forth, "was a great success. Our program wasn't all long-haired stuff. As a matter of fact, we played a good bit of light classical and some groovy music. Lawrence Tibbett, a regular joe, was well received by the audience. He's a terrific singer," Frenck added.

Tibbett, we were informed, will not give another concert in this theater. He'll be going to Germany and then home. We shouldn't feel bad, however, as we all can buy tickets upon reaching New York and delve into the finer things of life.

Commissary Because paint can't be secured and due to the lack of one good refrigerator, the new Commissary at the 779 Air Material Squadron, under the direction of Lt. Thomas Witek, isn't quite ready to do business. When asked about the situation, Corporal Victor Crabtree, accounting clerk, replied, "To the best of my knowledge, there is no paint of any sort available for us. Utilities at 529 Air Service Group have a beat-up ice box," explained the corporal, "but a lack of aluminum and glass is holding up repairs." He added, however, that the commissary is expected to open in the immediate future. Busily at work fingering papers, Vic kept up an amiable conversation. "We've been working for the past two weeks and a bit of business has come our way. The clubs, for instance, buy supplies through us while Quartermaster does the actual issuing. Once we're open to the individual, of course, the store will be similar to A&P or National, namely self-service." Variety of Goods A wide variety of goods will be carried, to include everything, as the proverbial saying goes, from soup to nuts. A staff of seven men is employed to make buying more convenient for the purchaser, although, as Corporal Crabtree puts it, "we're minus a butcher." Are there any promising young surgeons looking for a start in life?

Departure

Local boy Eugene S. Cohen went up to Leghorn this week for his return trip to America. During his stay in Italy, FO Cohen expressed a deep affection for the people of FAAB and the people of Foggia. He left, firmly convinced that the two can live together.

The Managing Editor of the Foggia Occupator began his journalistic activities on the paper as a sports writer. Cohen wrote his first story for the number one edition of this army publication nine months ago. "Just enough time to have a baby," chuckled Gene with a sense of humor that developed the Local Items style.

Important Contribution

Perhaps the most important contribution to the news-hungry people of the world, from this newspaper, were the photo releases of the food riots in Foggia by the Associated Press. Papers in all parts of the United States had access to them, and clippings from Chicago, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Indiana, and several New York papers have already been received with the pictures of Foggia. These photographs were taken on the day of the riot by FO Eugene S. Cohen.

Four years of college under the G.I. Bill of Rights await the one-time editor of the Foggia Occupator. One of them he expects to spend in the Italian universities. "You can say I'm going back as a professional student on the Army payroll," spoke the enthusiastic ex-managing editor.

Liquor Anywhere in Italy - Surveys have concluded that the American soldier of World War Two is more sober than his father but failed to state the fact that he also has the world's toughest stomach. No one here seems to give the slightest thought to the potency of Italian liquor. It is very seldom that you see the enticing labels of VO, Old Grandad, or other U.S. favorites. Therefore, everyone is falling into the habit of Italian whiskies, rums, and wines that have been dreamed up by the Italian distillers. There was the story of a sergeant who favored Genuine Scotch Whiskies over everything. He said every time he got looped on it, he had visions of being in charge of a chorus of girls teaching them how to "take it off." Having such an effect, the demand soon exceeded the supply. Then fake Genuine Scotch Whiskies, those which produced no visions, soon filled the shelves of the liquor stores. Italian "booze" at its worst does not hurt the user as much as the liquor brewed by the G.I. himself. Such concoctions as straight alcohol and juice, aftershave lotion, and distilled potato peelings are guaranteed to make anyone "take off" into a world of their own.

Affliction The saddest story of the week, we think, comes from Pfc. Herm Schroee, who works for the 529th Heavy Equipment Section. Herm was driving a weapons carrier in the vicinity of the tar pits at Foggia Main and was unfortunate enough to have a flat tire, but that was only the beginning of his troubles. Feeling somewhat unhappy but resigned to his misfortune, he returned to 529, picked up another tire, returned to the weapons carrier, and replaced the flat. It was with a sigh of relief that he lowered the jack. Finished? Well, not quite. The second tire was quite as flat as the first.

Astonished. Two Pfc's barged into Headquarters and Base mess hall this week and found they had to join a line of hungry G.I.'s waiting to get their trays and silverware. "I can't understand this place," said one of them. "I never come in here but people are eating."

Tours Around Foggia (This is the first of a series of articles exploring Foggia and its vicinity) 

The church of Monte Calvario on the San Severo road is about the best place to begin. Not only does it offer a wide variety of camera shots, but it is also a pleasurable tour. The Church of Monte Calvario, better known as the Church of the Crosses, was built around 1600 by the Spanish Padre, De Olivada. The name, Church of the Crosses, was later given to the church as it was built around a huge wooden cross carried there by pilgrims from the villages close by Foggia. These crusades demonstrated the religious belief of enduring hardships for Christ.

Chapels In The Garden 

Upon entering the gardens surrounding the main chapel, it becomes evident that even this beautiful edifice did not escape the ravages of war, for barbed wire and shells are abundant. The buildings, however, are being repaired, and they will soon regain their natural beauty.

In the center of the garden stand five chapels, utilized as burial places since in that era the modern cemetery was not known, and members of that religious order were interred in vaults underneath each chapel. Later, the relics were transferred to a crypt located in the basement of the main chapel.

When we began our exploration, the caretaker almost fell over backward in his desire to help us. He quickly ushered us inside the building, where the beautiful frescoes of Tintoretto (1518-1594), a Venetian painter of the Renaissance period, can plainly be seen. The building still retains some of its natural beauty, and one can easily imagine the charm of such a setting.

Weird Things 

Leading us down to the cellar, which was dark and stumbling with old age, he began to talk of the weird things we would see. Little did we know of the truth in this old character's words, but after groping around in the dark, we finally found a light bulb that managed to flicker every second or so. Before us was a small grotto filled almost to the top with human skulls and remnants of skeletons. He spoke quickly in mixed Italian and English, telling us that these were the remains of priests and nuns transferred from the chapels in the garden.

The Flight Of Stairs 

Coming up from the dark, we saw another set of stairs leading off into nowhere, so we tagged along. The stairs led us on a merry chase, going around corners so sharply we almost met ourselves coming back. When we reached the top, there was Foggia in the distance, and we were standing in an ancient belfry.

After that, it was "Chow," and the old caretaker wobbled over to a shady spot to sit and reminisce.

ITALY

The Constituent Assembly met at the Montecitorio Palace in Rome on Monday, where President Saragat of the Constituent Assembly read the speech of Mr. De Nicola, the provisional president of the Italian Republic. In his declaration, Mr. De Nicola stated, "The Republican form of government will assure future generations a climate of true democracy." He concluded his message with "God grant Italian Resurrection."

President of Ministers, Mr. De Gasperi, submitted the list of new ministers of the first government of the Italian Republic and stated, "The all-important problem is still that of foreign policy." With regard to the Trieste situation, Mr. De Gasperi said, "The Italian people want that country which is Italian." He also gave thanks to the countries of Latin America who made a common approach to the "Big Four" in favor of a right and just peace with Italy.

The government allotted four million lire for the reconstruction of the Foggia and Bari area. The grant will cover public works, including roads, government buildings, and railroads.

Two riders were killed and five more wounded when a group of gangsters, armed with guns, hand grenades, and daggers attacked a civilian truck near Cassino on the Rome-Naples road.

Unemployment threats and failures in conceding an increase in wages called for a general strike in three towns in the Bari province. Serious riots developed in Andria and Corato where demonstrators blocked all roads, while in Cerignola, six hundred workers plundered the nearby grain fields.

Why I Washed by Pfc. Robert I. G. Hoyt

"Dear Jack:

"I suppose you've heard that I'm no longer a cadet, and naturally you'll wonder why I was eliminated. Well, it actually didn't have anything to do with the way I fly. They can always find something even if you fly circles around them.

"What really happened was, I got PO'd at the Major. I was a little high in the Cadet Club on open-post night, and he was in there and saw me and said something about my blouse being unbuttoned. There was one button loose.

"Listen," I said, "Why don't you take that Boy-Scout stuff and put it where it belongs?" I really told him. He said something about 'impudence' and I said, "Why don't you go back to flying balloons, jerk; it'll go with your stomach!"

"So he called the MP's. He wanted to court-martial me, but of course he knew I had too much on him. Everybody knows he's drunk most of the time.

"So they washed me. I'm just as glad. A man's got to keep his self-respect. Well, Jack, give 'em hell in the Infantry, and let's hear from you.

"Be seeing you,
"Phil"

"Dear Sally:

"The real reason I washed out, sweetest, had lots to do with you just like everything else in my young life.

"You see, darling, an awful lot of what happens in cadets depends on how your instructor likes you. My instructor liked me okay at first, I guess, but something happened.

"The way it was, I met him in town one time, and his wife and sister were with him. We all had a drink together. It seems like his sister kind of fell for me, though I didn't say two words to her, and the next day my instructor tells me she wants a date and how about it? Naturally, I thought of you right away. I said no, I couldn't as I was practically engaged.

"He was pretty insistent about it, but I wouldn't give in. Finally, he got sore. The very next day I got a check ride, and they washed me. It's too bad in a way because I did want to fly, but as I've said to you before, honey, I don't think the kind of love that can't stand a test is worth much.

"By the way, don't say anything about this to the others—they might think I was silly.

"All my love,
"Phil"

"Dear Uncle Fred:

"Uncle Fred, I think I can tell you the real reason I washed out, but please don't tell Dad and Mom, as they'd just worry about it. I was washed out for what they call 'Flying accident due to pilot error'. I could have set them straight on that, but it wasn't worth it to me.

"The way it happened was this. I took my ship up the other day for practice acrobatics—solo, of course—and was about to come out of a spin when the controls caught. I got her down all right, but she was pretty well smashed up. I found out the mechanic was drunk during the pre-flight check and had left a wrench in the fuselage. It had caught in the control cables.

"I could have reported it that way, of course, but I happened to know the mechanic and what it would mean to him. He has a wife and three kids. If I reported him, he'd get a prison sentence for sure.

"So I let it go. As I said, it wasn't worth it to me. He has promised he'll never touch another drop, and that's reward enough for me.

"By the way, could you let me have a fiver? I had to bribe the crew chief not to report the mechanic, and am a little short.

"All my love,
(Yank Magazine) "Phil"

Foggia Boxing Team Takes On Pescara Huskies

July 18 --- When the Foggia boxing team takes on the Pescara Huskies at the Flagella Theatre this Tuesday, July 23rd, it will mark the second in the series of inter-city boxing matches now in progress.

One of the featured fighters of the evening will be 19-year-old Stewart Evans. Stew is a tall, well-built lad from Newton, Massachusetts, who loves to get in and "mix it up." The 172-pound GI recently slugged his way into a three-round decision over a badly beaten Carbonara and immediately won his way into the fans' hearts with his aggressiveness and boxing skill.

Another personality on Tuesday's fight card is "Pop" Mario, a middle-aged pugilist who keeps the audience roaring at his peculiar style. Mario, a short stocky fighter, bobs, weaves, and laughs his way through the bout, all of which tends to highly agitate his adversary. His best punch is a right jab delivered from behind the back during "close-in" fighting.

Joe DiGuart is a newcomer to fight fans in Foggia and was discovered while working in the 529 mess hall. Boxing promoters at the local gymnasium were impressed by his muscular build and persuaded Joe to work out at the gym. He showed up so well that they decided to put him against Pescara's best.

Outstanding fighters from Pescara will include Romeo Milete, Amateur Champion of Italy, and Frankie Franceschelli. Milete is a lad with lightning footwork and a darting left jab. He made a lasting impression on FAAB fans when he fought the 40 pounds heavier Zucco Zuccaroni to a standstill for five rounds, only to lose the decision by a hair. Franceschelli left an equally impressive record behind him in his only appearance in Foggia by defeating the popular Vince Russo decisively in five rounds.

Stateside • July 18 -- If "Prince Hal" Newhouser of the Detroit Tigers and Bob Feller of the Cleveland Indians keep up their current terrific winning pace, the league will see two thirty-game winners this season. Newhouser, at this writing, has seventeen victories tucked away while Feller is breezing along with sixteen decisions on the credit side. With the season only half over, the two aces have a fifty-fifty chance of hitting the thirty-game cycle. Feller is determined to crack "Rube" Waddell's strikeout record of 343 that has stood since 1904. "Rapid Robert" has 202 whiffs accredited with two months of action still to go.

By Jim Boyle  
• Due to the deactivation of the 345th Engineers, the team known as the 345th Rangers was forced to withdraw from the Foggia American League. The Rangers, at the time of their withdrawal, had won four and lost six while holding down the fourth spot in team standings. With the 345th team now out of the league, there are only five teams left of the original nine squads that opened the season.  
• "Watch out for the Special Service Specials" rings the cry from the watching baseball world. With the acquisition of "Tex" Childs, "Lefty" Elliot, Wilson Welker, and others from the once-powerful Security Barons, the team has improved overnight into a team that should get the title of "giant-killers" if they live up to this writer's predictions. Although definitely out of the running for the pennant, the Specials have no pressure on them during the games as those fighting for the flag. Proof of this was provided in the 1898th game. The Specials battled the new league leaders down the line and were finally nosed out in the late innings.  
• Let us not forget the big swimming meet to be held in Rome on the 2nd and 3rd of August. At the present time, there are eight swimmers and divers trying out for the team, and Cpl Lencowski would like to see at least twelve more spirited contestants come out and make the tournament a successful one for the Foggia entry.  
• Special Service announced that there will be a Theater Tennis Championship tourney at Caserta to be held from the 7th to 10th of August inclusively. Also to be held in the near future are badminton, baseball, and softball tournaments. The elimination process will take place in the Foggia-Bari area, and the outstanding team of the sector will enter the finals.

French Whitewashes Specials, 3-0

July 13 — "Bulldog" Drummond's timely double that drove home two runs in the sixth inning broke up a tight pitchers' battle between Bob French and the Specials' Lefty Elliot, as the 1898th Bulldozers triumphed over the Special Service nine 3-0, at the Foggia Stadium this afternoon.

Both pitchers hurled shutout ball until the eventful sixth inning when the Bulldozers scored three times to clinch the contest. Drummond's two-base blow scored Johnson and French with the winning runs.

French kept five Special Service singles well scattered in achieving his first shutout of the season. He displayed good control by striking out seven while walking none. Elliot whiffed eleven 'Dozers and gave up three walks.

Rebels Trim Yankees, 20-8

July 12 — Running up the largest total of runs yet obtained in league play, the 779 Rebels smashed the 529 Yankees by a stunning 20-8 score at Foggia Stadium this afternoon. The seventeen-hit attack was led by manager Steve Enright, who belted two singles and a pair of doubles in five trips to the plate. With the Yankees in a 3-2 lead in the third inning, the Rebels amassed eleven runs on seven hits as 15 batters strode to the plate. Enright set a new record by clouting two doubles in this one inning. Bill Falk, "Patchy" Thompson, and Don Dawson paced the winners with three hits apiece.

Three FAAB Officers Presented With Commendation Ribbon

Aug. 3 — In a special presentation ceremony at the monthly garrison review this morning, the Commendation Ribbon was presented to three FAAB officers by Colonel Robert K. Martin. The following officers received the award:

Major Harold L. Thayer - Accomplished the transition from combat operation to occupation and the move from Amendola to Foggia with efficiency in spite of loss of personnel.

Major William W. Berg - As executive officer, he administered the Second Bomb Group during the transition from combat operations to occupation. He secured recreational facilities and instituted and consolidated the Unit Personnel system.

Captain David S. Ives - Exercised sound judgment in the disposition of requisitioned property and did excellent work as Foggia Town Major during a difficult period. He helped to avoid undue distress, and under him, Italo-American relations became very much improved.

Siponto Officers Club

Beach Hotel

The Siponto Beach Hotel, which was to be used as a rest center for FAAB personnel, will not open, it was learned today. The beach is still restricted to swimmers because of the presence of mustard gas in the water. Recent investigation has disclosed the fact that currents are constantly carrying more of the gas in from the sea, where several gas bombs have been discovered, so the beach will, in all probability, not be reopened. The officers are abandoning their beach club and it will be turned over to the 6600th Engineers. The enlisted men's beach club will remain open.

Commissary Open for Business Aug. 2 — All FAAB personnel who applied for commissary ration books are advised that the books are now available in the payroll section of the Unit Personnel office. The commissary will officially open for business Monday, August 5, and store hours will be from nine AM until twelve-thirty PM daily except Sunday.

AES Installs New Generator July 30 -- The installation of a new generator has made it possible for the American Expeditionary Station in Foggia to resume its normal broadcasting schedule from six-thirty AM until twelve-fifteen AM, beginning today.

Flagella Installs New Equipment

July 31 — Flagella theatre manager, Corporal Heefner, announced today the installation of new equipment in the theatre. The equipment, recently received in a shipment from the States, includes Simplex Arc Lamp Projectors, a sound system, and a perforated screen.

Installation man, David F. Stimeling, stated that there would be a definite improvement in the acoustics as both high and low-frequency speakers will be used, and the sound will be evenly distributed throughout the theatre.

Corporal Heefner is expecting new movies from the States and hopes to be able to provide theatre schedules two weeks in advance in the near future.

FAAB Civilian Club Organizes Lottery

July 31 — The FAAB Civilian Club organized a lottery to give aid to the poorer employees of FAAB and their children. Any aid, such as old clothes or other articles of which the GIs have no further use, will be deeply appreciated by the Civilian Club and further seal the bond of friendship between the Italian civilians and U.S. troops stationed here. Contributions may be deposited before August 15 at the Editorial Office of the Foggia Occupator, where they will be forwarded to the director, Mr. Carmen Guidarelli.

The shipment, including baby foods, meat, fish, soups, vegetables, and milk, was flown by US ex-service men who worked throughout the day to get the vessel off on time. 20,000 gift parcels arrived last week at Naples from the United States in the "Elberton". 10,000 gift parcels arrived last week at Palermo from the United States in the "Middleburg Victory". The strong reaction of Italian public opinion against the conditions of peace has been expressed by the Italian papers. LOCAL ITEMS

About a week ago, the 838th Engineers moved into Foggia from Caserta to take the place of the 345th Engineers. When we visited their camp recently, everyone was anxious to show us around so that we could see the improvements in the past week despite the fire that started while they were preparing the Officer-Enlisted Men's Club for a stage show. Before it could be brought under control, one side of the building, with the exception of one room, was ravaged by flames. The room, which contained special service equipment, liquor, and beer rations, was undamaged except for the ceiling.

Rejuvenation Of The Caves

Lt. W. R. Bartley, the Special Service Officer, stated that plans in effect now call for the rejuvenation of the caves located in the rear of the camp. These caves will house a Chapel, Theatre, Day Rooms, Basketball Courts, and Club. "The Club will be finished in about a week," said Lt. Bartley, "and it will have the added attraction of being in a cool place. The rest of the rooms will be completed as soon as possible."

Just then, T/4 Harry A. Bell, the theatre manager, came forward with the information that the caves were over 200 years old and were originally used by the Vindita, a bandit tribe, as a den.

Hearing the "Diaveleers" playing in the next room, we asked Lt. Bartley if they had any more engagements in Foggia. "Yes," he replied, "we will play at the 55th Station Hospital next Thursday evening, and we might broadcast Saturday afternoon. What did you think of our orchestra when they played at the Red Cross?" We answered in accordance.

Chuckle.

Best quotation of the week overheard at the Red Cross: "When I was born, I was so dumbfounded that I couldn't speak for a year and a half."

The time has come, we believe, to outline briefly the function of the AES Ground Station. Here we met Pfc. Tom J. Paul, the noncom in charge, and his staff of two men, Pfc. Jim Pursley and Pfc. Don Priddy.

"Starting as early as 6 AM we have our hands full with this antique generator," Tom stated as we walked into the shed. "We have trouble getting cotton waste for our oil filter," he went on to say, nodding towards the generator, "but we expect two new generators in tomorrow or the next day from Naples. Because of the condition the motor is in, we must keep two men on duty at all times," he said, "and that means nineteen hours of work each day. Of course, we have our free time pretty well filled up, but somehow we manage to squeeze in a few moments to operate our 'Ham' radio. It means quite a bit to be able to reach almost any place in the world and in that way we can keep abreast with the world events."

Immense Transmitter

After that, we looked at the immense transmitter that would strike awe into the heart of any man.

"With these dials here on the front of the machine," Tom chuckled. "We can tell where the trouble is and quickly make the necessary repairs." Leading us around behind, he showed us the many wires and tubes that make up this giant mechanism. "These tubes on the right," he went on to say, pointing inside the cabinet, "are worth about seventy-three dollars. That will help to give you an idea of how much the machine costs."

Befanotrofio Orphanage Foggia Area, Italy — Only the sun and wind now rake the fields along the roads and the long beaches of Manfredonia, and kids without food or proper care lie in the roadside ditch, the sand, or field, abandoned by their mothers. In some, where strength remains, cries of anguish with never-ending tears pour out in hope that a Samaritan may overhear the call for aid and tend to their cares. Others just struggle with the disease inherited from their parents. 

The farmers, plowing their fields, stumble onto these stray infants. The beachcombers, sunning on the sands, rescue the drifting castaways before the tide can lay its claim. The travelers, interrupting their journey for a few minutes rest, find a bundle along the road. Rediscovered, the nucleus of tomorrow's civilization, for the present, is sheltered at the Befanotrofio Orphanage in Manfredonia.

A recent visit to the Befanotrofio Orphanage in Manfredonia brings the gratifying disclosure that conditions have been vastly improved since the orphanage was unofficially adopted at Easter time by the 55th Station Hospital. 

"I visited the Befanotrofio orphanage at Manfredonia yesterday, after an interval of two months, and I was delighted to find the improvements which have been made, and about which I had heard," wrote Mr. M. E. Wood, UNRRA Field Welfare Officer in this area, in a recent letter to the orphanage committee.

Sponsoring The Orphanage Although sponsoring the orphanage was originally the project of the 55th Station Hospital, interest in the campaign has since become widespread in the Foggia area. To take care of contributions and see to the proper dispensation of cash donations in the purchase of food, clothing, and medical supplies, a committee has been formed. Included in the committee are Lieutenant Elrie Rodgers - President, Mrs. M. Martin - Treasurer, Sergeant George - Secretary, Mrs. B. McCasland, Lieutenant Helen Bowerman, and Mrs. Melvin.

Facilities for the care of the foundlings were pitifully inadequate when the orphanage was first brought to the attention of the hospital staff. Due to a lack of bedding and beds, as many as six babies slept in a single small cot, and although the children received a sufficient amount of food, it was lacking in the proper vitamins resulting in a large number of malnutrition cases.

Efforts Of The Committee Through the efforts of the committee, aided by contributions from personnel throughout the Foggia area, beds, mattresses, sheets, and rubber matting have been provided for all the children, and their diet has been greatly improved. An appeal from the committee brought gift parcels of Cod Liver Oil and other vitamins from several stateside pharmaceutical companies with promises of more to follow.

More than 100,000 lire has been donated to the orphanage in the past two months from various sources, including proceeds from the weekly Friday-night boxing matches sponsored by the Ripple Lounge, church collections, and individual contributions.

Yankees Upset Sparkplugs 7-4  

July 27 — Ed McCaully, making his debut on the mound for the 529 Yankees, handcuffed the 955 Sparkplugs with three hits as the Yanks upset the Sparks 7-4 at Foggia Stadium this afternoon. McCaully's steady hurling, plus Ron Schaber's big day at the plate, brought the Yankees out of a seven-game losing streak and sent the stumbling Sparkplugs a full game behind the league-leading 1898s.  

No Hitter  

The Yankee hurler had a no-hitter within his grasp until the eventful sixth inning when Al Levick led off with a single. Nick Ingenito then drove one of McCaully's deliveries to left center field for his third home run of the season.  

Ron Schaber proved to be the big gun of the 529 attack as he drove out two singles and a triple in four tries. He figured in most of the Yankee scoring as he drove home three tallies and scored two. Lefty Owens and Wilmer Smith contributed two hits apiece for the victors.  

McCaully sent eleven Sparkplugs down via the strikeout route and walked two. Levick whiffed eight and walked four as he went the distance for the losers.

Sport Shots  
By Jim Boyle

The surprise of the past month has been the sustained batting slump suffered by one of the league's top-notch sluggers, Ed Greiner of the 1898th. Greiner, on the 26th of June, was sporting a slightly terrific batting average of .470. In the last five games, the pitcher and infielder of the league leaders has made but one safety in fourteen official times at bat, dropping to a .354 percentage. Of these fourteen appearances, he has gone down swinging seven times, which more than doubles his previous nine-game record of three strikeouts. "Ready Eddie" will undoubtedly snap out of his hitless streak if that age-old adage, "you can't keep a good man down," still holds true.

One of the main faults of the Foggia American league is the poor sportsmanship displayed by some of the teams. It is common knowledge that competent umpires are almost impossible to find. Instead of making the best with what is available, a few players insist on "baiting" the volunteer arbiters and taking advantage of them through technicalities. This isn't the big leagues, fellas, so let's play the game to win but have fun doing it win, lose or otherwise.

For you GI's that are tired of taking your favorite girl to the movies or to a night spot and are looking for some new place to go for entertainment, why not take her to the local gymnasium some evening about 7:00 o'clock to see a basketball game. The games thus far in the season have been thrillers from start to finish with plenty of action and scoring. A team always plays a better game with plenty of support, so why not give the boys a break and come on out? Who knows, your girl might even like the game. There are games almost every night. The schedule is available at the Red Cross.

Cid Apprehends Cable Thieves

August 7 — Approximately two months ago, the Bari road became the scene of activity similar to the great gold rush of '49, only in this instance, the prospectors were digging for copper and lead.

Another dissimilarity from the famous gold rush, one which brought the CID into the picture, was the fact that the copper and lead were not in their native state, having been laid in 1943 as an emergency communication cable by the U.S. Army. The subterranean cable, valued at four hundred thousand dollars, was strung between Foggia and Bari, buried at a depth of 30 inches, adjacent to the road.

According to CID agents Gilbert Zitterbart and Walter Vickrey, the Italian pick and shovel prospectors conducted their illegal activities under cover of darkness, and their discovery was due to the fact that they neglected to refill the ditches after removing the cable.

Approximately half of the cable has been stolen, the majority of it from the Foggia end of the line. Between Foggia and Cerignola, the cable has been entirely removed except for isolated lengths laid beneath intersecting roads.

Agent Vickrey stated that, to date, thirty-seven arrests have been made, and approximately twenty miles of the cable have been recovered. Some of the thieves were apprehended while staking out a line in preparation for their nighttime activities. One brazen youth was picked up pedaling his bicycle along the Bari road with a length of the cable in his possession. Agent Vickrey continued, "The case is practically closed. We expect to complete our arrests and recover the remainder of the cable in the next day or so."

QM Laundry and Dry Cleaning Establishment Swept by Fire, Destroys Plant and Equipment

Three GI, Two Civilian Fire Trucks Combat Blaze for Two Hours

CWO John McKenzie, Men from 838th Eng Save Clothes

Aug. 8 - A fire of undetermined origin swept the Quartermaster Laundry and Dry Cleaning establishment at ten o'clock this morning, completely destroying the plant and equipment. The office and warehouse, however, were undamaged by the blaze and only the clothing which was in the plant was lost.

Three GI fire trucks and two civilian trucks were called to combat the blaze, and they worked two hours to bring the fire under control.

Pfc. Paul M. Wood and Cpl Charles Calabrese, who were working in the laundry at the time, stated that the fire started with an explosion at approximately ten AM, followed almost immediately by several more explosions. A quantity of gasoline used for cleaning purposes was ignited by the explosions, and the entire plant was engulfed in a matter of minutes.

The quick thinking of Chief Warrant Officer John McKenzie and several of his men from 838th Engineers saved most of the clothes from the blaze. Aided by several enlisted men and civilian employees, they carried an estimated 95 percent of the clothing out of the building before it could be damaged by fire or water.

Pfc. Wood stated that the clothing had to be sorted out and it would be impossible to issue any laundry or cleaning at the present time. AES will announce the reopening date of the laundry.

Rest Tours Limited  
August 7 — Due to the unsettled conditions resulting from orders to inactivate Foggia Army Air Base, it will be impossible for personnel to attend Switzerland, Venice, and Paris Rest Camps, effective as of this date. Short trips to Capri and Rome will continue to be available as usual, stated Lieutenant Wesley R. Williams, Unit Personnel Officer.

Foggia Army Air Base Will Be Inactivated September 15th Aug. 10 Foggia Army Air Base will be inactivated September 15th according to a statement by Colonel Robert K. Martin, Commanding Officer. There is no definite information as to the disposition of personnel at the present time but Colonel Martin stated that, subject to the approval of the War Department, he was making an effort to have the majority of the men attached to PBS, in which case they will remain in the Foggia area until such time as they return to the States. The remainder of personnel will be transferred to the Ninth Air Force in Germany. Men desiring to reenlist for service in Germany are advised to notify their Commanding Officer immediately, to ensure their inclusion in the transfer orders. Personnel will, in all probability, be informed in which category they will be included, by the first of September.

Newest Development in the V.D. Campaign

Aug 5 — The newest development in the VD control campaign is a schedule of authorized daily visits to the civilian hospital, where prostitutes undergoing treatment are exposed to inspection by members of the conducted tour. This is for the purpose of showing FAAB personnel, at first hand, the horrible ravages of venereal disease. Approximately seventy-five percent of the prostitutes picked up for inspection are infected.

The personal observance program, which has been in effect for the past several weeks in Germany with favorable results, was introduced to Foggia by Colonel Robert K. Martin on his return from a recent trip to Furstenfelbruck, Germany. Medical Officer, Captain Diaz, stated that ten or twelve men from the various squadrons will make the daily inspection trip until the entire FAAB personnel has participated in the program.

Another step in the effort to wipe out VD will be the distribution of VD questionnaires in the near future. The questionnaires will be in the form of written examinations, and any man failing to answer the required number of questions will be given additional information on the prevention of VD.

The regular Saturday morning I & E programs will include VD films and lectures in the future to further aid in the campaign.

The VD rate in Foggia showed a decrease from 172 cases per thousand per annum in June to 62 cases per thousand per annum in July. Captain Diaz stated, "Although the decrease is a definite improvement, there are still 62 cases more than there should be."

Cigarette Ration Increase  
Aug. 7 — Cigarette ration in the Foggia PX has been increased to 12 packs per week as of Aug. 7. The 12-pack ration will exclude the purchase of cigars or tobacco. Men desiring cigars or tobacco will be allowed only 8 packs of cigarettes, but the tobacco ration will be increased accordingly.

Rhythm Aces To Broadcast Aug. 6 — Beginning Aug. 14, a new broadcast will hit the airwaves from the Foggia AES. The Rhythm Aces, Sergeant Wayne Commodore's popular 838th swing band, formerly the Diavelleers, will broadcast weekly on Wednesday afternoons from one-thirty until two PM. Ken Eill will do the announcing.

LOCAL ITEMS

Theatre  
Capitol Dora, the new German theatre, opened this week at the 6600 Engineers in the D Group area. To honor the occasion, "Spiced Wine," a novel by Heinrich Sperl adapted for the stage by Hinz Biering, was presented by a cast of German POWs. Capitol Dora was erected in its entirety by the Germans themselves with whatever material was available. The equipment permits not only the showing of movies but also the presentation of first-rate stage shows, as demonstrated this week. In the past, German POW entertainment was only for the prisoners themselves. "Spiced Wine" was the first German entertainment that most of the Americans here had ever seen. All who attended agree that the theatre, play, and acting were of high standards. The scenery of "Spiced Wine" was most realistic, showing a great amount of ingenuity. Of special note was the fountain in the town garden of act IV and the jeep driven out onto the stage, made up as a taxi, in act V. Though there were a number of feminine characters in the show, all parts were played by men. The quality of the impersonations impressed all. Worthy of special praise is the young man who played the part of Pfeiffer. His acting and singing were among the high spots of the comedy play.

It has come to our attention that Dave Fenton's radio program "Grab Bag" has received favorable mention from many sources and we believe that credit should be given where credit is due. The program, coming over the airwaves nightly, is versatile in the type of recordings put on and we believe that this studio production merits our gratitude.

In the past few weeks, however, we have noticed that the particular announcer is rather partial to the requests received. We think that some have been neglected.
